### Promote the new model

To finish the rollout, swap the priorities: `gpt-6.1-sol` at `0`, `gpt-6-luna` at `1`. Use the portal, or run
the CLI command from the previous section with `$PRIMARY` and `$CANDIDATE` swapped. Run the count again: every
request now shows `gpt-6.1-sol-…`. To roll back, swap them again. Clients never change.

<!-- /steps -->

## Go further

- **Canary in steps.** Move the weights from `95`/`5` to `80`/`20` to `50`/`50` while you watch errors, latency,
  and cost per model in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md). Weights must be at least
  `1`, so to stop sending traffic to a model, give it a higher priority number or remove it from the alias.
- **Prefer provisioned throughput.** Put a provisioned deployment at priority `0` and a pay-as-you-go
  deployment of the same model at priority `1`, so purchased capacity is used first. Test what happens when the
  provisioned deployment is saturated before you depend on it.
- **Balance regions or providers.** Register the same model from two Foundry accounts, or from Foundry and a
  custom provider, and give them weights in proportion to their quota.
- **Limit each model and the alias.** A token limit on a backend model, as in
  [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md), applies to that model. A limit
  on the alias applies to every request that calls `chat`.

## Clean up

Keep the gateway, the runtime key, and `gpt-6-luna` from lab 02. Later labs use them. Remove what you added in
this lab: the alias first, then the backend model, then the Foundry deployment.

In the portal, open `chat` in **Models** › **Aliases** and select **Delete**. Requests that use the alias fail
immediately; the backend models stay in the gateway. Then delete the `gpt-6.1-sol` model, and any alias that the
import created for it, from **Models**.

From a shell:

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/aliases/$ALIAS?$API"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$CANDIDATE?$API"
az cognitiveservices account deployment delete -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --deployment-name "$CANDIDATE"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/aliases/$ALIAS`?$API"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$CANDIDATE`?$API"
az cognitiveservices account deployment delete -g $FOUNDRY_RG -n $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT --deployment-name $CANDIDATE
```

If an alias that the portal import created still points to `gpt-6.1-sol`, delete that alias before the model.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "Select models with at least one common API format." | The selected backend models don't share an interface, for example an Anthropic Messages model and an OpenAI Chat Completions model | Put models that share an interface in the same alias. |
| "Weight must be a whole number from 1 to 100." or `weight must be between 1 and 100.` | A weight is `0`, negative, or above `100` | To stop traffic to a model, raise its priority number or remove it. |
| "Priority must be a whole number from 0 to 100." or `priority must be between 0 and 100.` | A priority is outside `0` to `100` | Use `0` for the preferred tier and higher numbers for the others. |
| "Each backend model can appear only once." or `backendModels must not contain duplicate model identities.` | The same backend model is listed twice | Combine the entries and adjust the weight. |
| All requests go to one model | The models have different priorities, so only the lowest number receives traffic | Give the models the same priority to split by weight. |
| `404` with `DeploymentNotFound` | The candidate backend model points to a Foundry deployment that doesn't exist | Create the deployment, or fix `deployment.resourceId` on the backend model. |
| `429` from the preferred model | The preferred deployment is out of capacity, and the gateway returns the error | Retry in the client, add capacity, or spread traffic with weights at the same priority. |

# Stream responses and count every token

Chat apps and agents stream their replies: the model sends text a few tokens at a time, so people start reading
after a second or two instead of waiting for the whole answer. Streaming used to be a blind spot for governance,
because a streamed Chat Completions response only reports token usage when the client asks for it. In this lab you
stream through the gateway with curl, PowerShell, and the OpenAI SDKs, read every event the client receives, and
then prove that a token limit still counts every streamed token.

![A streamed request passes the gateway's limits before the stream starts, and the gateway captures usage while the stream flows back to the client](../assets/diagrams/streaming-usage.svg "Token and cost limits are checked before the stream starts. While the stream flows back, the gateway records its token usage for limits, budgets, and Monitoring.")

<!-- widget: stream-usage -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need a gateway, an imported
  model, a callable alias, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- For the shell steps: `curl` and `jq` for Bash, or PowerShell 7.4 or later. For the CLI and IaC tracks: the
  [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with `az login`.
- For the Code track: Python 3.10 or later, or Node.js 22.18 or later.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group, for the token limit steps.

Set these variables once, from the lab folder (`labs/23-streaming-responses`). Every track and the **Verify**
section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider
export STREAM_ALIAS="$MODEL-stream"        # the token-limited alias that this lab creates

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export MODEL_URL="$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# A starting guess for the alias. Confirm it on the model's Aliases tab (lab 02) and replace it if it differs.
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG           = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY      = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER     = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL        = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider
$STREAM_ALIAS = "$MODEL-stream"             # the token-limited alias that this lab creates

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$MODEL_URL  = "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# A starting guess for the alias. Confirm it on the model's Aliases tab (lab 02) and replace it if it differs.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

> [!TIP]
> The Code track only needs `AI_GATEWAY_URL`, `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`, and `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`. If you skip the token
> limit steps, you can set those three by hand and skip the Azure CLI.

## How it works

Add `"stream": true` to a Chat Completions request and the gateway answers with `Content-Type:
text/event-stream`. The body is a series of server-sent events (SSE): each one is a `data:` line with a JSON chunk,
followed by a blank line. The gateway passes each chunk on as the model produces it, and the response carries
`x-accel-buffering: no`, which tells proxies such as NGINX not to hold it back.

This is what a streamed reply from a Foundry model looks like through the gateway:

| Chunk | `choices` | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt filter results | Empty `[]` | Content safety results for the prompt. `id` and `model` are empty strings. |
| Role | One choice | `delta.role` is `assistant` and `delta.content` is an empty string. |
| Content deltas | One choice | `delta.content` holds the next few characters of the reply. `usage` is `null`. |
| Finish | One choice | `finish_reason` is `stop`, or `length` when the reply hits `max_completion_tokens`. |
| Usage | Empty `[]` | `usage` with `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, and `total_tokens`. Sent when the client sets `stream_options.include_usage`. |
| `data: [DONE]` | Not JSON | The end of the stream. Stop reading. |

Two chunks have an empty `choices` array, so code that reads `choices[0]` on every chunk crashes on the first one.

**Where the gateway counts tokens.** A token limit or cost limit is checked **before** the gateway forwards the
request. When a counter is exhausted, the client gets an ordinary JSON error, such as `429` with `Retry-After`, and no
stream starts. Once a stream starts, it runs to the end, even if it takes the counter past the limit; the next request
is throttled. While the stream flows, the gateway records its token usage for token limits, cost limits, and
Monitoring.

**Usage without `include_usage`.** Since the [September 24, 2026 release](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/releases/2026-09-24),
the gateway makes sure it has a usage record for every streamed Chat Completions response, even when the client
doesn't set `stream_options.include_usage`, so the counters stay accurate. The release notes ask clients that parse
the events themselves to accept a usage-only chunk before `[DONE]`, even when they didn't ask for one. In our test
run in October 2026, a client that didn't set `include_usage` received no usage chunk, yet the token limit counted its
tokens exactly as it did for a client that asked. So write your client to work either way: skip chunks with an empty
`choices` array, and take usage from whichever chunk carries it.

The Responses API streams typed events instead: each `data:` line follows an `event:` line, and the last event,
`response.completed`, always carries the usage.

## Stream a response

Pick a track. Both stream the same request through the gateway and show the text as it arrives, the events, and
the usage.

<!-- track: cli | curl and PowerShell -->

### Watch the raw events

curl buffers its output by default; `-N` turns that off, so each event prints the moment it arrives. PowerShell's
`Invoke-RestMethod` and `Invoke-WebRequest` wait for the whole body, so the PowerShell script reads the stream
with `HttpClient`.

```bash title="Bash"
curl -sSN "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"stream\":true,\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Say hello in five words.\"}]}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/stream-chat.ps1 -Raw -Prompt "Say hello in five words."
```

Expected output (shortened; your text and IDs differ):

```text
data: {"choices":[],"created":0,"id":"","model":"","object":"","prompt_filter_results":[{"prompt_index":0,"content_filter_results":{…}}]}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"","refusal":null,"role":"assistant"},"finish_reason":null,"index":0,…}],"model":"gpt-6-luna-2026-09-22","object":"chat.completion.chunk",…,"usage":null}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Hi"},"finish_reason":null,"index":0,…}],…,"usage":null}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":" there"},"finish_reason":null,"index":0,…}],…,"usage":null}

…

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{},"finish_reason":"stop","index":0,…}],…,"usage":null}

data: [DONE]
```

### Stream with the script

The script prints the reply as it streams, then counts the events, measures the time to the first token, and shows
the usage chunk if the stream had one.

<!-- include: infra/stream-chat.sh -->

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/stream-chat.sh
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/stream-chat.ps1
```

On GitHub, open [stream-chat.sh](infra/stream-chat.sh) or [stream-chat.ps1](infra/stream-chat.ps1).

Expected output (your text and numbers differ):

```text
Streaming shows replies as they're generated, so users see progress right away. They can start reading before the full answer is ready. That makes the app feel more responsive than waiting for one complete message.

Events              43 (1 with an empty choices array)
First token         1.77 s
Usage chunk         none: run again with --usage to ask for one
HTTP status         200
Content-Type        text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
Served by           gpt-6-luna-2026-09-22
```

### Ask for usage at the end of the stream

Run the script again with the option that sets `"stream_options": {"include_usage": true}`:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/stream-chat.sh --usage
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/stream-chat.ps1 -Usage
```

Expected output:

```text
Streaming shows the reply as it's generated instead of waiting for the whole answer. You can start reading right away. That makes the app feel more responsive.

Events              35 (2 with an empty choices array)
First token         1.74 s
Usage chunk         prompt 19, completion 34, total 53
HTTP status         200
Content-Type        text/event-stream; charset=utf-8
Served by           gpt-6-luna-2026-09-22
```

The second empty-`choices` chunk is the usage chunk, the last one before `[DONE]`. `stream_options` is only valid
together with `"stream": true`; without it, the gateway returns `400`.

### Stream the Responses API

The Responses API names every event. List the event types in order, then read the usage from `response.completed`:

```bash title="Bash"
curl -sSN "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/responses" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"stream\":true,\"input\":\"Say hello in five words.\"}" > events.txt
grep '^event:' events.txt | uniq -c
sed -n 's/^data: {/{/p' events.txt | jq -c 'select(.type == "response.completed") | .response.usage'
rm events.txt
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; stream = $true; input = "Say hello in five words." } | ConvertTo-Json
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/responses" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
$lines = $r.Content -split "`n"
$prev = $null; $n = 0
foreach ($e in $lines -match '^event:') { if ($e -eq $prev) { $n++ } else { if ($prev) { '{0,4} {1}' -f $n, $prev }; $prev = $e; $n = 1 } }
'{0,4} {1}' -f $n, $prev
($lines -match '^data: \{' | ForEach-Object { $_.Substring(6) | ConvertFrom-Json } |
  Where-Object type -eq 'response.completed').response.usage | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
```

Expected output (your counts differ):

```text
   1 event: response.created
   1 event: response.in_progress
   1 event: response.output_item.added
   1 event: response.output_item.done
   1 event: response.output_item.added
   1 event: response.content_part.added
   7 event: response.output_text.delta
   1 event: response.output_text.done
   1 event: response.content_part.done
   1 event: response.output_item.done
   1 event: response.completed
{"input_tokens":12,"input_tokens_details":{"cache_write_tokens":0,"cached_tokens":0},"output_tokens":66,"output_tokens_details":{"reasoning_tokens":53},"total_tokens":78}
```

The first `output_item` pair is the model's reasoning item; the second is the message that carries the text. The
`reasoning_tokens` count shows why the first token can take a moment with a reasoning model.

<!-- track: code | Code -->

### Install the SDK

Each sample reads `AI_GATEWAY_URL`, `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`, and `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` from the environment. Run the
commands from the lab folder.

```bash title="Python"
cd infra
pip install -r requirements.txt     # the openai package
```

```bash title="TypeScript"
cd infra
npm install                         # the openai npm package
```

### Stream from code

Pass `stream=True` and iterate over the chunks. Skip chunks without `choices`, and keep the usage from the chunk that
has it.

```python title="Python"
stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain in two sentences why streaming makes chat apps feel faster."}],
    stream=True,
    stream_options={"include_usage": True},
)
usage = None
for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.usage:
        usage = chunk.usage
    if not chunk.choices:  # the prompt filter chunk and the usage chunk
        continue
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="", flush=True)
print(f"\nTokens used: {usage.total_tokens if usage else 'no usage chunk'}")
```

```typescript title="TypeScript"
const stream = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model,
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Explain in two sentences why streaming makes chat apps feel faster." }],
  stream: true,
  stream_options: { include_usage: true },
});
let usage: OpenAI.CompletionUsage | undefined;
for await (const chunk of stream) {
  if (chunk.usage) usage = chunk.usage;
  // choices[0] is undefined on the prompt filter chunk and the usage chunk.
  process.stdout.write(chunk.choices[0]?.delta?.content ?? "");
}
console.log(`\nTokens used: ${usage?.total_tokens ?? "no usage chunk"}`);
```

The Responses API streams typed events. Print `response.output_text.delta` events and read the usage from
`response.completed`:

```python title="Python"
for event in client.responses.create(model=model, input="Write a one-sentence status update.", stream=True):
    if event.type == "response.output_text.delta":
        print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
    elif event.type == "response.completed":
        print(f"\nTokens used: {event.response.usage.total_tokens}")
```

```typescript title="TypeScript"
const events = await client.responses.create({ model, input: "Write a one-sentence status update.", stream: true });
for await (const event of events) {
  if (event.type === "response.output_text.delta") process.stdout.write(event.delta);
  else if (event.type === "response.completed") console.log(`\nTokens used: ${event.response.usage?.total_tokens}`);
}
```

The full samples create the client, time the first token, and print both streams: open [stream.py](infra/stream.py)
and [stream.ts](infra/stream.ts).

### Run the sample

```bash title="Python"
python stream.py
```

```bash title="TypeScript"
node stream.ts      # Node.js 22.18 or later; on older versions run: npx tsx stream.ts
```

Expected output (your text differs):

```text
Chat Completions:
Streaming shows each response as it's generated instead of making you wait for the whole message, so you see progress right away. It also lets you start reading or reacting before the response is complete.
First token:      1.77 s
Tokens used:      74 (prompt 18, completion 56)

Responses API:
Streaming is running smoothly, with no interruptions reported.
Tokens used:      66 (input 16, output 50)
```

> The reply appears a few words at a time, and you can name the chunk that carries the usage in each API.

## Put a token limit on a streaming alias

To find out whether the gateway counts streamed tokens, give a new alias, `<model-name>-stream`, a deliberately low
limit: **1,000 tokens per minute for each caller identity**. It targets the same backend model as your alias from
lab 02, so clients that call that alias aren't affected.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Create the alias

1. Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway in the top bar.
2. Select **Models** › **Aliases** › **Add alias**.
3. On **Basics**, set **Alias name** to `<model-name>-stream`, for example `gpt-6-luna-stream`. Select **Next**.
4. On **Select models**, select your model in **Available backend models**. Select **Next**.
5. Keep the defaults on **Priority and weights**, select **Next**, then select **Create** on **Review**.

### Add the token limit

1. Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
   **Token rate limit**, then **Next**.
2. On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets**, select the `<model-name>-stream` alias, then **Next**.
3. On the **Details** step, set **Time period** to **Per minute**, **Allowed tokens** to `1000`, and
   **Counter dimensions** to **Caller identity**. Select **Create**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step](../assets/screens/policy-add-wizard.png "Policies › Add policy opens a three-step wizard: Type, Scope, Configure.")

> **Checkpoint**
> **Models** › **Aliases** lists `<model-name>-stream`, and **Policies** lists a **Token rate limit** of 1,000
> tokens per minute scoped to it.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the alias with its token limit

An alias carries its own `policies` array, so one `PUT` creates the alias and its limit together.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method put --url "$WS/aliases/$STREAM_ALIAS?$API" \
  --body "$(jq -cn --arg m "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL" '{properties: {
      description: "Streaming lab: 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller",
      backendModels: [{resourceId: $m}],
      policies: [{type: "tokenLimit", count: 1000, period: "minute", counterKey: ["identity"]}]}}')" \
  --query "{alias:name, policies:properties.policies}" -o json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
@{ properties = @{
    description   = "Streaming lab: 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller"
    backendModels = @(@{ resourceId = "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL" })
    policies      = @(@{ type = "tokenLimit"; count = 1000; period = "minute"; counterKey = @("identity") })
  } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put --url "$WS/aliases/$STREAM_ALIAS`?$API" --body "@body.json" `
  --query "{alias:name, policies:properties.policies}" -o json
Remove-Item body.json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The output shows your alias and one policy with `"type": "tokenLimit"`, `"count": 1000`, `"period": "minute"`,
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and `"scope": "resource"`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Deploy the template from lab 06

[Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md) ships a template that publishes a
token-limited alias for an existing model. Reuse it with the streaming alias name.

```bash title="Bash"
az deployment group create -g "$RG" -n 23-streaming-alias \
  --template-file ../06-token-limits/infra/main.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" providerName="$PROVIDER" modelName="$MODEL" aliasName="$STREAM_ALIAS" \
               allowedTokens=1000 period=minute counterKey="['identity']" \
  --query properties.outputs
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az deployment group create -g $RG -n 23-streaming-alias `
  --template-file ../06-token-limits/infra/main.bicep `
  --parameters gatewayName=$GATEWAY providerName=$PROVIDER modelName=$MODEL aliasName=$STREAM_ALIAS `
               allowedTokens=1000 period=minute counterKey="['identity']" `
  --query properties.outputs
```

On GitHub, open [main.bicep](../06-token-limits/infra/main.bicep).

> **Checkpoint**
> The outputs show `aliasName` set to your streaming alias, and **Policies** in the portal lists a
> **Token rate limit** scoped to it.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

Send bursts of streamed requests that each use about 220 tokens: first without asking for usage, then with it. If the
gateway only counted the tokens that clients report, the first burst would never be throttled.

<!-- steps -->

### Stream a burst without asking for usage

For each request, the script prints the status, `Retry-After`, the number of events, and the usage chunk, if any.

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/stream-burst.sh "$STREAM_ALIAS" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/stream-burst.ps1 -Model $STREAM_ALIAS -Requests 8
```

On GitHub, open [stream-burst.sh](infra/stream-burst.sh) or [stream-burst.ps1](infra/stream-burst.ps1).

Expected output (your counts differ):

```text
Request  Status  Retry-After  Events  Usage chunk
1        200     -            209     none
2        200     -            187     none
3        200     -            207     none
4        200     -            200     none
5        200     -            196     none
6        200     -            191     none
7        429     2            -       Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 2 seconds.
8        429     1            -       Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 1 seconds.
```

No stream carried a usage chunk, yet the gateway throttled request 7, after about 1,300 tokens. If it had
counted only the prompts, about 25 tokens each, the alias would have allowed roughly 40 requests.

> [!NOTE]
> A new alias or policy can take up to a minute to apply, and the counters catch up within a few seconds, so a fast
> burst can go a few hundred tokens past the limit. If every request returns `200`, wait a minute and run it again.

### Stream a burst with usage

Wait a minute for the window to reset, then run the same burst with `include_usage`:

```bash title="Bash"
sleep 60
./infra/stream-burst.sh --usage "$STREAM_ALIAS" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
Start-Sleep 60
./infra/stream-burst.ps1 -Model $STREAM_ALIAS -Requests 8 -Usage
```

Expected output:

```text
Request  Status  Retry-After  Events  Usage chunk
1        200     -            196     218 tokens
2        200     -            186     208 tokens
3        200     -            196     218 tokens
4        200     -            191     213 tokens
5        200     -            211     233 tokens
6        200     -            191     213 tokens
7        429     1            -       Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 1 seconds.
8        200     -            193     215 tokens
```

The throttle point is the same: the gateway counted the streams the same way whether or not the client asked for
usage. Request 8 succeeds again because it was sent after the `Retry-After` wait.

### Inspect a throttled streaming request

Run the burst once more and, while the alias is throttled, look at a full response:

```bash
curl -sS -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$STREAM_ALIAS\",\"stream\":true,\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

Expected output, when the limit is active:

```text
HTTP/2 429
content-type: application/json
retry-after: 3
content-length: 84

{ "statusCode": 429, "message": "Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 3 seconds." }
```

The throttled answer is plain JSON, not an event stream, because the gateway refused the request before it reached
the model. Check the status code before you start reading events, and honor `Retry-After`.

### Find the streamed calls in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring**. The streamed requests show their token counts next to the non-streamed ones, and the throttled
requests appear as `429` outcomes.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> Both bursts were throttled at the same request, the burst without `include_usage` included, and the throttled
> request returned a JSON `429` with `Retry-After` instead of a stream.

## Go further

- **Cap spend for streams.** A cost limit is estimated from the same usage record, so streamed calls count against
  budgets too. Try it in [Enforce cost budgets](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).
- **Shorten the time to the first token.** Reasoning models think before they write. For chat that needs a quick
  first word, set `reasoning_effort` to `low` or `none` where the model supports it, as the scripts in this lab do.
- **Stream from an agent.** Agent frameworks stream through the same endpoint. See
  [Connect agent frameworks to models and tools](../15-agent-frameworks/README.md).
- **Check your proxies.** Anything between the client and the gateway, such as a reverse proxy or an API layer of your
  own, must pass `text/event-stream` responses through without buffering.

## Clean up

Delete the streaming alias. Its token limit goes with it, and the backend model and your alias from lab 02 stay.
In the portal, open `<model-name>-stream` in **Models** › **Aliases** and select **Delete**. From a shell:

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/aliases/$STREAM_ALIAS?$API"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/aliases/$STREAM_ALIAS`?$API"
```

Keep the gateway, model, and key. The next labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `IndexError: list index out of range` in Python, or `Cannot read properties of undefined` in TypeScript | The code reads `choices[0]` on the prompt filter chunk or the usage chunk, which have no choices | Skip chunks whose `choices` array is empty, as the samples do. |
| The whole reply appears at once | curl runs without `-N`, PowerShell uses `Invoke-RestMethod`, or a proxy buffers the response | Use `curl -N`, read the stream with `HttpClient` as `stream-chat.ps1` does, and turn off response buffering in your proxy. |
| No usage chunk at the end of the stream | The client didn't set `stream_options.include_usage` | Set it when your app needs the numbers. The gateway counts the tokens for its limits either way. |
| `400` with `The 'stream_options' parameter is only allowed when 'stream' is enabled.` | The request sets `stream_options` without `"stream": true` | Send both, or neither. |
| `429` JSON response instead of a stream | A token limit on the alias, the model, or the gateway is exhausted | Wait for `Retry-After` seconds. The limit is checked before the stream starts, so no partial reply is lost. |
| The SDK sample never shows a `429` | The OpenAI SDKs retry `429` responses automatically and honor `Retry-After` | That's the behavior you want in an app. To see each `429`, create the client with `max_retries=0` (Python) or `maxRetries: 0` (TypeScript). |
| Every request in the burst returns `200` | The policy isn't active yet, or the burst used another alias | Check that `STREAM_ALIAS` matches the alias with the limit, wait a minute, and run the burst again. |

# Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint

Your agent teams want tools: documentation search, ticketing, internal APIs. If every agent connects to every
tool server directly, you end up with credentials in many places and no single point of control. In this lab
the platform team publishes **one governed MCP endpoint** on the gateway, starting with the public Microsoft
Learn MCP server, so agents get tools through the same front door they already use for models.

![One MCP endpoint on the gateway federates tools from several backends](../assets/diagrams/mcp-federation.svg "Clients connect to one MCP endpoint. The gateway authenticates them, applies policies, and federates the namespaced tools of every backend.")

## Before you begin

- Complete [Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md).
- A runtime API key, for example `app-first-call` from [lab 02](../02-first-model-call/README.md). If you don't have
  one yet, create it in the portal under **Access** › **Keys**, or, after
  you set the variables below, run `az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-first-call?$API" --body '{"properties":{}}'`
  and read its value with
  `az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-first-call/listSecrets?$API" --query primaryKey -o tsv`.
- For the CLI and IaC tracks: the [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or
  later, signed in with `az login`, plus `jq` for the Bash snippets. The CLI track calls the Azure Resource
  Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't manage the new `aigateways`
  resource type yet.
- For the **Verify** scripts: `curl` and `jq` (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later. The Code track also uses
  Python 3.10 or later and, optionally, VS Code.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

## How it works

An **MCP server** in AI Gateway is a federation point. You give it one or more **backends**, and the gateway
publishes all their tools at one Streamable HTTP endpoint:
`https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp`.

| Backend type | What you provide | What clients see |
|---|---|---|
| **MCP server** (remote) | A URL that speaks SSE or Streamable HTTP | The server's tools |
| **OpenAPI spec** | A JSON or YAML OpenAPI document (upload, URL, or inline) | Selected operations as tools. The operation summary or description becomes the tool description. |
| **Built-in connector** | A managed connection to a SaaS app, such as Microsoft 365, SharePoint, GitHub, or Salesforce | The connector's operations as tools |
| **Foundry Toolbox** | A Microsoft Foundry Toolbox source | The toolbox's tools |

Each backend can have a **namespace**. The gateway prefixes that backend's tools with it, as in
`learn_microsoft_docs_search`, so two backends can expose tools with the same name without conflict.

The gateway authenticates **clients**. In this lab they send a runtime key in the `api-key` header.
It authenticates to each **backend** separately, with **None**, **API key** (a header name and value),
**OAuth 2.0**, or **Managed identity**. Backend credentials are stored securely, are never exposed to clients,
and appear under **Connections**.

> [!NOTE]
> Registering a backend doesn't mean that AI Gateway translates every backend protocol into MCP. Pick the
> backend type that matches what the backend actually serves.

## Register the Learn MCP server

Pick one track. Each track creates the same MCP server: **`learn`**, with one backend, the public Microsoft
Learn MCP server at `https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp`, under the namespace `learn`. That server needs no
credentials, so the backend authentication is **None**.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the workflow

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **MCP servers** › **Add MCP server**. The full-page **Create MCP server** workflow has three steps:
**Basic info**, **Backends**, and **Tools**.

### Describe the server

On **Basic info**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Name** | `learn` (part of the endpoint URL; it can't be changed after creation) |
| **Display name** | `Microsoft Learn` |
| **Description** | `Search and fetch official Microsoft documentation and code samples.` |

Agents and people read the description to decide when to use the server, so keep it specific. Select **Next**.

### Add the Learn backend

On **Backends**, select **Add backend**. In **Choose a backend type**, select **MCP server**, then set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **URL** | `https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp` |
| **Namespace** | `learn` |
| **Authentication** | **None** |

The backend appears in the table with its **URL**, **Type**, **Authentication**, **Namespace**, and
**Required** columns. Leave **Required** on. Select **Next**.

### Publish all tools

On **Tools**, under **Tool availability**, keep **Allow all tools** ("Expose every tool from these backends,
including tools added in the future."). You narrow this down in
[Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md). Select **Create**.

### Copy the endpoint

The server's details page opens. When **Provisioning** shows that the server is ready, copy the
**Endpoint URL**. It ends in `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp`.

> **Checkpoint**
> **MCP servers** lists `learn`, and its details page shows an **Endpoint URL** and one backend with the
> namespace `learn`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the registration

MCP servers are `toolServers` child resources of the gateway's `default` workspace.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method put --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body '{
  "properties": {
    "type": "mcp",
    "displayName": "Microsoft Learn",
    "description": "Search and fetch official Microsoft documentation and code samples.",
    "endpoints": [{"kind": "mcp", "namespace": "learn", "required": true,
                   "mcp": {"transport": "streamableHttp", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp"}}]
  }}' \
  --query "{name:name,mcpEndpoint:properties.gatewayEndpoints[0].url}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
@{ properties = @{
    type        = 'mcp'
    displayName = 'Microsoft Learn'
    description = 'Search and fetch official Microsoft documentation and code samples.'
    endpoints   = @(@{ kind = 'mcp'; namespace = 'learn'; required = $true
                       mcp  = @{ transport = 'streamableHttp'; url = 'https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp' } })
  } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content -Path body.json
az rest --method put --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body '@body.json' `
  --query "{name:name,mcpEndpoint:properties.gatewayEndpoints[0].url}"
Remove-Item body.json
```

The last segment of the URL, `learn`, is the MCP server name. A `PUT` replaces an existing registration with
the same name, including its backends and policies, so use `PATCH` to change a registration that already
exists, as in the next section.

### Confirm the registration

The command is the same in Bash and PowerShell.

```bash
az rest --url "$WS/toolServers?$API" --query "value[].{name:name,sources:length(properties.endpoints)}" -o table
az rest --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --query "properties.{endpoints:endpoints,url:gatewayEndpoints[0].url}"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The table shows `learn` with `1` in the **Sources** column. The second command returns one endpoint with
> `"namespace": "learn"` and `"kind": "mcp"`, and a `url` that ends in `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Review the template

The template references your existing gateway and its `default` workspace, then declares one
`toolServers` resource. The optional `secondNamespace` parameter is used in the next section.

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

On GitHub, open [infra/main.bicep](infra/main.bicep).

> [!WARNING]
> A Bicep deployment sends a `PUT`, which replaces the whole MCP server, including backends and tool rules
> that you added in the portal. Deploy the template to a new server name, or keep the template as the only
> source of truth for this server.

### Deploy it

```bash title="Bash"
az deployment group create -g "$RG" \
  --template-file infra/main.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" serverName=learn namespace=learn \
  --query properties.outputs
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az deployment group create -g $RG `
  --template-file infra/main.bicep `
  --parameters gatewayName=$GATEWAY serverName=learn namespace=learn `
  --query properties.outputs
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The outputs include `mcpEndpoint`, ending in `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp`, and **MCP servers** in the
> portal lists `learn`.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Federate a second backend

Federation pays off when one endpoint combines several backends. To see it without extra credentials, add the
same public Learn server again under a second namespace, `docs`. Both backends expose a tool called
`microsoft_docs_search`, and the namespaces keep them apart. Mark the new backend as **not required**: if an
optional backend is unavailable, the gateway skips it instead of failing the whole MCP server.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add the backend

On the `learn` details page, select **Edit**, then go to **Backends**. Select **Add backend** › **MCP server**
and set **URL** to `https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp`, **Namespace** to `docs`, and **Authentication** to
**None**. In the backends table, turn **Required** off for the new row. Select **Save**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Add the source

A `PATCH` of `properties.endpoints` replaces the whole list of backends, so read the list, append the new
backend, and send the result back. Other settings, such as the description and policies, stay as they are.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --query properties.endpoints -o json \
  | jq -c '{properties: {endpoints: (map(select(.namespace != "docs")) + [{kind: "mcp", namespace: "docs",
      required: false, mcp: {transport: "streamableHttp", url: "https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp"}}])}}' > endpoints.json
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body @endpoints.json \
  --query "properties.endpoints[].{namespace:namespace,required:required,url:mcp.url}" -o table
rm endpoints.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$endpoints = @(az rest --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --query properties.endpoints -o json | ConvertFrom-Json |
  Where-Object namespace -ne 'docs')
$endpoints += @{ kind = 'mcp'; namespace = 'docs'; required = $false
                 mcp  = @{ transport = 'streamableHttp'; url = 'https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp' } }
@{ properties = @{ endpoints = $endpoints } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content -Path endpoints.json
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body '@endpoints.json' `
  --query "properties.endpoints[].{namespace:namespace,required:required,url:mcp.url}" -o table
Remove-Item endpoints.json
```

The filter drops an existing `docs` backend first, so running the command twice doesn't add it twice. A `GET`
doesn't return backend credentials. If a backend uses an API key, include its credential again in the body.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Redeploy with a second namespace

```bash
az deployment group create -g "$RG" \
  --template-file infra/main.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" serverName=learn namespace=learn secondNamespace=docs \
  --query properties.outputs
```

The template adds the second endpoint with `required: false`.

<!-- /tracks -->

> [!TIP]
> In production, the second backend is a different service. For an internal REST API, choose **OpenAPI spec**
> and point **Spec source** › **Fetch from URL** at its OpenAPI document. For an API that needs a key, set
> **Authentication** to **API key** with the **Header name** and **Key value** the backend expects. Clients
> never see that key.

> **Checkpoint**
> The `learn` server has two backends: `learn` (required) and `docs` (optional).

## Choose supported MCP versions

MCP is versioned by date. A client opens a connection by naming the protocol version it speaks, and the server
answers with the version both sides will use. AI Gateway negotiates one version for the whole MCP server, so
that version must work with **every backend** behind it.

| Supported MCP versions | What clients get |
|---|---|
| Not configured | The legacy defaults: `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and `2024-11-05`. The portal labels them **Legacy defaults**. |
| A list that you choose | Version restrictions. Clients negotiate only a version in the list, and a request whose `MCP-Protocol-Version` header names any other version is rejected with `400`. |

You can choose `2026-07-28`, `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and `2024-11-05`. Version
`2026-07-28` is the stateless revision of the specification: it replaces the `initialize` handshake and
sessions with a `server/discover` request, and every request carries `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Method`, and
`Mcp-Name` headers plus metadata in `params._meta`. Select it only when every backend supports it, and use an
MCP SDK that implements it rather than hand-written requests.

In this lab, pin the server to `2025-06-18`. At the time of writing, that's the version the Microsoft Learn MCP
server negotiates, so both backends, `learn` and `docs`, support it.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Pin the version

1. On the `learn` details page, find **Supported MCP versions**. Unless you changed it, it lists the legacy
   defaults.
2. Select **Edit**. On **Basic info**, open **Supported MCP versions** and keep only `2025-06-18` selected.
3. Go to **Backends**. Because the list changed, the portal asks you to recheck the backends: "Supported MCP
   versions changed. Edit and save each external MCP backend before saving this server." For each backend row,
   select **Edit**, then **Save** in **Edit MCP backend**. The portal checks which versions the backend
   supports before it saves the row.
4. Select **Save**.

If a backend doesn't support a selected version, **Edit MCP backend** shows "Backend isn't compatible with all
configured MCP versions." and lists the versions the backend reports. Return to **Basic info** and change the
list, or update the backend.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set the versions

A `PATCH` that sends only `properties.versions` keeps the backends, tool rules, and policies as they are.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" \
  --body '{"properties": {"versions": ["2025-06-18"]}}' --query properties.versions
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
@{ properties = @{ versions = @('2025-06-18') } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5 -Compress | Set-Content -Path body.json
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body '@body.json' --query properties.versions
Remove-Item body.json
```

Unlike the portal, the API doesn't ask the backends which versions they support. If you list a version that a
backend can't speak, the `PATCH` succeeds and clients that negotiate that version fail. See
[Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Redeploy with pinned versions

The `supportedVersions` parameter takes a comma-separated list, such as `2025-06-18` or
`2026-07-28,2025-06-18`. Leave it empty to keep the legacy defaults.

```bash title="Bash"
az deployment group create -g "$RG" \
  --template-file infra/main.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" serverName=learn namespace=learn secondNamespace=docs \
               supportedVersions=2025-06-18 \
  --query properties.outputs.supportedVersions.value
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az deployment group create -g $RG `
  --template-file infra/main.bicep `
  --parameters gatewayName=$GATEWAY serverName=learn namespace=learn secondNamespace=docs `
               supportedVersions=2025-06-18 `
  --query properties.outputs.supportedVersions.value
```

<!-- /tracks -->

### Check the negotiated version

Ask for an older version. The gateway answers with the version it will use:

```bash title="Bash"
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-03-26",
       "capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"}}}'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$mcp     = "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/toolservers/learn/mcp"
$headers = @{ 'api-key' = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY; Accept = 'application/json, text/event-stream' }
$body    = '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-03-26",
             "capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"pwsh","version":"1.0"}}}'
(Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri $mcp -Headers $headers -ContentType 'application/json' -Body $body).Content
```

The result includes `"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18"`. Now send a request that names a version outside the list:

```bash title="Bash"
curl -sS -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri $mcp -SkipHttpErrorCheck -ContentType 'application/json' `
  -Headers ($headers + @{ 'MCP-Protocol-Version' = '2026-07-28' }) -Body '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
"HTTP $($r.StatusCode) $($r.Content)"
```

The gateway rejects it with `400` and `Unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version` before any backend is called.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Supported MCP versions** shows `2025-06-18` on the details page and in **Catalog**, an `initialize` request
> for `2025-03-26` returns `2025-06-18`, and a `2026-07-28` request is rejected with `400`.

## Connect a client

Any MCP-compatible client or agent framework can use the endpoint. Store the runtime key in the client's
secret store, never in a file that you commit.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Use the Connect panel

On the `learn` details page, select **Connect**. The panel offers **VS Code** and **Cursor** (install through a
deep link) and **mcp.json** (raw configuration for any MCP-aware client). Replace any key placeholder with your
runtime key in the client's secret prompt, not in a committed file.

<!-- track: code | Code -->

### Add the server to VS Code

Create `.vscode/mcp.json` in a project, paste this configuration, and replace `<gateway>` with your gateway
name. The `inputs` entry makes VS Code prompt for the key instead of storing it in the file.

<!-- include: infra/mcp.json -->

On GitHub, open [infra/mcp.json](infra/mcp.json).

Start the `ai-gateway-learn` server from the `mcp.json` editor and paste your runtime key when prompted. In
Copilot Chat agent mode, the gateway's namespaced tools are now available, for example
`learn_microsoft_docs_search`.

### Call the tools from Python

This client uses the official [MCP Python SDK](https://pypi.org/project/mcp/) and sends the runtime key in the
`api-key` header.

<!-- include: infra/list_tools.py -->

On GitHub, open [infra/list_tools.py](infra/list_tools.py).

```bash title="Bash"
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r infra/requirements.txt
python infra/list_tools.py learn learn_microsoft_docs_search "How do I add a token limit in AI Gateway?"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
python -m venv .venv; .venv/Scripts/Activate.ps1
pip install -r infra/requirements.txt
python infra/list_tools.py learn learn_microsoft_docs_search "How do I add a token limit in AI Gateway?"
```

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### List the published tools

MCP clients start with a handshake: `initialize`, then `notifications/initialized`, then `tools/list`. The
script runs that handshake through your gateway, reads JSON or server-sent event (SSE) responses, and prints
every published tool. Run it from the lab folder.

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn
```

On GitHub, open [list-tools.sh](infra/list-tools.sh) or [list-tools.ps1](infra/list-tools.ps1).

Expected output (descriptions are shortened, and the tool list can change as the Learn server evolves):

```text
MCP endpoint: https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/learn/mcp
Server: <server-name-reported-by-the-gateway>  protocol: <negotiated-version>

Tool                                          Description
learn_microsoft_docs_search                   Search official Microsoft/Azure documentation to find the most relevan
learn_microsoft_code_sample_search            Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn docu
learn_microsoft_docs_fetch                    Fetch and convert a Microsoft Learn documentation webpage to markdown
docs_microsoft_docs_search                    Search official Microsoft/Azure documentation to find the most relevan
docs_microsoft_code_sample_search             Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn docu
docs_microsoft_docs_fetch                     Fetch and convert a Microsoft Learn documentation webpage to markdown

6 tools published
```

Each tool carries its backend's namespace. Use the exact names that your output shows in the next steps.

### Call a tool through the gateway

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn learn_microsoft_docs_search "How do I add a token limit in AI Gateway?"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_search -Query "How do I add a token limit in AI Gateway?"
```

After the tool list, the script prints the start of the search results that Microsoft Learn returned through
your gateway.

### Send a raw JSON-RPC request

The docs show the smallest possible request: a single JSON-RPC `tools/list` call. Streamable HTTP clients
should also accept both JSON and SSE responses.

```bash
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

The answer is JSON or an SSE `data:` line with a `result.tools` array. If the server answers with a JSON-RPC
`error` instead, it requires the full handshake. Use the script, which runs it for you.

### Prove that the gateway checks the caller

Send the same request without the key:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

The gateway rejects the request, typically with `401`, and no backend is called. Microsoft Learn is public,
but your MCP endpoint isn't.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The script lists namespaced tools from both backends, a tool call returns Microsoft Learn content, and a
> request without a key is rejected.

## Go further

- **Control the catalog.** Publish only approved tools, block risky ones, and rate-limit the server in
  [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md).
- **Screen tool traffic.** Content safety also screens tool inputs and responses on MCP servers. See
  [Screen prompts and responses with content safety](../08-content-safety/README.md).
- **Go keyless.** Grant callers the **AI Gateway User** role and send a Microsoft Entra token instead of a
  runtime key. See [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).
- **Watch tool traffic.** When Application Insights is configured, tool executions appear in **Monitoring** ›
  **Tools**. See [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md).
- **Onboard GitHub.** Add the GitHub MCP server, `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, as an **MCP server**
  backend with **API key** authentication: **Header name** `Authorization` and **Key value**
  `Bearer <your-github-token>`. The gateway stores the token, and clients never see it.
- **Give tools to an agent.** Point an agent framework at the endpoint in [Connect agent frameworks to models and tools](../15-agent-frameworks/README.md).

## Clean up

MCP servers don't add charges beyond the gateway itself. Keep `learn` if you continue with
[Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md), which builds on it.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the second backend or the server

To remove only the `docs` backend, select **Edit** on the `learn` details page, delete its row on **Backends**,
and select **Save**. To remove the whole server, select **Delete** on the details page.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the second source or the server

```bash title="Bash"
# Remove only the optional backend
az rest --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --query properties.endpoints -o json \
  | jq -c '{properties: {endpoints: map(select(.namespace != "docs"))}}' > endpoints.json
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body @endpoints.json --query "properties.endpoints[].namespace"
rm endpoints.json

# Or remove the whole MCP server
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Remove only the optional backend
$endpoints = @(az rest --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --query properties.endpoints -o json | ConvertFrom-Json |
  Where-Object namespace -ne 'docs')
@{ properties = @{ endpoints = $endpoints } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content -Path endpoints.json
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body '@endpoints.json' --query "properties.endpoints[].namespace"
Remove-Item endpoints.json

# Or remove the whole MCP server
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API"
```

An MCP server needs at least one backend, so the service rejects a `PATCH` that removes the last one. Delete
the server instead.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Redeploy or delete

Redeploy without `secondNamespace` to go back to one backend, or delete the server:

```bash
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API"
```

<!-- track: code | Code -->

### Remove the client configuration

Delete the `ai-gateway-learn` entry from `.vscode/mcp.json` and the `.venv` folder you created.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `401` from the MCP endpoint | The key is missing, revoked, or sent in the wrong header | Send a runtime key from **Access** › **Keys** in the `api-key` header. |
| `404` from the MCP endpoint | Wrong server name in the URL, or the server is still provisioning | List the servers with `az rest --url "$WS/toolServers?$API" --query "value[].name"` and use the exact name in `/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp`. |
| `406` or an error about the `Accept` header | The client doesn't accept both JSON and SSE | Send `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`, or use an MCP SDK. |
| `tools/list` returns an empty `tools` array | The registration is reachable but no backend returned tools | Check each backend's URL and authentication with `az rest --url "$WS/toolServers/<server-name>?$API" --query properties.endpoints`. |
| The whole server fails when one backend is down | That backend is **Required** | Turn **Required** off for backends that are nice-to-have, or fix the backend. |
| Backends or policies disappeared after a `PUT` or a Bicep deployment | A `PUT` replaces an existing registration with the same name | Change existing servers with `GET`, edit, `PATCH`, as in the CLI track, or `PUT` to a new name. |
| `PATCH` fails with "Tool server endpoints are required" | The request removes the last backend | Keep at least one backend, or delete the server. |
| `400` with `Unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version` | The client sent an `MCP-Protocol-Version` header that isn't in **Supported MCP versions** | Add the version to the list if every backend supports it, or let the client negotiate a listed version. |
| `404` with "Federation tools/list failed: required endpoint '…' returned error: Backend selected protocol version '…' instead of '…'" | **Supported MCP versions** includes a version that this backend doesn't support, and the client negotiated it | Keep only versions that every backend supports. In the portal, edit and save each backend to recheck it. |
| `400` with JSON-RPC error `-32603`, "The request cannot be completed using the requested protocol version." | A `2026-07-28` request reached a backend that doesn't support `2026-07-28` | Remove `2026-07-28` from **Supported MCP versions** until every backend supports it. |
| `400` with JSON-RPC error `-32602`, "Required MCP request metadata is missing or malformed." | A `2026-07-28` request lacks the `Mcp-Method` or `Mcp-Name` header, or `params._meta` | Use an MCP SDK that implements `2026-07-28` instead of hand-written requests. |
| The portal shows "Backend isn't compatible with all configured MCP versions." | The backend doesn't report support for every selected version | Return to **Basic info** and change **Supported MCP versions**, or update the backend. |
| Creating a server fails with `502 Bad Gateway`, or a Bicep deployment keeps running | Another MCP server in the gateway already uses the same display name | Choose a unique display name, for example with the Bicep `displayName` parameter. |

  - Block specific tools with patterns that take precedence over the allow list
