# Control which tools agents can call

The `learn` MCP server that you federated now publishes every tool from two backends. Your security team has
two requests: agents should **search** documentation but not fetch arbitrary pages, and the code sample tool
stays off until its review is done. Operations adds a third: a looping agent must not flood the backends. In
this lab you publish only the approved tools, block one explicitly, and give each caller a request budget.

![Tool controls on the MCP server decide which federated tools agents can list and call](../assets/diagrams/mcp-federation.svg "The gateway applies tool availability, blocked tools, and policies on the MCP server before it calls any backend.")

<!-- widget: tool-patterns {"tools":["learn_microsoft_docs_search","learn_microsoft_code_sample_search","learn_microsoft_docs_fetch","docs_microsoft_docs_search","docs_microsoft_code_sample_search","docs_microsoft_docs_fetch"],"allow":["*_search"],"block":["*code_sample*"]} -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). You need the `learn`
  MCP server with its `learn` and `docs` backends, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- The [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with
  `az login`, to set the variables below. The REST track calls the Azure Resource Manager REST API with
  `az rest`, and its Bash snippets also need `jq`.
- For the **Verify** scripts: `curl` and `jq` (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

## How it works

An MCP server has three layers of tool control. The gateway applies all of them before it calls a backend.

| Control | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool availability** | The server's **Tools** step | **Allow all tools** publishes every tool, including tools that backends add later. **Select exact tools** (a static list) or name patterns publish only matching tools. Tools that don't match aren't listed and can't be called. |
| **Blocked tools** | The server's **Tools** step | Names or patterns that the gateway refuses to run. Blocked patterns take precedence over the allow list. Blocked tools remain visible to clients, but the gateway blocks their execution. |
| **MCP server access** | The server's **Basic info** step, in edit mode | **Active** or **Blocked**. Blocked MCP servers can't be reached by clients, whatever their tool rules say. |
| **Request rate limit** policy | **Policies** | A number of **Calls** per **Renewal period** for each counter. Over the limit, the gateway answers `429` with `Retry-After`. |

Patterns use `*` for any number of characters and `?` for exactly one. This lab uses `*_search` to allow
both search tools and `*code_sample*` to block the code sample tool. Both patterns match whether or not you
include the namespace prefix, such as `learn_`, so they cover every backend of the server.

> [!NOTE]
> Tool availability, blocked tools, and server access are configured in the portal. There's no documented CLI
> or REST shape for them yet, so this lab doesn't show one. The request rate limit has both a portal and a REST
> track.

## Publish only approved tools

These steps edit the `learn` server in the portal. Make sure the patterns cover every tool that your agents
legitimately need before you save. Tools that don't match are no longer listed or callable.

<!-- steps -->

### Open the Tools step

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway. Select **MCP servers**,
open `learn`, select **Edit**, and go to the **Tools** step.

### Allow the search tools by pattern

Under **Tool availability**, select **Match tools by name pattern**. Depending on your portal version, the
option is labeled **Use name patterns**, and **Select exact tools** is also offered. In
**Allowed tool name patterns**, enter `*_search`. If your portal shows **Add pattern**, use it to add each
pattern on its own row.

### Block the code sample tool

Under **Blocked tools**, select **Add blocked tool** (or **Add**). In **Tool name or pattern**, enter
`*code_sample*` and select **Add**. The pattern appears under **Blocked tools**, with a note on whether it
matches tools in the discovered catalog.

![The Tools step with an allowed tool name pattern and a blocked pattern](../assets/screens/mcp-tool-controls.png "Edit MCP server › Tools: allowed name patterns publish matching tools, and blocked patterns stop matching tools from running. This example uses a pet store backend.")

### Save the server

Select **Save**.

### Check the catalog

Run the script from [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). This lab
includes a copy, so run it from this lab's folder. It lists the tools and calls an allowed one.

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn learn_microsoft_docs_search "What is AI Gateway?"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_search -Query "What is AI Gateway?"
```

On GitHub, open [list-tools.sh](infra/list-tools.sh) or [list-tools.ps1](infra/list-tools.ps1).

The list has four tools, the search tools and the code sample tools of both backends. The `*_fetch` tools are
gone because they don't match `*_search`. The code sample tools are still listed, because blocked tools stay
visible. The call to `learn_microsoft_docs_search` returns Microsoft Learn results.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `tools/list` returns four tools and no `*_fetch` tool, and an allowed search tool still works.

## Take the whole server offline

Sometimes you need to stop all tool traffic at once, for example while you investigate a misbehaving backend.
Blocking the server keeps its backends, tool rules, and policies, so you can turn it back on in one step.

<!-- steps -->

### Block the server

On the `learn` details page, select **Edit**. On **Basic info**, set **MCP server access** to **Blocked**, then
select **Save**.

### Confirm that clients can't connect

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn
```

The script stops at `initialize` with an HTTP error from the gateway. No backend is called.

### Turn the server back on

Select **Edit** again, set **MCP server access** to **Active**, and select **Save**. Run the script again to
confirm that the four tools are back.

<!-- /steps -->

## Rate-limit the MCP server

A request rate limit counts calls instead of tokens. That suits tools, where one agent in a loop can send
hundreds of calls a minute. Pick one track. Both produce the same policy on the `learn` server: **5 calls per
30 seconds for each caller identity**. The limit is deliberately low so you can trigger it quickly.

<!-- widget: request-rate {"calls":5,"window":30} -->

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
**Request rate limit**, then **Next**.

### Choose the MCP server

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select the `learn` MCP server, then **Next**.

### Configure the limit

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Calls** | `5` |
| **Renewal period** | **30 seconds** |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

The other renewal periods are **60 seconds**, **2 minutes**, and **5 minutes**. **Caller identity** gives each API
key, and each Entra caller, its own counter. If you select no counter dimension, all callers share one
counter. Select **Create**.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists a **Request rate limit** with the `learn` MCP server as its scope.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current policies

Policies live inline in the MCP server's `properties.policies` array. A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**,
so always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to change.

```bash title="Bash"
URL="$WS/toolServers/learn"
az rest --url "$URL?$API" --query properties.policies
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$URL = "$WS/toolServers/learn"
az rest --url "$URL`?$API" --query properties.policies
```

The command prints nothing if the server has never had a policy.

### Replace the request rate limit and keep everything else

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$URL?$API" -o json | jq -c '{properties: {policies: (
    [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "requestRateLimit")]
    + [{type: "requestRateLimit", callsPerPeriod: 5, periodSeconds: 30, counterKey: ["identity"]}])}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$current  = az rest --url "$URL`?$API" -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'requestRateLimit' })
$policies += [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'requestRateLimit'; callsPerPeriod = 5; periodSeconds = 30; counterKey = @('identity') }

@{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content -Path policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$URL`?$API" --body '@policies.json' --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

The commands read the whole MCP server, not just `properties.policies`, because the array is missing until the
server has had a policy. `periodSeconds` is the renewal period in seconds. The portal offers `30`, `60`, `120`, and
`300`. `counterKey` is an array with `identity`, `ipAddress`, or both. An empty array gives all callers one
shared counter.

> [!TIP]
> The same `GET`, merge, `PATCH` pattern sets policies on models, aliases, and the `default` workspace. Only the
> URL changes.

> **Checkpoint**
> The `PATCH` returns your other policies unchanged plus one entry like this:
>
> ```json
> {
>   "callsPerPeriod": 5,
>   "counterKey": ["identity"],
>   "periodSeconds": 30,
>   "scope": "resource",
>   "type": "requestRateLimit"
> }
> ```

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

The rate limit counts the calls you make while you verify, too. Every MCP request counts, including the two
handshake messages that each script run starts with. Wait 30 seconds between steps so each one starts with a
fresh window.

<!-- steps -->

### Call a blocked tool

The code sample tool is still listed, but the gateway refuses to run it:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn learn_microsoft_code_sample_search "Python MCP client"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn -Tool learn_microsoft_code_sample_search -Query "Python MCP client"
```

The tool list prints as before, and then the script reports that the `tools/call` request failed and prints
the gateway's error. The Learn backend never receives the call.

### Run the burst

Wait 30 seconds, then send a handshake followed by eight `tools/list` requests:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/trigger-request-rate.sh learn 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/trigger-request-rate.ps1 -Server learn -Requests 8
```

On GitHub, open [trigger-request-rate.sh](infra/trigger-request-rate.sh) or
[trigger-request-rate.ps1](infra/trigger-request-rate.ps1).

Expected output (your `Retry-After` values will differ):

```text
Request  Method                      Status  Retry-After
1        initialize                  200     -
2        notifications/initialized   202     -
3        tools/list                  200     -
4        tools/list                  200     -
5        tools/list                  200     -
6        tools/list                  200     -
7        tools/list                  200     -
8        tools/list                  429     4
9        tools/list                  429     3
10       tools/list                  429     2

Last response body:
{ "statusCode": 429, "message": "Rate limit is exceeded. Try again in 2 seconds." }
```

The counter is approximate, so the gateway can let a call or two beyond the limit through before the first
`429`. `Retry-After` counts down to the end of the current 30-second window, so it can be anything from 1 to 30
seconds.

### Inspect one throttled response

Right after the burst, while you're still throttled, send one raw request and look at the status line and
headers. If it returns `200`, the window has already renewed. Run the burst again, then this command.

```bash
curl -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

The status line is `HTTP/2 429`, the headers include `retry-after`, and the body is the same JSON error. The
`Retry-After` value tells the client how many seconds to wait. Agent frameworks should back
off for that long instead of retrying in a tight loop.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The `*_fetch` tools are no longer listed, a call to the blocked code sample tool fails, an allowed search
> tool works, and calls over the limit in a 30-second window get `429` with `Retry-After`.

## Go further

- **Prefer exact names for sensitive servers.** Patterns also publish tools that a backend adds later. Where
  your portal offers **Select exact tools**, use it for servers whose new tools need a review first.
- **Block destructive operations everywhere.** For a server built from an OpenAPI spec, keep
  **Allow all tools** and add blocked patterns such as `*_delete_*` so new read operations appear
  automatically but deletions never run.
- **Set a default for every MCP server.** Add a **Request rate limit** with **Gateway** scope in
  [Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md).
- **Inspect tool calls for attacks.** Add Agent 365 tool threat protection in
  [Protect tool calls with Agent 365 threat protection](../19-tool-threat-protection/README.md).

## Clean up

A 5-call limit will throttle real agents. Remove it, and open the tool catalog again, before you continue.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the policy and restore the catalog

1. Select **Policies**, open the **Request rate limit** that's scoped to `learn`, and delete it.
2. Open **MCP servers** › `learn` › **Edit** › **Tools**. Select **Allow all tools**, remove the
   `*code_sample*` blocked pattern, and select **Save**.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the policy

```bash title="Bash"
URL="$WS/toolServers/learn"
az rest --url "$URL?$API" -o json \
  | jq -c '{properties: {policies: [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "requestRateLimit")]}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$URL      = "$WS/toolServers/learn"
$current  = az rest --url "$URL`?$API" -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'requestRateLimit' })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content -Path policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$URL`?$API" --body '@policies.json' --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

Then restore the catalog in the portal: open **MCP servers** › `learn` › **Edit** › **Tools**, select
**Allow all tools**, remove the `*code_sample*` blocked pattern, and select **Save**.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, the `learn` MCP server, and your key. The next labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A tool you blocked still appears in `tools/list` | Expected. Blocked tools remain visible, but the gateway blocks their execution | Call the tool to confirm that it's blocked. To hide a tool, leave it out of the allow list instead. |
| `tools/list` returns no tools | The allow list matches nothing, or the server access is **Blocked** | Check the patterns against the exact tool names, and set **MCP server access** to **Active**. |
| An allowed tool is blocked | A blocked pattern also matches it. Blocked patterns take precedence | Make the blocked pattern narrower, for example `*code_sample*` instead of `*sample*`. |
| `429` on the first request of a run | The previous step used up the window, or a **Gateway** scope rate limit also applies | Wait for `Retry-After`, and review **Policies** for every limit that covers the MCP server. |
| Never `429` | The policy is on another asset, it was saved moments ago, or the burst spans two windows | Check the policy's scope, wait a minute after you save it, and run a longer burst, for example `./infra/trigger-request-rate.sh learn 12`. |
| Other policies vanished after the REST call | `PATCH` replaces the whole `policies` array | Always `GET`, merge, then `PATCH`, as shown in the REST track. |

  responses, too.

  MCP server.

  calls for prompt injection and sensitive data.

<!-- https://azure.github.io/ai-gateway/labs/06-token-limits/ -->
---
title: Throttle tokens per caller with token limits
summary: Cap how many tokens each app, agent, or user can consume per minute, hour, or day, and watch the gateway answer with 429 and Retry-After before your backend capacity runs out.
category: governance
level: Beginner
duration: 25
tracks: [portal, cli, rest, iac]
order: 6
illustration: diagrams/token-limits.svg
tags: [tokenLimit, TPM, quota, "429", Retry-After, noisy neighbor]
objectives:
  - Explain how a token limit counts tokens per caller and per time window
  - Add a token rate limit to a model in the portal, with the Azure CLI, or with the REST API
  - Publish a separately limited alias with Bicep, without touching existing clients
  - Trigger a 429 response, read Retry-After, and find the throttled calls in Monitoring
prereqs:
  - 02-first-model-call
---

# Throttle tokens per caller with token limits

Your gateway now serves several apps from one model deployment. One batch job sends long prompts in a tight
loop and eats the deployment's tokens-per-minute (TPM) capacity, so every other app starts to fail. In this lab
you give each caller its own token allowance at the gateway, so a noisy neighbor gets a `429` with
`Retry-After` and everyone else keeps working.

![A token limit gives each caller its own allowance in front of a shared model deployment](../assets/diagrams/token-limits.svg "Each caller identity gets its own token counter. When a counter is exhausted, the gateway answers 429 without calling the backend.")

<!-- widget: token-limit {"limit":1000,"period":"minute"} -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need a gateway, an imported
  model, a callable alias, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- For the CLI, REST, and IaC tracks: the [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli)
  2.75 or later, signed in with `az login`, plus `jq` for the Bash snippets. The CLI track calls the Azure
  Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't manage the new
  `aigateways` resource type yet.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export MODEL_URL="$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# A starting guess for the alias. Confirm it on the model's Aliases tab (lab 02) and replace it if it differs.
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER   = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL      = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$MODEL_URL  = "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# A starting guess for the alias. Confirm it on the model's Aliases tab (lab 02) and replace it if it differs.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

> [!TIP]
> Not sure which alias your clients call? Open the model in **Models** and check its **Aliases** tab. The value
> in the request `model` field must match an alias exactly.

## How it works

A token limit is a policy that the gateway evaluates **before** it forwards a request. It keeps a counter of
the tokens that each caller consumed in the current window. While the counter is under the limit, the request
goes through and the tokens in the response are added to the counter. When the counter reaches the limit, the
gateway answers `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header and never calls the backend.

| Setting | Portal label | JSON field | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Allowance | **Allowed tokens** | `count` | Positive integer |
| Window | **Time period** | `period` | `minute` (TPM), `hour`, `day` (quota) |
| Who gets a counter | **Counter dimensions** | `counterKey` | An array: `["identity"]` (each API key, or each Entra tenant + object ID), `["ipAddress"]`, or both |

You can attach a token limit to a **model** (applies to every alias that targets it), to an **alias** (only
callers that use that name), or to the **gateway** (a default for every compatible model, including models you
add later). Every applicable policy is checked, and any one of them can block the request.

> [!NOTE]
> The backend deployment has its own capacity, shown as **Token rate limit (TPM)** on the model's details page.
> The gateway limit is how you *share* that capacity fairly. Set per-caller limits so that the sum of your busiest
> callers stays below the deployment's TPM.

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

## Add a token limit to the model

Pick one track. Each track produces the same policy on your model: **1,000 tokens per minute for each caller
identity**. The limit is deliberately low so you can trigger it in a few requests. The IaC track takes a
different route, explained in its first step.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
**Token rate limit**, then **Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step](../assets/screens/policy-add-wizard.png "Policies › Add policy opens a three-step wizard: Type, Scope, Configure.")

### Choose where the limit applies

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select your model, then **Next**.

> [!TIP]
> **Gateway** scope applies the limit to every compatible asset, including models you add later. It's a good
> default for production. You'll try it in [Go further](#go-further).

### Configure the allowance

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Time period** | **Per minute** |
| **Allowed tokens** | `1000` |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Create**. The policy appears in the **Policies** list with your model as its scope.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists a **Token rate limit** for your model with 1,000 tokens per minute and the
> **Caller identity** counter.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set the token limit

Policies live in the model's `properties.policies` array, and a `PATCH` replaces the whole array. So read the
array, swap in the token limit, keep every other policy, and write it back.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:([(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]
      + [{type:"tokenLimit",count:1000,period:"minute",counterKey:["identity"]}])}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$p = (az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies
$p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' }) +
     @(@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; count = 1000; period = 'minute'; counterKey = @('identity') })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

`period` accepts `minute`, `hour`, or `day`. `counterKey` is an array with `identity`, `ipAddress`, or both.

### Confirm the policy

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --query properties.policies -o json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --query properties.policies -o json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The output contains `"type": "tokenLimit"` with `"count": 1000`, `"period": "minute"`,
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and `"scope": "resource"`, which the service adds to every model policy.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current policies

Policies live inline in the model's `properties.policies` array. A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**, so
always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to change.

```bash
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

### Replace the token limit and keep everything else

```bash title="Bash"
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '
  [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]
  + [{"type":"tokenLimit","count":1000,"period":"minute","counterKey":["identity"]}]')"

az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' })
$policies += [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; count = 1000; period = 'minute'; counterKey = @('identity') }

$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json'
Remove-Item patch.json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus one `tokenLimit` entry with
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]` and `"scope": "resource"`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Choose what to declare

A Bicep deployment sends a `PUT`, which replaces the whole resource. Redeclaring a model you imported in the
portal risks dropping settings you didn't copy. Instead, this template **adds a new alias**,
`<model-name>-limited`, that targets the same backend model and carries its own token limit. Existing clients
keep calling the original alias. Callers that you move to the new alias get the allowance.

This is also a common production pattern: one backend model, several aliases, and a different limit for each
audience (for example `gpt-chat` for interactive apps and `gpt-batch` for offline jobs).

### Review the template

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

On GitHub, open [infra/main.bicep](infra/main.bicep).

### Deploy it

```bash title="Bash"
az deployment group create -g "$RG" \
  --template-file infra/main.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" providerName="$PROVIDER" modelName="$MODEL" \
               allowedTokens=1000 period=minute counterKey="['identity']" \
  --query properties.outputs

export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$MODEL-limited"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az deployment group create -g $RG `
  --template-file infra/main.bicep `
  --parameters gatewayName=$GATEWAY providerName=$PROVIDER modelName=$MODEL `
               allowedTokens=1000 period=minute counterKey="['identity']" `
  --query properties.outputs

$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "$MODEL-limited"
```

`counterKey` is an array parameter. Pass `"['ipAddress']"` to count per client IP address, or
`"['identity','ipAddress']"` for both. The single quotes inside the value survive both Bash and PowerShell.

> **Checkpoint**
> In the portal, **Models** shows the `<model-name>-limited` alias, and **Policies** lists a
> **Token rate limit** scoped to it.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

Send a burst of requests that each use about 225 tokens. With a 1,000-token budget, the first few succeed, and
then the gateway starts answering `429`.

<!-- steps -->

### Run the burst

From the lab folder, run the script for your shell. For each request it prints the status, `Retry-After`, the
tokens used, and the backend deployment's own `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` header.

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/trigger-token-limit.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/trigger-token-limit.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 8
```

On GitHub, open [trigger-token-limit.sh](infra/trigger-token-limit.sh) or
[trigger-token-limit.ps1](infra/trigger-token-limit.ps1).

Expected output (your token counts will differ):

```text
Request  Status  Retry-After  Tokens used  Backend tokens left
1        200     -            231          9977
2        200     -            214          9977
3        200     -            220          9977
4        200     -            221          9977
5        200     -            223          9977
6        200     -            229          9977
7        429     1            -            -
8        200     -            222          9977
```

The gateway stops this caller once it passes 1,000 tokens, while the backend deployment still has most of its
capacity left: that's the point of a per-caller limit. `Retry-After` says how many seconds to wait, and a request sent
after that wait can succeed again, as request 8 shows. The gateway doesn't add its own remaining-tokens header, so
watch the status and `Retry-After`.

> [!NOTE]
> The gateway counts a request's tokens after the response, and its counters catch up within a few seconds, so a
> fast burst can go a few hundred tokens past the budget before the first `429`. A new or changed policy can also
> take up to a minute to apply. If every request returns `200`, wait a minute and run the burst again.

### Inspect one throttled response

Look at the full headers and body of a single throttled call:

```bash
curl -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

The status line is `HTTP/1.1 429`, and `Retry-After` tells the client how many seconds to wait. Well-behaved
SDKs, including the OpenAI SDKs, honor `Retry-After` automatically when they retry.

### Prove the counter is per caller

Create a second runtime key in **Access** › **Keys**, set it as `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` in a new terminal, and
run the burst again while the first key is still throttled. The second key starts with a full allowance,
because **Caller identity** gives every key its own counter.

### Find the throttled calls in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring**. The dashboard shows `429` outcomes and policy impact next to token consumption, and the
**Traces** tab shows the policy span that blocked each request.

![The Monitoring overview showing requests, outcomes, and token consumption](../assets/screens/monitoring-overview.png "Monitoring shows throttled requests and token use per model and API key.")

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> You saw `200` responses until the allowance ran out, then `429` with `Retry-After`. A second key wasn't
> affected, and the backend received no calls while the limit was active.

## Go further

- **Set a gateway-wide default.** Add a second **Token rate limit** with **Gateway** scope and a generous
  allowance, such as `100000` per minute. New models get a guardrail the moment you import them, and you keep
  the stricter model or alias limits on top.
- **Add a daily quota.** Combine a per-minute limit (smooths bursts) with a **Per day** limit (caps total use).
  Both are checked on every request.
- **Limit by IP address.** For a public demo with one shared key, use **Caller IP address** so each visitor
  gets their own counter.
- **Budget in dollars instead of tokens.** Token counts don't reflect model prices. To cap spend, continue
  with [Enforce cost budgets](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).

## Clean up

The policy doesn't cost anything, but a 1,000-token limit will throttle real traffic. Remove it, or raise it
to a production value, before you continue.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the policy

Select **Policies**, open the **Token rate limit** you created, and delete it. If you created a second runtime
key for testing, revoke it in **Access** › **Keys**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the policy

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$p = (az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies
$p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

This removes only the token limit and keeps every other policy on the model. To keep a limit for real traffic
instead, run the **Set the token limit** step again with a production `count`, such as `100000`.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the policy

```bash
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]')"
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Delete the limited alias

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/aliases/$MODEL-limited?$API"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az rest --method delete --url "$WS/aliases/$MODEL-limited?$API"
```

Or select the alias in **Models** and delete it in the portal. The backend model and its original alias stay.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, model, and key. The next labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Every request returns `200`, never `429` | The limit is on a different model or alias than the one you call, or the window reset between requests | Check that the request `model` matches an alias of the limited model. Run the burst without pauses. |
| `429` on the very first request | Another token limit with a lower allowance applies, for example a **Gateway** scope policy, or the counter is shared because **Counter dimensions** is empty | Review **Policies** for every limit that covers the model. Pick **Caller identity** for per-caller counters. |
| `403` with `LlmCostQuotaExceeded` | A **Cost limit** blocked the call, not the token limit | See [Enforce cost budgets](../07-cost-budgets/README.md). |
| `429` without a gateway token limit | The backend deployment ran out of TPM | Raise the deployment's capacity in Foundry, or lower per-caller gateway limits so their sum fits. |
| Other policies vanished after the REST call | `PATCH` replaces the whole `policies` array | Always `GET`, merge, then `PATCH`, as shown in the REST track. |
| `ValidationError` with target `counterKey` | `counterKey` is a string such as `"Identity"`, uses another value, or is missing | Send an array with `identity`, `ipAddress`, or both, for example `"counterKey": ["identity"]`. |

- [Enforce cost budgets with per-key overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md): cap spend in dollars per caller.
- [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md): see which callers hit their limits.
- [Publish model aliases across providers](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md): give each audience its own alias and limit.
- Docs: [Policies in AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/policies).

# Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides

Your FinOps team has a problem that token limits can't solve: a thousand tokens on a premium reasoning model
costs many times more than a thousand tokens on a mini model, so "tokens per day" says nothing about the bill.
They want every app to have a **daily budget in dollars**, a bigger envelope for the production support bot,
and a separate allowance for a data science lead who signs in with Microsoft Entra ID. In this lab you set
that up as a cost limit at the gateway, so a caller who runs out of budget is stopped before the model is
called.

![A cost limit can apply to one model or to the whole gateway, with overrides for specific callers](../assets/diagrams/policy-scopes.svg "A cost limit attached to a model budgets spend on that model. Attached at gateway scope, it tracks one budget per caller across all models.")

<!-- widget: budget {"amount":5,"period":"day"} -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md). This lab reuses the
  **Policies** › **Add policy** wizard and the idea of per-caller counters.
- Complete [Issue and rotate runtime API keys](../10-api-keys/README.md). You need **two** runtime keys from
  **Access** › **Keys**, for example `app-dev` (gets the default budget) and `support-bot` (gets an override).
- Recommended: configure Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md)
  and send a few requests first, so **Monitoring** can show estimated spend before you choose a budget.
- Optional, for the Entra override: a user or service principal that can call the gateway with Microsoft
  Entra ID. [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md) shows how.
- For the REST track: the [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later,
  signed in with `az login`, plus `jq` for the Bash snippets.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.

Set these variables once. Both tracks and the **Verify** section reuse them. Use the `app-dev` key here.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export MODEL_URL="$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
# Paste the app-dev runtime key from Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER   = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL      = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$MODEL_URL  = "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
# Paste the app-dev runtime key from Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

## How it works

After each model response, the gateway **estimates its cost** from the tokens the provider reported and the
model's public pricing, broken down by token category. A cost limit adds that estimate to the caller's
counter for the current renewal period. Before it forwards the next request, the gateway checks the counter.
Once spend reaches the budget, the gateway answers `403` with the error code `LlmCostQuotaExceeded` and never
calls the backend. Responses also carry a header with the remaining budget.

| Setting | Portal label | JSON field | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Budget | **Budget amount** | `amount` | US dollars, for example `5` |
| Window | **Renewal period** | `period` | `hour`, `day`, `week`, `month`, `year` (**Hourly** … **Yearly**) |
| Who gets a counter | **Counter dimensions** (shown as **Budget counted by**) | `counterKey` | An array: `["identity"]` (the API key, or the Entra tenant ID + object ID) or `["ipAddress"]` |
| Exceptions | **Overrides** | Portal only | A different amount for an API key or Entra identity |
| Policy identity | Not shown | `id` | Stable ID. Editing the amount keeps accumulated spend. |

Renewal periods are **fixed calendar windows**, not rolling windows: a **Daily** budget starts fresh at the
beginning of each day, not 24 hours after the first call. Attach the policy to a **model** to budget spend on
that model, or at **Gateway** scope to track **one budget per caller across all models**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A cost limit is a guardrail, not an invoice. Spend is estimated from public pricing, and because gateway
> instances update counters concurrently, concurrent requests can briefly **overshoot** the budget before every
> instance sees the latest spend.

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

## Add a cost limit to the model

Pick one track. Both produce the same default budget on your model: **$5 per day for each caller identity**.
Overrides for specific callers are configured in the portal, so the REST track ends there too.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
**Cost limit**, then **Next**.

### Choose where the budget applies

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select your model, then **Next**.

> [!TIP]
> Choose **Gateway** ("Apply to all compatible assets") when the budget should cover **every** model a caller
> uses, including models you import later. A gateway-scoped cost limit tracks one budget across all models
> instead of one per model.

### Set the default budget

On the **Details** step, under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Budget amount** | `5` (US dollars) |
| **Renewal period** | **Daily** |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Next**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Caller identity** gives each API key, and each Entra caller, its own counter. If you select no dimension, every
> caller shares one counter for the policy. **Caller IP address** can't be combined with overrides: the portal asks
> you to remove all overrides or switch to caller identity before saving.

### Give an API key a bigger budget

On the **Overrides** step, under **API keys**, select **Add**. In the new row, pick your `support-bot` key in
**API key** and set **Budget amount** to `50`. Each key can have only one override.

### Give a Microsoft Entra identity its own budget

Under **Microsoft Entra identities**, select **Add**. In **Add Microsoft Entra identities override**, choose how
**Match requests by** works:

- **Specific Microsoft Entra identity**: search for a user by name or email. For a service principal, enter its
  **object ID**, not its application (client) ID.
- **Custom token claim combination**: add one or more **Claim name** and **Value** pairs, for example `appid`
  and the client ID of an internal app. Every claim condition must match the validated token.

Set **Budget amount** to `20`, then select **Add**.

![The Overrides step with one Microsoft Entra identity override and one custom token claims override](../assets/screens/policy-cost-limit-entra-overrides.png "Overrides (optional): API key overrides match a specific key; Microsoft Entra overrides match one identity or a combination of validated token claims. The first matching override wins.")

Overrides are evaluated in the order you add them, and the **first match wins**. A claim combination never
pools callers into a shared budget: with identity counting, each matching identity gets the override amount
on its own counter.

### Create the policy

Select **Create**. Back in **Policies**, open the new **Cost limit** to review it.

![The Cost limit details page showing behavior, configuration, and the assets it applies to](../assets/screens/policy-cost-limit-details.png "The details page explains the trigger and the 403 LlmCostQuotaExceeded response, and lists Budget amount, Renewal period, Budget counted by, and Applies to.")

> **Checkpoint**
> The **Cost limit** details page shows **Budget amount** $5.00, **Renewal period** **Daily**, **Budget
> counted by** **Caller identity**, and your model under **Applies to**. Select **Edit** to see your overrides.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current policies

This track calls the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension
doesn't manage the new `aigateways` resource type yet. Policies live inline in the model's
`properties.policies` array. A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**, so always read it first and keep the
policies you didn't mean to change.

```bash
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

### Add or update the cost limit and keep everything else

A cost limit carries a stable `id`. Editing the amount of an existing policy **keeps its accumulated spend**,
so the merge below updates an existing `costLimit` in place (keeping its `id` and any overrides) and only
creates a new one, with a fresh GUID, when none exists.

```bash title="Bash"
BUDGET=5
PERIOD=day
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c \
  --argjson amount "$BUDGET" --arg period "$PERIOD" --arg id "$(uuidgen | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z')" '
  .properties.policies // [] | . as $p
  | if any($p[]; .type == "costLimit")
    then [$p[] | if .type == "costLimit"
                 then (.amount = $amount | .period = $period | .counterKey = ["identity"])
                 else . end]
    else $p + [{"type":"costLimit","id":$id,"amount":$amount,"period":$period,"counterKey":["identity"]}]
    end')"

az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$BUDGET = 5
$PERIOD = 'day'
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ })
$cost     = $policies | Where-Object { $_.type -eq 'costLimit' } | Select-Object -First 1
if ($cost) {
  $cost | Add-Member -NotePropertyName amount -NotePropertyValue $BUDGET -Force
  $cost | Add-Member -NotePropertyName period -NotePropertyValue $PERIOD -Force
  $cost | Add-Member -NotePropertyName counterKey -NotePropertyValue @('identity') -Force
} else {
  $policies += [pscustomobject]@{
    type = 'costLimit'; id = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString(); amount = $BUDGET; period = $PERIOD; counterKey = @('identity')
  }
}

$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json'
Remove-Item patch.json
```

`period` accepts `hour`, `day`, `week`, `month`, or `year`. `counterKey` is an array: `["identity"]`, or
`["ipAddress"]` to count per client IP address.

### Add overrides in the portal

Configure overrides for API keys and Microsoft Entra identities in the portal: select **Policies**, open the
**Cost limit**, select **Edit**, and use the **Overrides** step as described in the portal track. The merge
above keeps those overrides when you change the amount later.

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus one `costLimit` entry with its `id`,
> `"amount": 5.0`, `"period": "day"`, `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and `"scope": "resource"`.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

A $5 budget takes a while to spend, so temporarily lower it, run a short series of requests with the `app-dev`
key (which has no override), and watch the gateway switch from `200` to `403`.

<!-- steps -->

### Lower the budget for the test

In the portal, open the **Cost limit**, select **Edit**, set **Budget amount** to `0.01`, and **Save**. On the
REST track, run the merge again with `BUDGET=0.01` (PowerShell: `$BUDGET = 0.01`).

If your model is an inexpensive mini or nano model, use `0.001` so a handful of calls is enough. Because
editing keeps accumulated spend, the very first request might already be blocked if `app-dev` spent more than
the new budget earlier today.

### Run the requests

From the lab folder, run the script for your shell. It prints the status, the error code, the tokens used, and
any response header whose name mentions budget, cost, or remaining.

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/trigger-cost-limit.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 10
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/trigger-cost-limit.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 10
```

On GitHub, open [trigger-cost-limit.sh](infra/trigger-cost-limit.sh) or
[trigger-cost-limit.ps1](infra/trigger-cost-limit.ps1).

Expected output (your token counts, the number of successful calls, and the header values will differ):

```text
Request  Status  Error code               Tokens used  Budget headers
1        200     -                        220          …
2        200     -                        225          …
3        200     -                        218          …
4        403     LlmCostQuotaExceeded     -            …
5        403     LlmCostQuotaExceeded     -            …
```

How many calls succeed depends on the model's price. A call or two more than you expect is the small overshoot
described in [How it works](#how-it-works).

### Inspect one blocked response

Look at the full headers and body of a single blocked call:

```bash
curl -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

The status line is `HTTP/1.1 403`, and the body contains `LlmCostQuotaExceeded`. Scan the headers for the one
that reports the remaining budget, and compare it with a successful response from a key that still has budget.
Unlike a token limit, which frees up as the window rolls, the caller stays blocked until the next calendar
renewal period starts or you raise the budget.

### Prove the override and the per-caller counters

Set `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` to the `support-bot` key in a new terminal (repeat the variable block) and run the
script again. Every request succeeds, because that key has its own counter and a $50 override. If you added an
Entra override, call the gateway with that identity's token as shown in
[Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md): it gets its own counter too, keyed
by tenant ID and object ID.

### Review estimated spend in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights, open **Monitoring**. **Estimated model cost** and **Top models** show
the spend the gateway estimated, and the dashboard attributes it to individual API keys and models.

![The Monitoring overview with estimated model cost, model calls, and top models by estimated cost](../assets/screens/monitoring-overview.png "Monitoring estimates model cost from observed tokens and public pricing, and breaks it down by model and API key.")

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `app-dev` got `200` responses until its estimated spend reached the budget, then `403`
> `LlmCostQuotaExceeded`. `support-bot` wasn't affected, and the backend received no calls from `app-dev` while
> it was blocked.

## Go further

- **Cap spend across all models.** Add a second **Cost limit** with **Gateway** scope, for example $200
  **Monthly**. Each caller then has one budget across every model, including models you import later. With
  REST, run the same merge against the gateway workspace:
  `https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default?api-version=2025-09-01-preview`
  (`"${WS}?$API"` from the variable block).
- **Combine with token limits.** Keep a per-minute **Token rate limit** to smooth bursts and a **Cost limit**
  to cap spend. Both are checked on every request, and either one can block.
- **Budget by role or app.** Use **Custom token claim combination** overrides, for example a `roles` claim with
  an app role value, so everyone with that role gets a different per-identity amount.
- **Chargeback by team.** Export `tid`, `oid`, or a custom claim to cost metrics in
  [Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry](../14-otel-chargeback/README.md).

## Clean up

A $0.01 budget blocks real traffic. Delete the policy, or raise it to a production value, before you continue.
Raising the amount takes effect immediately, because the accumulated spend is kept and compared with the new
budget.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove or raise the budget

Select **Policies**, open the **Cost limit** you created, and select **Delete**, or select **Edit** and set a
production **Budget amount**. If you created runtime keys only for this lab, revoke them in **Access** › **Keys**.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the cost limit

```bash
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "costLimit")]')"
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

To keep the policy instead, run the merge again with a production budget, for example `BUDGET=100`.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, model, and keys. The next labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Every request returns `200`, never `403` | The cost limit is on a different model than the alias you call, your key has an override, or the model is so cheap that the calls haven't reached the budget | Check **Applies to** on the policy details page, use a key without an override, and lower the budget to `0.001` or send more requests. |
| `403` `LlmCostQuotaExceeded` on the first request | The key already spent more than the new amount in this period (spend is kept when you edit), or a **Gateway** scope cost limit is exhausted | Review every **Cost limit** in **Policies**. Raise the amount, or wait for the next renewal period. |
| An Entra override doesn't apply | An earlier override matched first, the caller used an API key, or you entered a service principal's application ID | Remove the earlier override and add them again in the order you want. Call with an Entra token. Use the service principal's **object ID**. |
| **Caller IP address** can't be selected in **Counter dimensions** | The policy has overrides | Remove all overrides, or keep **Caller identity**. |
| `429` instead of `403` | A **Token rate limit** or **Request rate limit** blocked the call, or the backend ran out of capacity | See [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md). |
| Other policies vanished after the REST call | `PATCH` replaces the whole `policies` array | Always `GET`, merge, then `PATCH`, as shown in the REST track. |
| `ValidationError` with target `counterKey` | `counterKey` is a string such as `"Identity"`, or it's missing | Send an array, for example `"counterKey": ["identity"]`. A cost limit always needs `counterKey`. |

## Next steps

- [Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md): combine gateway-scoped budgets with other guardrails.
- [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md): see estimated spend by API key and model.
- [Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry](../14-otel-chargeback/README.md): build chargeback reports by team or identity.
- Docs: [Policies in AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/policies).

# Screen prompts and responses with content safety

Your gateway now serves a customer-facing assistant and several internal agents, on models from more than one
provider. Your responsible AI review asks for one consistent rule: every prompt and every response is screened
for harmful content, whichever model or tool handles it. In this lab you add a **content safety** policy at the
gateway, tune it per category, and see what a blocked call looks like to a client.

![The request lifecycle through authentication, policies, the backend, and telemetry](../assets/diagrams/request-lifecycle.svg "Content safety is one of the policies that the gateway evaluates on every request. When it blocks a call, the client gets 400.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle {"focus":"contentSafety"} -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need a
  gateway, an imported model, a callable alias, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- For the CLI and REST tracks: the [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75
  or later, signed in with `az login`, plus `jq` for the Bash snippets. The CLI track calls the Azure Resource
  Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't manage the new `aigateways`
  resource type yet.
- For the **Verify** script: `curl` and `jq` (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export MODEL_URL="$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER   = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL      = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$MODEL_URL  = "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

## How it works

A content safety policy screens prompts, tool inputs, and responses with Azure AI Content Safety. It rates
content in four categories: **Hate**, **Self-harm**, **Sexual**, and **Violence**. You set a severity threshold
for each category independently. When content reaches the threshold, the gateway blocks the call and returns
`400`. A blocked prompt never reaches the backend.

The threshold is the lowest severity that gets blocked, so a **lower** threshold blocks **more**:

| Portal label | CLI and REST value | What it blocks |
|---|---|---|
| **Strict** | `Low` | The most content: low, medium, and high severity |
| **Balanced** (default) | `Medium` | Medium and high severity |
| **Lenient** | `High` | Only the most concerning, high-severity content |
| **Off** | `None` | Nothing in this category |

You can attach content safety to **models** and **MCP servers**. On an MCP server, it screens the tool inputs
that agents send and the results that tools return. Every applicable policy is evaluated, and any one of them
can block the call.

> [!NOTE]
> Foundry deployments have their own **Content filter**, shown on the model's details page in **Models**. That
> filter runs inside Foundry, for that one deployment. The gateway policy runs before the backend, applies the
> same rules to models from any provider and to MCP tool traffic, and is managed by the platform team in one
> place. Keep both: a request has to pass each of them.

## Add content safety to the model

Pick one track. Each track produces the same policy on your model: **Balanced** (`Medium`) for Hate,
Self-harm, and Sexual, and **Strict** (`Low`) for Violence. The stricter Violence threshold makes the test in
**Verify** more likely to show a block, using only a mild, non-graphic prompt.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Security**, select **Content safety**, then
**Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step](../assets/screens/policy-add-wizard.png "Policies › Add policy opens a three-step wizard: Type, Scope, Details.")

### Choose the model

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select your model, then **Next**.

### Set the thresholds

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, choose how strictly
each category is filtered:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Hate** | **Balanced** |
| **Violence** | **Strict** |
| **Self-harm** | **Balanced** |
| **Sexual** | **Balanced** |

Select **Create**. The policy appears in the **Policies** list with your model as its scope.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists a **Content safety** policy for your model.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set the policy

Policies live in the model's `properties.policies` array, and a `PATCH` replaces the whole array. So read the
array, swap in the content safety policy, keep every other policy, and write it back.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:([(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "contentSafety")]
      + [{type:"contentSafety",hateSeverity:"Medium",selfHarmSeverity:"Medium",sexualSeverity:"Medium",violenceSeverity:"Low"}])}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$p = (az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies
$p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'contentSafety' }) +
     @(@{ type = 'contentSafety'; hateSeverity = 'Medium'; selfHarmSeverity = 'Medium'; sexualSeverity = 'Medium'; violenceSeverity = 'Low' })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

Each of `hateSeverity`, `selfHarmSeverity`, `sexualSeverity`, and `violenceSeverity` accepts `None`, `Low`,
`Medium`, or `High`. Set all four explicitly.

### Confirm the policy

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --query properties.policies -o json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --query properties.policies -o json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The output contains `"type": "contentSafety"` with `"violenceSeverity": "Low"`, `"Medium"` for the other
> three categories, and `"scope": "resource"`, which the service adds to every model policy.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current policies

Policies live inline in the model's `properties.policies` array. A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**, so
always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to change.

```bash
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

### Replace the content safety policy and keep everything else

```bash title="Bash"
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '
  [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "contentSafety")]
  + [{"type":"contentSafety","hateSeverity":"Medium","violenceSeverity":"Low","sexualSeverity":"Medium","selfHarmSeverity":"Medium"}]')"

az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'contentSafety' })
$policies += [pscustomobject]@{
  type = 'contentSafety'; hateSeverity = 'Medium'; violenceSeverity = 'Low'; sexualSeverity = 'Medium'; selfHarmSeverity = 'Medium'
}

$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json'
Remove-Item patch.json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus one `contentSafety` entry with
> `"violenceSeverity": "Low"` and `"scope": "resource"`.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

Test the policy with **benign prompts only**. You don't need harmful content to see how the gateway behaves,
and you should never write it to test a filter.

<!-- steps -->

### Run the test prompts

From the lab folder, run the script for your shell. It sends two prompts: a neutral question, and a request
for a short, non-graphic scene from a historical novel. It prints the status and the start of the response or
the error for each one.

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/test-content-safety.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/test-content-safety.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
```

On GitHub, open [test-content-safety.sh](infra/test-content-safety.sh) or
[test-content-safety.ps1](infra/test-content-safety.ps1).

Example output:

```text
Prompt    Status  Finish reason   Response or error
neutral   200     stop            Teams put an API gateway in front of AI models to centralize access con
fiction   400     -               <the gateway's content safety error message>
```

The neutral prompt returns `200`. The fiction prompt can go either way, and your results will vary: Content
Safety rates both the prompt and the model's response, and a mild battle scene sits close to the **Strict**
Violence threshold. If it returns `400`, the gateway blocked it and the error message says why. If it returns
`200`, the content was rated below the threshold.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> If the fiction prompt passes, don't make it more graphic to force a block. The point of this test is to
> understand thresholds with safe input, not to probe the filter. Use **Monitoring** and real, representative
> traffic in a test environment to tune thresholds.

### Relax one category

Set **Violence** back to **Balanced** (`Medium`) with the track you used, then run the script again. For
example, with the CLI, change only `violenceSeverity` and keep everything else:

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:[(.properties.policies // [])[]
      | if .type == "contentSafety" then .violenceSeverity = "Medium" else . end]}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$p = @((az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ })
$p | Where-Object type -eq 'contentSafety' | ForEach-Object { $_.violenceSeverity = 'Medium' }
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

A prompt that **Strict** blocked is more likely to pass at **Balanced**. Prompts that passed before still pass.

### Check the Foundry content filter

Open **Models**, select your model, and find **Content filter** on its details page. That is the Foundry
deployment's own filter, separate from the gateway policy. When Foundry's filter acts instead of the gateway,
the error or the `finish_reason` comes from the backend, and it can mention `content_filter`.

### Find blocked calls in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring** and look for `400` outcomes on your model. Review them before and after every threshold change.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The neutral prompt returned `200`, you saw how the borderline prompt fared at **Strict** and at **Balanced**,
> and you can tell a gateway block (`400` from the content safety policy) from a Foundry content filter result.

## Go further

- **Screen tool traffic.** Add a **Content safety** policy to the `learn` MCP server from
  [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). In the wizard, pick the MCP
  server on the **Scope** step. With REST, use the same `contentSafety` object on
  `.../workspaces/default/toolServers/learn`.
- **Make it the default.** Apply **Balanced** content safety to every model and MCP server, including future
  ones, in [Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md).
- **Tune per category.** Start every category at **Balanced**, tighten the ones that matter most for your
  audience, and turn a category **Off** only with a documented exception.

## Clean up

A **Strict** threshold can block legitimate traffic. Remove the model policy before you continue. The next
lab sets a gateway-wide baseline instead.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the policy

Select **Policies**, open the **Content safety** policy that's scoped to your model, and delete it.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the policy

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "contentSafety")]}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$p = (az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies
$p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'contentSafety' })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

This removes only the content safety policy and keeps every other policy on the model.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the policy

```bash
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "contentSafety")]')"
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, model, and key. The next labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary prompts return `400` | A threshold is too strict for your traffic, or another content safety policy, such as a **Gateway** scope policy, also applies | Review **Policies** for every content safety policy that covers the model. Move categories from **Strict** to **Balanced** and retest with representative prompts. |
| Nothing is ever blocked | The policy is on a different model or alias than the one you call, or a category is **Off** | Check the policy's scope and that the request `model` matches an alias of that model. |
| `400` that mentions `content_filter`, or `finish_reason` is `content_filter` | The Foundry deployment's **Content filter** acted, not the gateway | Review the deployment's content filter in Foundry. The gateway policy is managed separately. |
| `400` that isn't about content | The request itself is invalid, for example an unknown model alias | Read the error message, and check the request body and the alias. |
| `ValidationError` such as `contentSafety.violenceSeverity must be one of: Low, Medium, High, None.` | A severity uses a portal label such as `Strict` or `Balanced` | Use the API values from the table in [How it works](#how-it-works): `Low`, `Medium`, `High`, or `None`. |
| Other policies vanished after the `PATCH` | `PATCH` replaces the whole `policies` array | Always `GET`, merge, then `PATCH`, as shown in the CLI and REST tracks. |

  every model and MCP server.
- [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md): limit which tools agents can reach.
- [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md): find `400` outcomes and the policy that caused them.
- Docs: [Policies in AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/policies).
