# Set gateway-wide policy baselines

Your gateway now serves several models and MCP servers, and teams add new ones every week. Some assets have
carefully tuned policies, and some have none at all. The platform and security teams agree on a baseline that
every asset gets by default: a generous token limit, a request rate limit, **Balanced** content safety, and
runtime access only from approved networks. In this lab you apply that baseline once, at **Gateway** scope,
and keep tighter asset policies on top of it.

![Policies at gateway scope and on models, aliases, MCP servers, and future assets](../assets/diagrams/policy-scopes.svg "A Gateway scope policy covers every compatible asset, including assets added later. Asset policies add narrower rules on top.")

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md) and
  [Screen prompts and responses with content safety](../08-content-safety/README.md), including their
  **Clean up** sections. You need a gateway, an imported model, a callable alias, and a runtime API key from
  **Access** › **Keys**.
- The [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with
  `az login`, plus `jq` (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later. The REST and Policy as code tracks and **Verify** call
  the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't manage the new
  `aigateways` resource type yet.
- For **Verify**: `curl` (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.
- The public IP addresses or CIDR ranges your callers use. Once the IP filter is on, calls from anywhere else get
  `403`.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export MODEL_URL="$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo

# The public IP address this machine uses on the internet, and the ranges the IP filter allows.
export MY_IP="$(curl -s https://api.ipify.org)" && echo "$MY_IP"
export ALLOWED_CIDRS="$MY_IP/32"           # comma-separated, for example "$MY_IP/32,198.51.100.0/24"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER   = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL      = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$MODEL_URL  = "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput

# The public IP address this machine uses on the internet, and the ranges the IP filter allows.
$env:MY_IP = Invoke-RestMethod https://api.ipify.org; $env:MY_IP
$env:ALLOWED_CIDRS = "$($env:MY_IP)/32"    # comma-separated, for example "$($env:MY_IP)/32,198.51.100.0/24"
```

## How it works

A policy with **Gateway** scope is stored on the gateway's `default` workspace instead of on one asset. It
applies to every compatible model, alias, and MCP server, including assets you add later, without another
policy update. Asset policies keep working alongside it. The gateway evaluates every applicable policy before
it forwards a request, and if any one of them blocks, the client gets an error and the backend is never
called. So an asset policy can make the rules **tighter** for one asset, but it can't loosen the baseline.

This lab's baseline:

| Policy | Applies to | Baseline value | Blocked calls get |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Token rate limit** | Models | 100,000 tokens per minute, per caller identity | `429` with `Retry-After` |
| **Request rate limit** | Models and MCP servers | 600 calls per 60 seconds, per caller identity | `429` with `Retry-After` |
| **Content safety** | Models and MCP servers | **Balanced** (`Medium`) for all four categories | `400` |
| **IP filter** | Models and MCP servers | **Allow listed IPs only**: your CIDR ranges | `403` |

A Gateway scope **Cost limit** is one budget across all models; you can add it in
[Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md). Agent 365 tool threat
protection can't be set at Gateway scope; it applies to individual MCP servers.

> [!WARNING]
> The IP filter applies to **runtime** calls. You keep managing the gateway in the portal and with `az rest`,
> so you can always fix the list. But every caller outside it gets `403`: teammates, CI pipelines, hosted
> agents, and your own machine when you switch networks or VPN. Remove it in [Clean up](#clean-up).

## Apply the baseline

Pick one track. Each track creates the same four policies at **Gateway** scope. Both scripted tracks use
`az rest` against the gateway's `default` workspace.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add the token rate limit

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, select **Token rate limit**, then **Next**.

On the **Scope** step, select **Gateway** ("Apply to the entire gateway workspace, including applicable assets
added later."), then **Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Scope step with Gateway selected](../assets/screens/policy-gateway-scope.png "On the Scope step, Gateway applies the policy to every compatible asset, including assets added later.")

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Time period** | **Per minute** |
| **Allowed tokens** | `100000` |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Create**.

### Add the request rate limit

Select **Add policy** again. Select **Request rate limit**, then **Gateway** scope, and set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Calls** | `600` |
| **Renewal period** | **60 seconds** |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Create**.

### Add content safety

Select **Add policy**. Under **Security**, select **Content safety**, then **Gateway** scope. Set **Hate**,
**Violence**, **Self-harm**, and **Sexual** to **Balanced**, then select **Create**.

### Add the IP filter

Select **Add policy**. Under **Security**, select **IP filter**, then **Gateway** scope, and set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Action** | **Allow listed IPs only** |
| **IP addresses / CIDR ranges** | Your `ALLOWED_CIDRS` value, for example `198.51.100.7/32` |

Use CIDR notation for every entry: `/32` for a single IPv4 address. Check the value against `echo "$MY_IP"`
before you select **Create**.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists four policies whose scope is **Gateway**: **Token rate limit**, **Request rate limit**,
> **Content safety**, and **IP filter**.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the Gateway scope policies

Gateway scope policies live inline in the `properties.policies` array of the gateway's `default` workspace.
A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**, so always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to
change.

```bash title="Bash"
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"

az rest --method get --url $URL --query properties.policies
```

### Merge the baseline and keep everything else

The baseline replaces any existing policy of the same four types and keeps every other entry, such as a
Gateway scope cost limit.

```bash title="Bash"
BASELINE="$(jq -cn --arg cidrs "$ALLOWED_CIDRS" '[
  {"type":"tokenLimit","count":100000,"period":"minute","counterKey":["identity"],"scope":"workspace"},
  {"type":"requestRateLimit","callsPerPeriod":600,"periodSeconds":60,"counterKey":["identity"],"scope":"workspace"},
  {"type":"contentSafety","hateSeverity":"Medium","violenceSeverity":"Medium","sexualSeverity":"Medium","selfHarmSeverity":"Medium"},
  {"type":"ipFilter","action":"Allow","cidrRanges":($cidrs | split(",") | map(gsub("\\s"; "")) | map(select(length > 0)))}
]')"
jq '.[] | select(.type == "ipFilter")' <<<"$BASELINE"    # check the allowed ranges before you apply

POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c --argjson baseline "$BASELINE" '
  [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type | IN($baseline[].type) | not)] + $baseline')"

az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$baseline = @(
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; count = 100000; period = 'minute'; counterKey = @('identity'); scope = 'workspace' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'requestRateLimit'; callsPerPeriod = 600; periodSeconds = 60; counterKey = @('identity'); scope = 'workspace' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'contentSafety'; hateSeverity = 'Medium'; violenceSeverity = 'Medium'; sexualSeverity = 'Medium'; selfHarmSeverity = 'Medium' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'ipFilter'; action = 'Allow'; cidrRanges = @($env:ALLOWED_CIDRS -split ',' | ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } | Where-Object { $_ }) }
)
$baseline | Where-Object type -eq 'ipFilter' | ConvertTo-Json    # check the allowed ranges before you apply

$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -notin $baseline.type })
$policies += $baseline

$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json'
Remove-Item patch.json
```

> [!NOTE]
> When you create a token or request rate limit at **Gateway** scope, the portal writes `"scope": "workspace"`
> into the policy object. The REST and Policy as code tracks include the same field so that every track creates
> the same policy. `counterKey` is an array: `["identity"]` gives each API key or Entra caller its own counter.
> If the API rejects a field, create the policy once in the portal, then copy its shape from the `GET` response.

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus `tokenLimit` and `requestRateLimit` entries
> with `"counterKey": ["identity"]` and `"scope": "workspace"`, and `contentSafety` and `ipFilter` entries
> with your ranges in `cidrRanges`. The service adds `"scope": "resource"` to the last two.

<!-- track: iac | Policy as code -->

### Choose what to declare

Gateway scope policies live on the gateway's `default` workspace. The sample Bicep templates only reference
that workspace as `existing`. Declaring it in your own template would send a `PUT` that replaces the whole
workspace resource, including settings that the template doesn't list. Instead, keep the baseline in a policy
file that goes through code review, and apply it with a script that does the same `GET`, merge, and `PATCH` as
the REST track.

### Review the policy file

<!-- include: infra/baseline-policies.json -->

On GitHub, open [infra/baseline-policies.json](infra/baseline-policies.json).

The `ipFilter` entry holds a placeholder from the `203.0.113.0/24` documentation range. The script never applies
it: it replaces `cidrRanges` with your `ALLOWED_CIDRS` value and stops if that value is missing or isn't in CIDR
notation.

### Preview the change

From the lab folder, print the merged policy array without changing anything:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/apply-baseline.sh --dry-run
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -DryRun
```

The PowerShell script reads `$env:ALLOWED_CIDRS` unless you pass `-AllowedCidrs`.

### Apply it

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/apply-baseline.sh
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY
```

<!-- include: infra/apply-baseline.sh -->

On GitHub, open [infra/apply-baseline.sh](infra/apply-baseline.sh) or
[infra/apply-baseline.ps1](infra/apply-baseline.ps1).

> [!TIP]
> Run the script from a pipeline with an identity that can change the gateway, and change the baseline only
> through pull requests to `baseline-policies.json`. Post the `--dry-run` output in the pull request so
> reviewers see the exact policy array before it's applied.

> **Checkpoint**
> The script prints four Gateway scope policies (`tokenLimit`, `requestRateLimit`, `contentSafety`, and
> `ipFilter`) plus any other policies you already had.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

Check that the baseline covers your model and MCP servers, that your own calls still pass, and that a tighter
asset policy still takes effect on top of it.

<!-- steps -->

### Review the baseline in the portal

Select **Policies**. The four baseline policies show **Gateway** in the **Scope** column. Policies you add to
a model, alias, or MCP server show that asset instead.

### Call the model from your IP address

From the lab folder, send one chat completion:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/check-call.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/check-call.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
```

On GitHub, open [check-call.sh](infra/check-call.sh) or [check-call.ps1](infra/check-call.ps1).

Expected output:

```text
Status: 200
Reply:  A gateway-wide policy baseline is a default set of rules that applies to every asset ...
```

Your call passed all four baseline policies: your IP address is on the allow list, you're far below both rate
limits, and the prompt is benign. If you completed
[Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md), run
`../04-federate-mcp-tools/infra/list-tools.sh learn` (PowerShell:
`../04-federate-mcp-tools/infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn`). The MCP server is covered by the same IP
filter, request rate limit, and content safety policies, and it still lists its tools.

### Layer a stricter model policy

Add a deliberately low token limit to your model only, the same one you used in lab 06. A model `PATCH`
replaces the model's whole `policies` array, so merge it with what's there:

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:([(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]
      + [{type:"tokenLimit",count:1000,period:"minute",counterKey:["identity"]}])}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$p = (az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies
$p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' }) +
     @(@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; count = 1000; period = 'minute'; counterKey = @('identity') })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

Then send a burst with the script from lab 06:

```bash title="Bash"
../06-token-limits/infra/trigger-token-limit.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
../06-token-limits/infra/trigger-token-limit.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 8
```

After three or four requests, the gateway returns `429`. The baseline allows 100,000 tokens per minute, but the
model's tighter limit is evaluated too, and it blocks. Remove the model limit and run the burst again:

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$p = (az rest --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies
$p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$MODEL_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

All eight requests now return `200`, because only the generous baseline applies.

### See the IP filter block a call (optional)

Point the allow list at a documentation address that can't be yours, call the model, then restore your range.

- **Portal:** in **Policies**, select **Edit** on the **IP filter** policy, set the ranges to
  `203.0.113.10/32`, and save.
- **Script (Bash):** `ALLOWED_CIDRS="203.0.113.10/32" ./infra/apply-baseline.sh`
- **Script (PowerShell):** `./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -AllowedCidrs "203.0.113.10/32"`

Run `check-call` again. It now returns `Status: 403`, and the request never reaches the model. Restore your
range in the portal, or run the script again without the override (`./infra/apply-baseline.sh`, or the
PowerShell script without `-AllowedCidrs`), and check that `check-call` returns `200`. If you still see the old
result, wait a minute and retry.

### Watch outcomes in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring** and compare `400`, `403`, and `429` outcomes before and after the baseline. A sudden rise in
`403` usually means a caller's network isn't on the allow list.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** shows four **Gateway** scope policies. Your own call returned `200`, a stricter model limit
> still returned `429` on top of the baseline, and you know how a blocked IP address looks (`403`).

## Go further

- **Cap spend gateway-wide.** Add a **Cost limit** with **Gateway** scope for one budget across all models, as
  described in [Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).
- **Tighten tool traffic.** Keep the baseline and add stricter controls to individual MCP servers in
  [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md) and
  [Protect tool calls with Agent 365 threat protection](../19-tool-threat-protection/README.md).
- **Keep the allow list for inbound traffic.** Inbound private endpoints and turning off public network access
  aren't available for AI Gateway yet, so the IP filter is how you restrict who can call the gateway. To keep
  the gateway's traffic to your backends private, see
  [Lock down backend traffic with private networking](../18-private-networking/README.md).
- **Count Entra callers.** With `identity` counters, each Entra caller gets its own allowance. Move clients to
  keyless calls in [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).

## Clean up

Remove the baseline before you continue, especially the IP filter: later labs call the gateway from hosted
agents and other networks, which would get `403`. In your own environment, you can keep the other three
policies and replace the IP filter with your organization's egress ranges.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the baseline

Select **Policies**. For each of the four policies with **Gateway** scope, select **Delete**. Remove the
**IP filter** first.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the baseline

```bash
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[]
  | select(.type | IN("tokenLimit","requestRateLimit","contentSafety","ipFilter") | not)]')"
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}"
```

Every other Gateway scope policy stays.

<!-- track: iac | Policy as code -->

### Remove the baseline

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/apply-baseline.sh --remove
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -Remove
```

The script removes the policy types listed in `baseline-policies.json` and keeps every other Gateway scope
policy.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, model, and key. The next labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Every call returns `403` | Your public IP address changed (new network, VPN, or hotspot), or your network reaches the gateway from a different address than the one `api.ipify.org` reported | Check `curl -s https://api.ipify.org` again and update the IP filter. If you use a proxy or split-tunnel VPN, ask your network team for the egress ranges. Management calls still work, so you can always fix the list. |
| Teammates, pipelines, or hosted agents get `403` | Their egress addresses aren't on the allow list | Add their CIDR ranges, or remove the IP filter until you know them. |
| Ordinary prompts return `400` | Content safety blocked them, from the baseline or from a stricter asset policy | Review every **Content safety** policy that covers the asset in **Policies**, and retest with representative prompts. |
| `429` much earlier than the baseline allows | A tighter token or request rate limit on the model, alias, or MCP server applies | Review **Policies** for every limit that covers the asset. The lowest applicable limit wins. |
| The `PATCH` returns a validation error about `counterKey` or `scope` | `counterKey` is a string such as `"Identity"` instead of an array, or the shape differs from what the API version expects | Use `"counterKey": ["identity"]`. If it still fails, create that policy once in the portal at **Gateway** scope, read the shape with the `GET`, and use it in your script or policy file. |
| `Set ALLOWED_CIDRS ...` or `Use CIDR notation ...` from the script | `ALLOWED_CIDRS` is empty, or an entry has no prefix length | Set it to comma-separated CIDR ranges, for example `"$MY_IP/32"`. |
| Other Gateway scope policies vanished after the REST call | `PATCH` replaces the whole `policies` array | Always `GET`, merge, then `PATCH`, as shown in the REST track and the script. |
| `jq: command not found` | `jq` isn't installed | Install `jq`, or use the PowerShell commands. |

  baseline.
- [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md): track `400`, `403`, and `429` outcomes per
  policy.
- [Lock down backend traffic with private networking](../18-private-networking/README.md): route the gateway's
  backend traffic through your virtual network.
- Docs: [Policies in AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/policies).

# Issue and rotate runtime API keys

Three callers now use your gateway: the `app-dev` web app, the `support-bot` agent, and a data scientist's
notebook that was shared with the whole company, key included. In this lab you give each caller its own runtime
API key, keep the values in a secret store, rotate the bot's key without taking it offline, and revoke the
leaked notebook key. Because every key is a separate caller identity, you can also see who used what.

![Callers reach the gateway with an API key or a Microsoft Entra token, and the gateway reaches providers with its own credentials](../assets/diagrams/identity-boundaries.svg "Inbound, apps send an api-key header or a Microsoft Entra token. Outbound, the gateway uses its managed identity or a provider key that it stores. Callers never receive backend credentials.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle {"focus":"auth"} -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md). You need the gateway, its resource
  group, and its runtime URL.
- Recommended: complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md),
  so you have a model alias to call. The checks in this lab call that alias. The gateway answers `404` for an
  alias it doesn't know before it checks the key, so without a real alias the checks can't tell accepted keys
  from rejected keys.
- Permission to manage the gateway's keys, for example **Contributor** on its resource group. Reading a key
  value needs `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/apiKeys/listSecrets/action`, which **Contributor** includes.
- Optional: an Azure Key Vault that uses Azure RBAC, where you have **Key Vault Secrets Officer**. You can create
  one below.
- Optional, for usage and cost per key: monitoring configured in
  [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md).
- For the CLI track and the **Verify** scripts: the
  [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with `az login`.
  The CLI track calls the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension
  doesn't manage the new `aigateways` resource type yet. The Bash scripts use `curl`; the PowerShell scripts need
  PowerShell 7 or later.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-alias>"      # an alias you can call, for example the one from lab 02
# export KEY_VAULT="<key-vault>"             # optional: uncomment to keep key values in Key Vault

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG                   = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY              = "<gateway>"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-alias>"      # an alias you can call, for example the one from lab 02
# $KEY_VAULT          = "<key-vault>"        # optional: uncomment to keep key values in Key Vault

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
```

<details>
<summary>No Key Vault yet? Create one for this lab.</summary>

Key Vault names are globally unique, 3 to 24 characters. The vault uses Azure RBAC, and you get
**Key Vault Secrets Officer** so you can write and read secrets. A new role assignment can take a few minutes to
apply.

```bash title="Bash"
export KEY_VAULT="kv-aigw-$RANDOM"
az keyvault create -g "$RG" -n "$KEY_VAULT" --enable-rbac-authorization true -o none
az role assignment create --role "Key Vault Secrets Officer" \
  --assignee "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" \
  --scope "$(az keyvault show -n "$KEY_VAULT" --query id -o tsv)" -o none
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$KEY_VAULT = "kv-aigw-$(Get-Random -Maximum 99999)"
az keyvault create -g $RG -n $KEY_VAULT --enable-rbac-authorization true -o none
az role assignment create --role "Key Vault Secrets Officer" `
  --assignee (az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv) `
  --scope (az keyvault show -n $KEY_VAULT --query id -o tsv) -o none
```

</details>

## How it works

A runtime API key is a gateway resource with a name and two values, **primary** and **secondary**.
Both values work at the same time, which is what makes rotation without downtime possible. Clients send either
value in the `api-key` header. The model endpoint also accepts it as a bearer token, which is how OpenAI SDKs
send their API key, but a request with both headers gets `400`. The gateway validates the key before it applies
policies or forwards the request, so a missing, wrong, rotated, or deleted value, or a suspended key, gets
`401 Unauthorized` and never reaches a model.

A key is gateway-scoped: it grants access to every published model and MCP server on the gateway. Each key is
also a separate caller identity, which token limits, cost limits, and Monitoring use to tell callers apart.
That's why every app, agent, or user should get its own key.

| Task | Portal (**Access** › **Keys**) | Azure CLI (`az rest` on `$GW/apiKeys/<name>`) |
|---|---|---|
| Create a key | **Create API key** | `PUT` |
| Read a value | **View keys** (primary value) | `POST .../listSecrets` (primary and secondary values) |
| Rotate | **Rotate key** (primary value) | `POST .../regeneratePrimaryKey` or `.../regenerateSecondaryKey` |
| Block temporarily | — | `PATCH` with `state` set to `suspended`, then back to `active` |
| Revoke | **Delete** | `DELETE` |

The gateway also has a built-in key named `master`. Don't hand it out; create named keys instead.

## Create a key for each app

Create three keys: `app-dev` for the web app, `support-bot` for the agent, and `old-notebook`, which stands in
for the key that leaked. Pick one track.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Create the first key

1. In the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), open your gateway and select **Access** › **Keys**.
2. Select **Create API key**.
3. In **Key name**, enter `app-dev`, and select **Create**.
4. The **API key created successfully** dialog shows the value. Select **Copy & done**.

Store the value right away; the next section shows where. After you close the dialog, only people with the
`apiKeys/listSecrets/action` permission, such as Contributors, can display the value again, with **View keys**.

### Create the other two keys

Repeat the steps for `support-bot` and `old-notebook`. Names must be unique, ignoring case; a duplicate gets
`A key named "..." already exists.` The portal derives the key's resource name from **Key name**: lowercase, with
every character other than letters, digits, and hyphens replaced by `-`. Use that resource name with the CLI.

### Load a value in your shell

Select the **…** (**More actions**) button on the `app-dev` row, select **View keys**, and copy the value. Paste it
into your shell for the checks in this lab:

```bash title="Bash"
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the keys

The key's name is the last segment of its URL, and the body can be empty. The service sets the key's display
name itself, so identify keys by `name`.

```bash title="Bash"
for KEY in app-dev support-bot old-notebook; do
  az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/$KEY?$API" --body '{"properties":{}}' -o none
done
az rest --url "$GW/apiKeys?$API" --query "value[].{name:name, state:properties.state}" -o table
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
'{"properties":{}}' | Set-Content apikey.json
foreach ($key in "app-dev", "support-bot", "old-notebook") {
  az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/$key`?$API" --body "@apikey.json" -o none
}
Remove-Item apikey.json
az rest --url "$GW/apiKeys?$API" --query "value[].{name:name, state:properties.state}" -o table
```

The list also shows the built-in `master` key, and every key is `active`. `PUT` and `GET` never return key
values.

### Load a value in your shell

The `listSecrets` action returns `primaryKey` and `secondaryKey`. Capture the value in a variable instead of
printing it:

```bash title="Bash"
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-dev/listSecrets?$API" \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-dev/listSecrets?$API" `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
```

<!-- /tracks -->

From the lab folder, send one request with the `app-dev` key:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/check-key.sh app-dev
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/check-key.ps1 -Label app-dev
```

The script sends a tiny Chat Completions request and prints only the last four characters of the key. On GitHub,
open [check-key.sh](infra/check-key.sh) or [check-key.ps1](infra/check-key.ps1).

<!-- include: infra/check-key.sh -->

> **Checkpoint**
> **Access** › **Keys** lists `app-dev`, `support-bot`, and `old-notebook`, and the check prints
> `HTTP 200  accepted` for `app-dev`.

## Store the key outside your code

A runtime key opens every model and MCP server on the gateway, so treat it like a password:

- **Local development:** set an environment variable for the session, as in this lab, and read it in code, for
  example `os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"]` in Python. If you keep it in a `.env` file, add the file to
  `.gitignore`.
- **Hosted apps:** keep the value in Azure Key Vault. App Service and Azure Functions resolve
  [Key Vault references](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/app-service-key-vault-references) in app
  settings, and Azure Container Apps can
  [reference Key Vault secrets](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/manage-secrets).
- **Pipelines:** use the secret store of your CI system, or read the value from Key Vault at run time.
- **Never** put the value in source code, a committed `.env` file, build logs, notebooks, chat, or tickets.

If you set `KEY_VAULT`, store the `app-dev` and `support-bot` values there. The commands print only the secret
IDs. Each secret is named `<key>-api-key`, which is the name the rotation script updates later.

```bash title="Bash"
for KEY in app-dev support-bot; do
  az keyvault secret set --vault-name "$KEY_VAULT" -n "$KEY-api-key" \
    --value "$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/$KEY/listSecrets?$API" --query primaryKey -o tsv)" \
    --tags aigateway-key="$KEY" key-type=primary --query id -o tsv
done
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
foreach ($key in "app-dev", "support-bot") {
  $value = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/$key/listSecrets?$API" --query primaryKey -o tsv
  az keyvault secret set --vault-name $KEY_VAULT -n "$key-api-key" --value $value `
    --tags aigateway-key=$key key-type=primary --query id -o tsv
}
Remove-Variable value
```

An app, or you, then reads the value from the vault instead of from the gateway:

```bash title="Bash"
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az keyvault secret show --vault-name "$KEY_VAULT" -n app-dev-api-key --query value -o tsv)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az keyvault secret show --vault-name $KEY_VAULT -n app-dev-api-key --query value -o tsv
```

> [!NOTE]
> The portal track can store the values the same way: run the commands above, or add the secrets to the vault in
> the Azure portal.

## Rotate a key without downtime

Rotate keys on a schedule, and whenever someone who had a value leaves the team. Regenerating a value invalidates
that value only, and right away. The trick is to regenerate the value that no client is using.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Save the current value

You use the old value later to prove that it stopped working. On the `support-bot` row, select **…**
(**More actions**) › **View keys**, copy the value, and paste it into your shell:

```bash title="Bash"
read -rsp "Current support-bot value: " OLD_SUPPORT_BOT && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT = Read-Host "Current support-bot value" -MaskInput
```

### Rotate the key

1. On the `support-bot` row, select **…** (**More actions**) › **Rotate key**.
2. The `Rotate "support-bot" key?` dialog warns that the current value stops working immediately and that the
   new value is displayed once. Select **Rotate**.
3. In **API key rotated successfully**, copy the new value and update the client, or the `support-bot-api-key`
   secret in Key Vault.

> [!NOTE]
> The portal rotates the **primary** value in place, so a client that still sends the old value gets `401` until
> you update it. To rotate without downtime from the portal, replace the key instead: create `support-bot-v2`,
> move the client to it, and then delete `support-bot`. The new key is a new caller identity, so move any
> cost-limit overrides to it, and expect Monitoring to report it separately. The CLI track avoids both trade-offs
> with the secondary value.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Save the current value

Clients use the primary value today. Keep it so you can prove later that it stopped working:

```bash title="Bash"
OLD_SUPPORT_BOT="$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot/listSecrets?$API" \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot/listSecrets?$API" `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
```

### Regenerate the unused secondary value

No client uses the secondary value, so regenerating it breaks nothing:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/rotate-key.sh support-bot secondary
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/rotate-key.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -KeyName support-bot -KeyType secondary # -KeyVault $KEY_VAULT
```

The script calls the key's `regenerateSecondaryKey` action with `az rest`, reads the new value with
`listSecrets`, and prints only its last four characters. If `KEY_VAULT` is set in Bash, or you pass `-KeyVault` in PowerShell,
it also writes the new value to the `support-bot-api-key` secret. On GitHub, open
[rotate-key.sh](infra/rotate-key.sh) or [rotate-key.ps1](infra/rotate-key.ps1).

<!-- include: infra/rotate-key.sh -->

### Move the client to the secondary value

Update the client's configuration to the new secondary value and restart it, or let it reload the Key Vault
secret. Both values are valid now, so no request fails during the switch. The old primary value still works:

```bash title="Bash"
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT" ./infra/check-key.sh "old primary"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/check-key.ps1 -ApiKey $OLD_SUPPORT_BOT -Label "old primary"
```

### Regenerate the primary value

When every client uses the secondary value, regenerate the primary. This invalidates the old value, wherever it
might have been copied:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/rotate-key.sh support-bot primary
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/rotate-key.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -KeyName support-bot -KeyType primary # -KeyVault $KEY_VAULT
```

Next time, rotate in the other direction: regenerate the primary, move clients to it, then regenerate the
secondary. With Key Vault, the secret always holds the newest value, so clients that reload it move along
automatically.

<!-- /tracks -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT" ./infra/check-key.sh "rotated value"` (or
> `./infra/check-key.ps1 -ApiKey $OLD_SUPPORT_BOT -Label "rotated value"`) prints `HTTP 401`.

## Revoke a leaked key

When a key leaks, revoke it first and investigate afterward. Deleting a key invalidates both of its values
immediately, and anyone who holds them gets `401`. Pick one track.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Save the leaked value

You use it to prove that the key no longer works. On the `old-notebook` row, select **…** (**More actions**) ›
**View keys**, copy the value, and paste it into your shell:

```bash title="Bash"
read -rsp "Leaked value: " LEAKED_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$LEAKED_KEY = Read-Host "Leaked value" -MaskInput
```

### Delete the key

Select the check box on the `old-notebook` row, and then select **Delete**. The `Delete "old-notebook" key?`
dialog warns that applications using the key will no longer authenticate to the gateway and that the action
can't be undone. Select **Delete**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Save the leaked value and delete the key

```bash title="Bash"
LEAKED_KEY="$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/old-notebook/listSecrets?$API" \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
az rest --method delete --url "$GW/apiKeys/old-notebook?$API"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$LEAKED_KEY = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/old-notebook/listSecrets?$API" `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
az rest --method delete --url "$GW/apiKeys/old-notebook?$API"
```

### Suspend a key instead

To block a key while you investigate, without deleting it, set its `state` to `suspended`. Calls with the key
get `401` until you set it back to `active`. The **Verify** section expects `support-bot` to work, so set it
back to `active` before you continue:

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" \
  --body '{"properties":{"state":"suspended"}}' --query properties.state -o tsv
# Later, to let the key work again:
az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" \
  --body '{"properties":{"state":"active"}}' --query properties.state -o tsv
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
'{"properties":{"state":"suspended"}}' | Set-Content keystate.json
az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" --body "@keystate.json" --query properties.state -o tsv
# Later, to let the key work again:
'{"properties":{"state":"active"}}' | Set-Content keystate.json
az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" --body "@keystate.json" --query properties.state -o tsv
Remove-Item keystate.json
```

Each command prints the new state, `suspended` or `active`.

<!-- /tracks -->

Then clean up after the leak: remove the value from the notebook and its history, and check
**Monitoring** for calls made with the key.

> [!NOTE]
> If the caller behind a leaked key must keep its identity, for example because a cost-limit override or
> Monitoring history is tied to it, regenerate **both** values instead of deleting the key. Run
> `./infra/rotate-key.sh <key> primary` and then `./infra/rotate-key.sh <key> secondary` (or the PowerShell
> script with `-KeyType`), and give the caller the new value.

## See usage and cost per key

Each key is a caller identity, so Monitoring can break usage down by key. This needs the monitoring setup from
[Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md) and a few requests with each key.

1. Select **Monitoring** › **Models**.
2. **Active caller identities** counts the API keys and Microsoft Entra identities with observed activity.
3. **Model usage by caller identity** compares caller identities by estimated model cost, tokens, and calls.
4. Use the **All caller identities** filter to scope the page to one key, for example `support-bot`. Keys appear
   by name, marked **API key**.

The same identity drives enforcement. A **Cost limit** counted by **Caller identity** gives each key its own
budget:

![A Cost limit policy with a $100 monthly budget counted by caller identity](../assets/screens/policy-cost-limit-details.png "A Cost limit counted by caller identity: each API key gets its own $100 monthly budget, and a caller that reaches it gets 403 LlmCostQuotaExceeded.")

To set budgets and limits per key, continue with
[Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).

## When to move to Microsoft Entra ID

API keys are the fastest way to start, but the docs don't recommend them for production.

| | Runtime API key | Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC |
|---|---|---|
| What the gateway sees | One named key | A user, agent, or workload identity in your tenant |
| What it can call | Every published model and MCP server | What its role grants: **AI Gateway User** (models and tools), **AI Gateway Models User**, or **AI Gateway Tools User**, at gateway, alias, or MCP server scope |
| Secret to protect | The key value | None with a managed identity; tokens are short-lived |
| Rotation | You rotate and redistribute values | Microsoft Entra ID issues new tokens |
| Good fit | Prototypes, labs, and tools that only accept a key | Production apps, agents, and per-user access |

Move to Microsoft Entra ID with
[Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).

## Verify

Run the checks from the lab folder. Only current values should get through; the rotated value, the deleted key,
and a request without a key should all get `401`.

<!-- steps -->

### Load the app-dev key

If `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` no longer holds the `app-dev` value, load it again from Key Vault, with
`listSecrets`, or by pasting it, as in [Create a key for each app](#create-a-key-for-each-app).

### Run the checks

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/check-key.sh app-dev
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT" ./infra/check-key.sh "rotated value"
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$LEAKED_KEY" ./infra/check-key.sh "deleted key"
./infra/check-key.sh --no-key
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/check-key.ps1 -Label app-dev
./infra/check-key.ps1 -ApiKey $OLD_SUPPORT_BOT -Label "rotated value"
./infra/check-key.ps1 -ApiKey $LEAKED_KEY -Label "deleted key"
./infra/check-key.ps1 -NoKey
```

Expected output (your key endings differ):

```text
app-dev        ...Q7xk  HTTP 200  accepted
rotated value  ...m2Rd  HTTP 401  rejected: the key is missing, invalid, rotated, suspended, or deleted
deleted key    ...Vt9a  HTTP 401  rejected: the key is missing, invalid, rotated, suspended, or deleted
no key         -        HTTP 401  rejected: the key is missing, invalid, rotated, suspended, or deleted
```

### Check that the rotated key still works

Load a current `support-bot` value from **View keys**, Key Vault, or `listSecrets`, and run the check again.
After the CLI flow, both the new primary and the new secondary value work. The check prints `HTTP 200`:

```bash title="Bash"
read -rsp "Current support-bot value: " SUPPORT_BOT && echo
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$SUPPORT_BOT" ./infra/check-key.sh support-bot
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$SUPPORT_BOT = Read-Host "Current support-bot value" -MaskInput
./infra/check-key.ps1 -ApiKey $SUPPORT_BOT -Label support-bot
```

<!-- /steps -->

## Go further

- **Prompt for the key in MCP clients.** VS Code can ask for the key when it starts an MCP server instead of
  storing it in `mcp.json`. See [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md).
- **Get a rotation reminder.** Set an expiry date on the Key Vault secret with
  `az keyvault secret set-attributes --expires`, and subscribe to the vault's `SecretNearExpiry` event.
- **Automate rotation.** Run the rotation script from a scheduled pipeline that signs in with a workload
  identity, with a pause between the secondary and primary steps for clients to reload.
- **Limit each key.** Give every key its own token allowance with
  [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md).

## Clean up

Keep `app-dev` and `support-bot`:
[Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md) gives them different budgets.
Delete any other keys you created for testing, such as `support-bot-v2`, in **Access** › **Keys** (check box,
then **Delete**), or with the CLI:

```bash
az rest --method delete --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot-v2?$API"
```

If you created a Key Vault only for this lab, delete it. Key Vault keeps deleted vaults for a retention period
and reserves the name; purge it if you want to reuse the name right away:

```bash
az keyvault delete -n "$KEY_VAULT"
az keyvault purge -n "$KEY_VAULT"
```

Clear the key values from your shell with `unset AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY OLD_SUPPORT_BOT LEAKED_KEY SUPPORT_BOT`
(Bash) or `Remove-Variable OLD_SUPPORT_BOT, LEAKED_KEY, SUPPORT_BOT; Remove-Item Env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`
(PowerShell). Delete the gateway only when you finish all labs, as described in
[Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md#clean-up).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A new key gets `401` | The value has a space or line break, or an MCP client sends it in `Authorization` instead of `api-key` | Copy the value again and send it as `api-key: <value>`. |
| `400` with `Specify either an API key or an Authorization header, not both` | The client sends an `api-key` header and an `Authorization` header | Send one of them. With an OpenAI SDK, pass the key as the SDK's API key and remove the extra header. |
| `401` right after **Rotate key** in the portal | Portal rotation replaces the primary value immediately | Give the client the value from **API key rotated successfully**. Next time, use the CLI secondary-value flow. |
| "The key was created, but its value couldn't be retrieved." | You don't have `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/apiKeys/listSecrets/action` | Use **Rotate key** to get a new value, or ask someone with that permission, such as a Contributor, to read it. |
| `check-key` prints `not checked` with `HTTP 404` | The gateway doesn't know the alias in `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`, so it never checked the key | Set `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL` to an alias from **Models**, for example the one from lab 02. |
| A key that worked gets `401`, and nobody rotated it | The key is `suspended` | Check `state` with the list command, and set it back to `active` if the suspension is over. |
| `check-key` prints `key accepted, but the call failed` | The key works, but `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL` isn't an alias you can call, or a policy blocked the request | Set `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL` to an alias from **Models**, for example the one from lab 02. |
| `Forbidden` from `az keyvault secret set` or `secret show` | You have no data-plane role on the vault, or the role assignment hasn't applied yet | Assign **Key Vault Secrets Officer** on the vault and wait a few minutes. |
| Monitoring shows no caller identities | Monitoring isn't configured, or the time range has no traffic | Complete [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), send requests with each key, and widen the time range. |

## Next steps

- [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md): replace keys with identities and
  roles.
- [Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md): give `app-dev` and
  `support-bot` different budgets.
- [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md): see usage and cost for each key.
- Docs: [Security and identity in AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/security-identity).

# Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC

A security review of your AI platform found runtime API keys in `.env` files, CI logs, and a shared notebook.
Every key grants every model and tool on the gateway, nobody can say which person is behind a key, and
rotation means chasing every team. The platform team wants callers to use **their own Microsoft Entra
identity** instead: access granted by Azure RBAC, scoped to one model alias or MCP server when needed, and
removed automatically when someone leaves a group. In this lab you grant a data-plane role, call a model with
an Entra token from the playground, the command line, and code, and see what the gateway answers when the role
is missing.

![Callers authenticate inbound to the gateway, and the gateway authenticates outbound to each backend](../assets/diagrams/identity-boundaries.svg "Inbound, callers present a Microsoft Entra token and Azure RBAC decides which models and tools they can use. Outbound, the gateway uses its own identity, which you configure in lab 12.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need a gateway with at least
  one model alias.
- The [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with
  `az login` to the tenant that holds the gateway. The commands call the Azure Resource Manager REST API with
  `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't manage the new `aigateways` resource type yet.
- For the CLI track in Bash: [jq](https://jqlang.org/download/), which decodes the token and reads the reply.
- Permission to **create role assignments** on the gateway: **Owner**, **User Access Administrator**, or
  **Role Based Access Control Administrator**. **Contributor** can manage the gateway but can't grant roles.
  If you don't have one of these, ask an administrator to run the role assignment step for you.
- For the Code track, one of: Python 3.9 or later, Node.js 22.18 or later, or the .NET 8 SDK or later.

You don't need an API key in this lab. Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse
them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az rest --url "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL?$API" \
  --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
export MY_OBJECT_ID="$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)"
# Prove that nothing in this lab uses a key.
unset AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG       = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY  = "<gateway>"
$PROVIDER = "<provider-name>"              # for example foundry-models
$MODEL    = "<model-name>"                 # the backend model name under that provider

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# For Foundry imports, the default alias matches the deployment's model name.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az rest --url "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/${MODEL}?$API" `
  --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
$MY_OBJECT_ID = az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv
# Prove that nothing in this lab uses a key.
Remove-Item Env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

## How it works

Access to AI Gateway crosses two trust boundaries. **Inbound**, your app authenticates to the gateway
endpoint. **Outbound**, the gateway authenticates to each model or tool with its own credential, which you
set up in [Call backends with managed identities](../12-backend-identity/README.md).

For inbound Entra access, the caller gets an access token for the audience `https://azure-api.net/aigateway`
and sends it in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. The gateway validates the token at its edge, then
checks the caller's Azure RBAC role assignments for the model alias or MCP server in the request. Without a
matching role, it answers `403` before any policy or backend runs. These roles grant **runtime** access only,
not gateway administration.

| Role | Role ID | Grants | Assignable at |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI Gateway User | `caad7a21-134e-43f4-a550-c5ffc17e051c` | List and invoke models, list and call MCP tools | Gateway, model alias, or MCP server |
| AI Gateway Models User | `a6b68e3d-a1f0-4c60-8678-237c050cf4ea` | List and invoke models | Gateway or model alias |
| AI Gateway Tools User | `dce03f8d-857f-4e40-a90d-67770fa6ecd2` | List and call tools within MCP servers | Gateway or MCP server |

| Caller | Token type | Scope to request |
|---|---|---|
| App that signs users in with MSAL | Delegated (on behalf of the user) | `https://azure-api.net/aigateway/Data.All` |
| Service principal, managed identity, or agent identity | App-only | `https://azure-api.net/aigateway/.default` |
| You, signed in to the Azure CLI | Delegated | `az account get-access-token --resource https://azure-api.net/aigateway` |

Policies that count by **Caller identity**, such as the token limits and budgets in labs 06 and 07, keep
working: for Entra callers, the gateway combines the token's tenant ID (`tid`) and object ID (`oid`), so each
principal gets its own counter.

## Grant a data-plane role

Grant yourself **AI Gateway Models User** on the whole gateway. Do this once, whichever track you follow to
call the gateway afterward. Role scopes are Azure resource IDs:

| Scope | Resource ID |
|---|---|
| Gateway | `/subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/<gateway>` |
| Model alias | `<gateway resource ID>/workspaces/default/aliases/<alias>` |
| MCP server | `<gateway resource ID>/workspaces/default/toolServers/<mcp-server-name>` |

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start a role assignment

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), select your gateway, and select
**Access** › **Entra ID** › **Add role assignments**.

### Choose access

On **Choose access**, pick what the identities can use:

- **All models and tools in the gateway** grants **AI Gateway User** at the gateway.
- **All models in the gateway** grants **AI Gateway Models User** at the gateway.
- **All tools in the gateway** grants **AI Gateway Tools User** at the gateway.
- **Specific resources** lets you select model aliases and MCP servers under **Resources**, then choose one
  compatible **Role** for all of them.

Select **All models in the gateway**, then **Next**.

![The Add role assignments wizard on the Choose access step](../assets/screens/access-entra-role-assignments.png "Choose gateway-wide access, or select specific model aliases and MCP servers and apply one compatible role.")

### Select identities

On **Select identities**, set **Assign access to** to **User, group, or service principal**, search for your
own account by name, and choose **Select**. In production, prefer an Entra group so membership controls
access. To grant an app running in Azure, set **Assign access to** to **Managed identity** and pick it by
subscription and resource type. You can also enter a principal object ID directly. Select **Next**.

### Review and assign

On **Review + assign**, confirm the role, identities, and scopes, then select **Assign**.

> **Checkpoint**
> Your account appears in **Access** › **Entra ID** with the **AI Gateway Models User** role on the gateway.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the role assignment

`az role assignment create` needs the principal's object ID, the role ID, and the full scope:

```bash title="Bash"
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$MY_OBJECT_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type User \
  --role "a6b68e3d-a1f0-4c60-8678-237c050cf4ea" \
  --scope "$GATEWAY_ID"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az role assignment create `
  --assignee-object-id $MY_OBJECT_ID `
  --assignee-principal-type User `
  --role "a6b68e3d-a1f0-4c60-8678-237c050cf4ea" `
  --scope $GATEWAY_ID
```

### Use the helper for other roles and scopes

The lab's helper script maps `user`, `models`, and `tools` to the role IDs, builds the scope for the gateway,
a model alias, or an MCP server, and defaults to the signed-in user:

```bash title="Bash"
./infra/assign-roles.sh models                              # AI Gateway Models User on the gateway
./infra/assign-roles.sh models "alias:$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"    # ...on one model alias only
./infra/assign-roles.sh tools "mcp:<mcp-server-name>"       # AI Gateway Tools User on one MCP server
./infra/assign-roles.sh user gateway <group-object-id> Group
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
./infra/assign-roles.ps1 -Role models
./infra/assign-roles.ps1 -Role models -Scope "alias:$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
./infra/assign-roles.ps1 -Role tools -Scope "mcp:<mcp-server-name>"
./infra/assign-roles.ps1 -Role user -PrincipalId <group-object-id> -PrincipalType Group
```

<!-- include: infra/assign-roles.sh -->

On GitHub, open [assign-roles.sh](infra/assign-roles.sh) or [assign-roles.ps1](infra/assign-roles.ps1).

For a managed identity, pass its **principal** (object) ID with the type `ServicePrincipal`, for example
from `az identity show -g <resource-group> -n <identity-name> --query principalId -o tsv`.

### Confirm the assignment

```bash title="Bash"
az role assignment list --scope "$GATEWAY_ID" \
  --query "[?principalId=='$MY_OBJECT_ID'].{Role:roleDefinitionName, Scope:scope}" -o table
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az role assignment list --scope $GATEWAY_ID `
  --query "[?principalId=='$MY_OBJECT_ID'].{Role:roleDefinitionName, Scope:scope}" -o table
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The list shows **AI Gateway Models User** with the gateway's resource ID as the scope.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Review the template

The template grants one AI Gateway role to one principal at the gateway, a model alias, or an MCP server. It
names the assignment with `guid()` of the scope, principal, and role, so redeploying it changes nothing.

<!-- include: infra/role-assignment.bicep -->

### Deploy it

```bash title="Bash"
az deployment group create -g "$RG" \
  --template-file infra/role-assignment.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" principalId="$MY_OBJECT_ID" principalType=User role=models \
  --query properties.outputs
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az deployment group create -g $RG `
  --template-file infra/role-assignment.bicep `
  --parameters gatewayName=$GATEWAY principalId=$MY_OBJECT_ID principalType=User role=models `
  --query properties.outputs
```

To grant one alias only, add `scope=alias scopeName="$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"`. For an MCP server, use `role=tools
scope=mcp scopeName=<mcp-server-name>`. For a group or managed identity, pass its object ID with
`principalType=Group` or `principalType=ServicePrincipal`.

If you already hold the role at the same scope from another track, the deployment fails with
`RoleAssignmentExists`, because that assignment has a different name. You have the access you need, so carry on.

> **Checkpoint**
> The `roleAssignmentId` output ends with a GUID under the gateway's resource ID, and
> **Access** › **Entra ID** in the portal lists you with **AI Gateway Models User**.

<!-- /tracks -->

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Role assignments can take several minutes to apply. Until then, Entra calls return `403`. Wait a few
> minutes and retry before you change anything else.

## Call the gateway with a token

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Open the playground with Entra ID

Select **Catalog** and pick your model. In the playground toolbar, the **Authentication** list has a
**Token** group with **Microsoft Entra ID** ("Use your signed-in identity.") and an **API key** group with
your runtime keys. When your role allows invoking the model, the portal selects **Microsoft Entra ID** for you.
It checks your permissions through the control plane, so you also need `Microsoft.Authorization/permissions/read`
on the gateway, which **Reader** and higher roles include.

If **Microsoft Entra ID** is disabled, the tooltip tells you to grant access under **Access** › **Entra ID**.
Wait for the role to apply and refresh the page.

### Send a prompt

With **Microsoft Entra ID** selected, send `In one sentence, why use Microsoft Entra ID instead of API keys?`.
The playground's code examples follow the authentication method you select.

> **Checkpoint**
> The model answers, and the **Authentication** list shows **Microsoft Entra ID**, not a key name.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Get a token

The Azure CLI can issue a token for the AI Gateway audience with your sign-in:

```bash title="Bash"
export AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN="$(az account get-access-token \
  --resource https://azure-api.net/aigateway --query accessToken -o tsv)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN = az account get-access-token `
  --resource https://azure-api.net/aigateway --query accessToken -o tsv
```

Access tokens are short-lived, typically about an hour. Run the command again when you get a `401`.

### Look inside the token

Decode the token's payload (the middle segment) to see what the gateway checks:

```bash title="Bash"
jq -R 'split(".")[1] | gsub("-";"+") | gsub("_";"/") | @base64d | fromjson
  | {aud, tid, oid, scp, appid}' <<< "$AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$payload = ($env:AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN -split '\.')[1].Replace('-', '+').Replace('_', '/')
$payload = $payload.PadRight($payload.Length + (4 - $payload.Length % 4) % 4, '=')
[Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String($payload)) |
  ConvertFrom-Json | Select-Object aud, tid, oid, scp, appid
```

`aud` is `https://azure-api.net/aigateway`, `scp` includes `Data.All` because the CLI gets a delegated token
for you, and `tid` plus `oid` identify you to per-caller policies.

### Call the model with the bearer token

```bash title="Bash"
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Say hello in five words.\"}]}" \
  | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$body = @{
  model    = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
  messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "Say hello in five words." })
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
$response = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN" } `
  -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
$response.choices[0].message.content
```

> [!WARNING]
> Send a token or a key, never both. A request with an `Authorization` header and an `api-key` header gets `400`.

> **Checkpoint**
> The model replies, and no `api-key` header was sent.

<!-- track: code | Code -->

### Install the packages

Each sample uses `DefaultAzureCredential`, which uses your Azure CLI or IDE sign-in on a laptop and a managed
identity or workload identity when the code runs in Azure. No key or secret appears in code or config.

```bash title="Python"
cd infra
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate     # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

```bash title="TypeScript"
cd infra
npm install
```

```bash title="C#"
cd infra
dotnet restore
```

### Review the sample

The only change from an API-key client is where the credential comes from:

```python title="Python"
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential, get_bearer_token_provider
from openai import OpenAI

token_provider = get_bearer_token_provider(
    DefaultAzureCredential(), "https://azure-api.net/aigateway/.default")

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1",
    api_key=token_provider,   # called before each request, sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>
)
```

```typescript title="TypeScript"
import { DefaultAzureCredential, getBearerTokenProvider } from "@azure/identity";
import OpenAI from "openai";

const getToken = getBearerTokenProvider(
  new DefaultAzureCredential(), "https://azure-api.net/aigateway/.default");

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: `${gatewayUrl}/default/models/openai/v1`,
  apiKey: getToken,   // called before each request, sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>
});
```

```csharp title="C#"
var credential = new DefaultAzureCredential();
AccessToken token = await credential.GetTokenAsync(
    new TokenRequestContext(new[] { "https://azure-api.net/aigateway/.default" }));

request.Headers.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", token.Token);
```

The OpenAI SDKs for Python (1.106 or later) and TypeScript (5.18 or later) accept a function as the API key.
They call it before each request and send the result as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and the Azure
Identity token provider refreshes the token before it expires. The C# sample calls the REST endpoint with
`HttpClient` and asks the credential for a token before each call, which also returns a cached token until
it's close to expiry. Don't use an `AzureOpenAI` client here: the gateway exposes the OpenAI v1 API at
`/default/models/openai/v1`.

The complete samples add input checks and print the reply and token usage:

<!-- include: infra/call_with_entra.py -->

<!-- include: infra/call-with-entra.ts -->

<!-- include: infra/CallWithEntra.cs -->

On GitHub, open [call_with_entra.py](infra/call_with_entra.py), [call-with-entra.ts](infra/call-with-entra.ts),
and [CallWithEntra.cs](infra/CallWithEntra.cs) with [CallWithEntra.csproj](infra/CallWithEntra.csproj).

### Run it

```bash title="Python"
python call_with_entra.py
```

```bash title="TypeScript"
node call-with-entra.ts
```

```bash title="C#"
dotnet run
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The sample prints the model's reply and the tokens used, with `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` unset.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

Prove that access now follows the role assignment, not a key.

<!-- steps -->

### Confirm the keyless call succeeds

Run the curl call or a code sample from the previous section. It returns `200` with a reply.

### Send a token for the wrong audience

A token for Azure Resource Manager is valid, but not for AI Gateway:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(az account get-access-token --query accessToken -o tsv)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

The gateway answers `401`: authentication failed, so the role was never checked.

### Remove the role and try again

Remove your assignment, wait a few minutes, get a fresh token, and repeat the curl call:

```bash
az role assignment delete --assignee "$MY_OBJECT_ID" \
  --role "a6b68e3d-a1f0-4c60-8678-237c050cf4ea" --scope "$GATEWAY_ID"
```

The gateway now answers `403`: you're authenticated, but no role allows you to invoke the model. In the
playground, the same error offers **Review access**, which opens the role assignments, and
**Copy access request**, which copies your identity, the suggested role, and the scope for an administrator.

### Restore access

Assign the role again (portal, `az role assignment create`, or `./infra/assign-roles.sh models`), wait for it
to apply, and confirm the call returns `200`.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> You called a model with no API key, got `401` for a token with the wrong audience, and `403` while your
> identity had no role.

## Go further

- **Narrow the scope.** Replace the gateway-wide assignment with **AI Gateway Models User** on a single alias
  (`./infra/assign-roles.sh models "alias:<alias>"`). Calls to other aliases now return `403`.
- **Grant tools only.** Give an agent **AI Gateway Tools User** on one MCP server from
  [Federate MCP tools](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md), so it can list and call those tools but not
  invoke models.
- **Run without a user.** Deploy the Python sample to an Azure service with a managed identity, assign the
  role to that identity's principal ID, and the same code runs with app-only tokens for the `.default` scope.
  Agent identities work the same way.
- **Budget per person.** Add a cost limit with **Caller identity** as the counter dimension and an override for one Entra identity in
  [Enforce cost budgets](../07-cost-budgets/README.md). Each `tid` and `oid` pair gets its own budget.
- **See who called.** In **Monitoring** › **Settings**, **Token claim attributes** exports claims such as
  `tid`, `oid`, `appid`, and `azp` as `azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.<claim>` attributes on logs, traces,
  and metrics. See [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md).

## Clean up

Role assignments don't cost anything. Keep yours if you'll continue with Entra-based labs. Otherwise remove
it, and revoke any runtime keys you no longer need in **Access** › **Keys**.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the role assignment

Select **Access** › **Entra ID**, find your assignment, and remove it.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the role assignment

```bash title="Bash"
az role assignment delete --assignee "$MY_OBJECT_ID" \
  --role "a6b68e3d-a1f0-4c60-8678-237c050cf4ea" --scope "$GATEWAY_ID"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az role assignment delete --assignee $MY_OBJECT_ID `
  --role "a6b68e3d-a1f0-4c60-8678-237c050cf4ea" --scope $GATEWAY_ID
```

<!-- track: code | Code -->

### Remove local files

Delete `infra/.venv`, `infra/node_modules`, or `infra/bin` and `infra/obj`. Then remove the role assignment
with the Portal or Azure CLI track.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `401` on every Entra call | The token is expired, or it was issued for another audience, such as Azure Resource Manager | Request a new token for `https://azure-api.net/aigateway` (`.default` for app-only callers). Check `aud` in the decoded token. |
| `403` right after you assigned the role | Role assignments take several minutes to apply | Wait and retry with a fresh token. In the playground, use **Back to playground** after reviewing access. |
| `403` for one model or MCP server only | The role is scoped to a different alias or MCP server, or the role doesn't cover it (Models User on an MCP server, Tools User on a model) | Assign a compatible role at the gateway or at that alias or MCP server. |
| `403` even though the role is correct | A gateway policy (for example a cost limit), the request proxy, or the backend rejected the call | Read the error code in the response body before changing permissions. `LlmCostQuotaExceeded` comes from a cost limit. |
| `AuthorizationFailed` when you create the assignment | You have **Contributor**, which can't write role assignments | Ask an **Owner**, **User Access Administrator**, or **Role Based Access Control Administrator** to assign the role. |
| `DefaultAzureCredential failed to retrieve a token` | No sign-in is available to the credential chain | Run `az login`, or sign in to the Azure extension in your IDE, then rerun the sample. |

- Docs: [Security and identity](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/security-identity) and
  [Access models through AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/model-access).
