- [Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md): turn the report into budgets per
  key, identity, or claim.
- [Connect agent frameworks to models and tools](../15-agent-frameworks/README.md): give each agent its own key or
  identity so the report shows it.
- [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md): move callers from keys to identities
  that carry claims.
- Docs: [Observability](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/observability)


<!-- https://azure.github.io/ai-gateway/labs/15-agent-frameworks/ -->
---
title: Connect agent frameworks to models and tools
summary: Point Microsoft Agent Framework, the OpenAI Agents SDK, and LangChain with LangGraph at the gateway's OpenAI-compatible model endpoint and its MCP endpoint, so every model and tool call an agent makes passes through gateway policies and shows up in Monitoring.
category: agents
level: Intermediate
duration: 30
tracks: [code]
order: 15
illustration: diagrams/architecture.svg
tags: [Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain, LangGraph, MCP, OpenAI-compatible, Python]
objectives:
  - Configure a framework's model client with the gateway's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, an alias, and a runtime key
  - Load governed tools from the gateway's MCP endpoint in each framework
  - Run the same agent in Microsoft Agent Framework, the OpenAI Agents SDK, and LangGraph
  - Prove that the gateway authenticates and records every model and tool call the agent makes
prereqs:
  - 02-first-model-call
  - 04-federate-mcp-tools
---

# Connect agent frameworks to models and tools

Your teams build agents with different frameworks, and each one wires its own model keys and tool servers. Nobody
can say which agent called what, and a policy change means touching every codebase. In this lab you point three
popular frameworks at one gateway: two URLs and one header, and every model and tool call the agent makes is
governed and observable in the same place.

![Agents call models and MCP tools through AI Gateway](../assets/diagrams/architecture.svg "Agents keep their framework. The gateway sits between them and every model and tool they call.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need the
  gateway URL, a callable alias, and a runtime key. Create a dedicated key for this agent under **Access** ›
  **Keys**, for example `docs-agent`, so its traffic is easy to find.
- Complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). The samples use the
  `learn` MCP server from that lab. Any MCP server on your gateway works.
- Python 3.10 or later. The samples were tested together on Python 3.13 with the versions in
  [infra/requirements.txt](infra/requirements.txt).
- Optional: monitoring from [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), to see the agent's calls.

## How it works

Agent frameworks talk to models through an OpenAI-compatible client and to tools through an MCP client. Point both at
the gateway. The model client takes the runtime key as its API key, which it sends as a bearer token that the
model endpoint accepts. The MCP client sends the same key in the `api-key` header, the only place the MCP endpoint
reads it.

The framework still owns orchestration, memory, and state. The gateway authenticates each call, applies the policies
on the alias, the MCP server, and the gateway, routes the alias to its provider, and records telemetry for every call
that leaves the agent. Changing a model, a policy, or a tool list then needs no agent code change.

| Framework | Model client | MCP tools | Model API |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft Agent Framework | `OpenAIChatClient` | `MCPStreamableHTTPTool` | Responses |
| OpenAI Agents SDK | `OpenAIChatCompletionsModel` with `AsyncOpenAI` | `MCPServerStreamableHttp` | Chat Completions |
| LangChain and LangGraph | `ChatOpenAI` | `MultiServerMCPClient` (langchain-mcp-adapters) | Chat Completions |

All three use the same two endpoints. The gateway serves both model APIs on the model endpoint:

- Model: `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/models/openai/v1`
- MCP: `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp`

## Set up the samples

<!-- steps -->

### Install the packages

From the lab folder, create a virtual environment in `infra` and install the pinned packages.

```bash title="Bash"
cd infra
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
cd infra
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### Configure the environment

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in your values. The samples build both endpoints from `AI_GATEWAY_URL`. The
[agent access docs](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/agent-access) name the full endpoints
`AI_GATEWAY_MODEL_ENDPOINT` and `AI_GATEWAY_MCP_ENDPOINT`. They point to the same URLs.

<!-- include: infra/.env.example bash -->

On GitHub, open [infra/.env.example](infra/.env.example).

```bash title="Bash"
cp .env.example .env
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
Copy-Item .env.example .env
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `.env` holds a secret. Keep it out of source control, and in production read the key from your platform's secret
> store or switch to Microsoft Entra ID.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `pip list` shows `agent-framework-core`, `openai-agents`, and `langchain-mcp-adapters`, and `.env` has your four
> values.

## Point the model client at the gateway

Each framework takes the gateway's model endpoint as its base URL, the alias as the model name, and the runtime key
as its API key.

<!-- steps -->

### Configure the model client

```python title="Agent Framework"
# The model endpoint accepts the key as the SDK's bearer token. Adding an api-key header as well gets a 400.
client = OpenAIChatClient(
    model=model,
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1/",
    api_key=api_key,
)
```

```python title="OpenAI Agents SDK"
client = AsyncOpenAI(
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1",
    api_key=api_key,
)
# ...
model=OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(model=model, openai_client=client),
```

```python title="LangGraph"
model = ChatOpenAI(
    model=model_name,
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1",
    api_key=api_key,
)
```

Don't add an `api-key` default header to the model client as well: the gateway rejects a request that has both an
`api-key` and an `Authorization` header with `400`.

> [!NOTE]
> The OpenAI Agents SDK sample turns off the SDK's built-in tracing, which otherwise exports traces to OpenAI. The
> gateway already records each model and tool call.

<!-- /steps -->

## Add the gateway's MCP tools

The MCP client connects to one MCP server on the gateway and sends the same key. The agent only sees the tools that
the server publishes, after the gateway's tool controls.

<!-- steps -->

### Connect to the MCP endpoint

```python title="Agent Framework"
mcp_tool = MCPStreamableHTTPTool(
    name="gateway-tools",
    url=f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{server}/mcp",
    static_headers={"api-key": api_key},
    approval_mode="never_require",
    request_timeout=60,
)
```

```python title="OpenAI Agents SDK"
async with MCPServerStreamableHttp(
    name="gateway-tools",
    params={
        "url": f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{server}/mcp",
        "headers": {"api-key": api_key},
        "timeout": 60,
    },
    cache_tools_list=True,
    client_session_timeout_seconds=60,
) as mcp_server:
```

```python title="LangGraph"
mcp_client = MultiServerMCPClient(
    {
        "gateway-tools": {
            "transport": "streamable_http",
            "url": f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{server}/mcp",
            "headers": {"api-key": api_key},
        }
    }
)
tools = await mcp_client.get_tools()
```

The `learn` tools only read documentation, so the Agent Framework sample runs them without asking for approval. For
tools that change data, set `approval_mode="always_require"` on the MCP tool and handle the approval requests in your
app. Also narrow the tool list on the gateway, as in
[Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md), so every agent gets the same limits.

### Build the agent

```python title="Agent Framework"
async with mcp_tool:
    agent = Agent(client=client, name="docs-agent", instructions=INSTRUCTIONS, tools=mcp_tool)
    result = await agent.run(question)
    print(result.text)
```

```python title="OpenAI Agents SDK"
agent = Agent(
    name="docs-agent",
    instructions=INSTRUCTIONS,
    model=OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(model=model, openai_client=client),
    mcp_servers=[mcp_server],
)
result = await Runner.run(agent, question)
print(result.final_output)
```

```python title="LangGraph"
agent = create_agent(model, tools, system_prompt=INSTRUCTIONS)
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
```

`create_agent` from LangChain builds a LangGraph graph that loops between the model and the tools. LangGraph keeps
orchestration and state, while AI Gateway applies policies and records telemetry for every call leaving the agent.

<!-- /steps -->

## Run the agents

<!-- steps -->

### Run each sample

Run the sample for each framework from the `infra` folder, with the virtual environment active. Pass a question as
arguments to override the default one.

```bash title="Agent Framework"
python agent_framework_agent.py
```

```bash title="OpenAI Agents SDK"
python openai_agents_agent.py
```

```bash title="LangGraph"
python langgraph_agent.py
```

Expected output: a line such as `Model <model-name> and MCP server learn through https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com`
(the LangGraph sample also prints how many tools it loaded), then a short answer about AI Gateway that cites
Microsoft Learn URLs. The answer differs between runs and frameworks.

### Review the full samples

<!-- include: infra/agent_framework_agent.py -->

<!-- include: infra/openai_agents_agent.py -->

<!-- include: infra/langgraph_agent.py -->

On GitHub, open [agent_framework_agent.py](infra/agent_framework_agent.py),
[openai_agents_agent.py](infra/openai_agents_agent.py), and [langgraph_agent.py](infra/langgraph_agent.py).

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> All three samples print an answer that cites at least one `learn.microsoft.com` URL, which means each agent called
> a model and an MCP tool through the gateway.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Prove the gateway is in the path

Run one sample with a wrong key. The gateway rejects the agent's first call with `401`, before any model or tool
runs.

```bash title="Bash"
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="not-a-key" python langgraph_agent.py
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = "not-a-key"; python langgraph_agent.py; Remove-Item Env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
```

Expected output: a traceback that ends with a `401 Unauthorized` error for the MCP endpoint, because each sample
connects to the MCP server before it calls the model. A key set in your shell takes precedence over `.env`.

### See the agent in Monitoring

If you set up monitoring in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), wait a few minutes and
open **Monitoring**. On **Overview**, **Model calls** and **Tool calls** both grew. On **Tools**, the `learn`
server shows up in **Usage by tool server**, and **Tool usage by caller identity** shows the agent's key. A run
usually makes at least two model calls: one that asks for a tool and one that writes the answer. Open
**Traces** to see each call with its gateway policies.

<!-- /steps -->

## Go further

- **Give each agent an identity.** Create one runtime key per agent, as in
  [Issue and rotate runtime API keys](../10-api-keys/README.md), so Monitoring and cost limits can tell agents apart.
  For production, drop keys: send a Microsoft Entra token for `https://azure-api.net/aigateway` from the agent's
  managed identity or agent identity, with the **AI Gateway User** role, as in
  [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).
- **Govern the agent, not the code.** Add a token limit to the alias with
  [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md), or a request rate limit to the MCP
  server. The agent gets `429` responses without any code change, so handle `Retry-After` in long-running agents.
- **Swap models behind the alias.** Retarget the alias to another model or provider, as in
  [Publish models from any provider behind stable aliases](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md). The agents keep
  working with the same `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`.
- **Use .NET.** The [.NET hosted agent sample](https://github.com/Azure-Samples/simple-foundry-hosted-agent-dotnet-aigateway)
  connects Microsoft Agent Framework for .NET to a gateway. With the AI Gateway tier, pass the runtime key as the
  client's API key and don't add an `api-key` header to model calls.
- **Other SDKs.** For the GitHub Copilot SDK and other frameworks, use their model and MCP configuration points with
  the same endpoints, and confirm the endpoint formats and authentication they support.

## Clean up

- Delete `infra/.env`, because it holds a key, and `infra/.venv` if you don't need it.
- If you created a key just for this lab, revoke it under **Access** › **Keys**.

Keep the gateway, the alias, and the `learn` MCP server. Other labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `401` from the model or MCP endpoint | The key is missing, wrong, or revoked, or the header isn't sent | Check `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` in `.env` and that the key exists under **Access** › **Keys**. A value set in your shell overrides `.env`. |
| `404` from the MCP endpoint | `AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER` doesn't match an MCP server name | Copy the name from **MCP servers**, or the endpoint from the server's page. |
| A `4xx` error that mentions the model | `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL` isn't a callable alias | Copy the alias exactly from the model's **Aliases** tab. |
| The agent answers without citing any URL | The MCP server publishes no tools, or tool controls block them | Run `list_tools.py` from [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md) and check the server's tool controls. |
| `429` responses | A token limit or rate limit on the alias, MCP server, or gateway | Expected when a policy applies. Wait for `Retry-After`, or raise the limit. |
| `ModuleNotFoundError` | The virtual environment isn't active | Activate `.venv` and run `pip install -r requirements.txt` again. |

## Next steps

  agent in Microsoft Foundry with the same gateway wiring.
- [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md): replace the agent's key with an
  identity.
- [Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry](../14-otel-chargeback/README.md): report each agent's tokens and
  estimated cost.
- Docs: [Connect agents to AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/agent-access)

# Deploy a Foundry hosted agent behind AI Gateway

Your team wants to run an agent in Microsoft Foundry, but the platform team needs every model call and every tool
call to be governed and visible in one place. In this lab you deploy a small Microsoft Agent Framework agent to
Foundry Hosted Agents. Its Foundry project has no model deployments and no tool connections: the agent reaches its
model and its tools only through AI Gateway, with a key of its own.

![A Foundry hosted agent calls a model alias and the Learn MCP server through AI Gateway](../assets/diagrams/hosted-agent.svg "Foundry runs the agent. AI Gateway governs its model calls and its MCP tool calls.")

## Before you begin

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md) and
  [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). The agent calls the alias from lab 02 and the `learn` MCP
  server from lab 04.
- An Azure subscription where you can create a resource group and a Foundry resource, and assign roles, for example
  **Owner**. azd gives the agent's identity access to its Foundry project.
- These tools:
  - [Azure Developer CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/developer/azure-developer-cli/install-azd) (azd) 1.34.2
    or later, signed in with `azd auth login`
  - Python 3.13 or later. With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) installed, azd uses it
    to create the agent's virtual environment.
  - Git
- For the Azure CLI track: the [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later,
  signed in with `az login` to the same tenant, plus `jq` for the Bash snippets. The CLI track calls the Azure
  Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't manage the new
  `aigateways` resource type yet.

> [!WARNING]
> `azd up` creates a Foundry resource, and the hosted agent and its model calls are billable. Run
> [Clean up](#clean-up) when you're done.

## How it works

The agent lives in [`infra/`](infra/), a complete azd project:

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`infra/azure.yaml`](infra/azure.yaml) | Declares a Foundry project with no model deployments, and the hosted agent `gateway-agent`: Python 3.13, code deploy, 0.5 CPU, 1 GiB, Responses protocol |
| [`infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py`](infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py) | The agent: one model client and one MCP tool, both pointing at the gateway |
| [`infra/src/gateway-agent/requirements.txt`](infra/src/gateway-agent/requirements.txt) | Pinned dependencies, compiled from `requirements.in`. Foundry builds the agent from this file. |

The agent has two outbound paths, and both end at AI Gateway:

- **Model.** An `OpenAIChatClient` points at the gateway's model endpoint, `/default/models/openai/v1/`, and sends
  your lab 02 alias as `model`. The runtime key is the SDK's API key, so it travels as `Authorization: Bearer`.
  The model endpoint accepts a runtime key either that way or in an `api-key` header.
- **Tools.** An `MCPStreamableHTTPTool` points at the gateway's `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp` endpoint with the
  same key in the `api-key` header. The MCP endpoint accepts keys only in that header: a bearer token there must be
  a Microsoft Entra token.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Send a key in one header only. If a request carries both `api-key` and `Authorization`, the gateway rejects it
> with `400` and "Specify either an API key or an Authorization header, not both". Older samples set a placeholder
> API key and add an `api-key` header, which the OpenAI SDK turns into exactly that request.

| Piece | Name in this lab | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Model alias | Your alias from lab 02, in `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL` | AI Gateway |
| MCP server | `learn`, at `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp` | AI Gateway |
| Runtime API key | `hosted-agent` | AI Gateway |
| Foundry resource and project | In resource group `rg-<env>`; the project is named after the azd environment | Foundry, created by azd |
| Hosted agent | `gateway-agent` | Foundry, created by azd |

Foundry runs the agent. AI Gateway decides what the agent may call, counts its tokens, and records every call.

## Give the agent its own key

A dedicated key makes the agent a separate caller identity: its token limits, cost limits, and Monitoring data
don't mix with other apps. Pick one track.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Create the key

1. In the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), open your gateway and select **Access** › **Keys**.
2. Select **Create API key**.
3. In **Key name**, enter `hosted-agent`, and select **Create**.
4. The **API key created successfully** dialog shows the value. Select **Copy & done**.

### Load the values in your shell

Paste the key without echoing it, then set the gateway URL from the gateway's **Overview** page and the alias from
lab 02:

```bash title="Bash"
read -rsp "hosted-agent key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://<gateway>.<region>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "hosted-agent key" -MaskInput
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://<gateway>.<region>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02
```

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set your variables

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG                   = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY              = "<gateway>"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02

$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
```

### Create the key and load its value

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/hosted-agent?$API" --body '{"properties":{}}' -o none
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/hosted-agent/listSecrets?$API" \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
'{"properties":{}}' | Set-Content apikey.json
az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/hosted-agent?$API" --body "@apikey.json" -o none
Remove-Item apikey.json
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/hosted-agent/listSecrets?$API" `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
```

<!-- /tracks -->

> **Checkpoint**
> **Access** › **Keys** lists `hosted-agent` as active, and your shell has `AI_GATEWAY_URL`, `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`,
> and `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`.

## Configure the azd project

<!-- steps -->

### Get the lab files

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway.git
cd ai-gateway/labs/16-foundry-hosted-agent/infra
azd ext install microsoft.foundry
```

`microsoft.foundry` installs the Foundry extensions for azd, including `azure.ai.agents`, which adds the
`azd ai agent` commands.

### Create an azd environment

The environment name also names the resource group, `rg-<env>`, and the Foundry project. Choose a region where
Foundry Hosted Agents are available, for example `eastus2`.

```bash
azd env new aigw-lab16 --location eastus2
```

### Pass the gateway settings to the agent

[`azure.yaml`](infra/azure.yaml) maps four azd environment values to the agent's environment variables:

```yaml
env:
  AI_GATEWAY_URL: ${AI_GATEWAY_URL}
  AI_GATEWAY_MODEL: ${AI_GATEWAY_MODEL}
  AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY: ${AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY}
  AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER: ${AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER}
```

Set them from your shell:

```bash title="Bash"
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_URL "$AI_GATEWAY_URL"
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MODEL "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY "$AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER learn
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_URL $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MODEL $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER learn
```

azd keeps the values in `.azure/aigw-lab16/.env`, which Git ignores, and passes them to the agent locally and in
Foundry. Anyone who can read the agent's definition in Foundry can also read the key; see
[Go further](#go-further) for keyless options.

<!-- /steps -->

## Read the agent

[`main.py`](infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py) is the whole agent. The model client and the MCP tool are the only
places it talks to the network, and both point at the gateway:

```python
client = OpenAIChatClient(
    model=model,
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1/",
    api_key=api_key,
)

tools = MCPStreamableHTTPTool(
    name="gateway-tools",
    url=f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{mcp_server}/mcp",
    static_headers={"api-key": api_key},
    approval_mode="never_require",
    load_prompts=False,
    request_timeout=60,
)
```

`ResponsesHostServer` serves the agent on the Responses protocol at port 8088, the same way locally and in Foundry.
The agent sets `store` to `false` on its model calls, because the hosting server already keeps the conversation
history. Tool approval is off because the Learn tools are read-only.

<!-- include: infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py -->

On GitHub, open [main.py](infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py) and [azure.yaml](infra/azure.yaml).

## Run the agent locally

<!-- steps -->

### Start the agent

From the `infra` folder:

```bash
azd ai agent run
```

azd creates a virtual environment, installs `requirements.txt`, starts the agent on `http://localhost:8088`, and
opens Agent Inspector, where you can chat with the agent and see its tool calls. Add `--no-client` to skip Agent
Inspector.

### Ask a question

In a second terminal, from the same folder:

```bash
azd ai agent invoke --local "Which Learn page explains Azure API Management key concepts? One sentence and the URL."
```

Expected output: an answer that cites a `learn.microsoft.com` URL, for example:

```text
[local] The Learn page "What is Azure API Management?" explains its key concepts.
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/api-management-key-concepts
```

Behind that answer, the agent made a model call that asked for a tool, one or more Learn tool calls, and a model
call that wrote the answer, all through the gateway. Stop the agent with **Ctrl+C**.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The local agent answers with a Microsoft Learn URL.

## Deploy to Foundry

<!-- steps -->

### Provision and deploy

```bash
azd up
```

azd asks for a subscription if the environment doesn't have one. Then it creates `rg-aigw-lab16` with a Foundry
resource and a project that has hosted agents enabled, uploads `src/gateway-agent` as a code package, and creates the
hosted agent. Foundry builds it from `requirements.txt`. It takes about five minutes, and ends with:

```text
SUCCESS: Your application was deployed to Azure in 2 minutes 31 seconds.
```

### Invoke the hosted agent

```bash
azd ai agent invoke gateway-agent "Which Learn page explains Azure API Management key concepts? One sentence and the URL."
```

Expected output: the same kind of answer, now from Foundry. The first call can take 10 to 20 seconds while the
agent starts.

```text
Agent:        gateway-agent (remote)
...
[gateway-agent] The Learn page titled "What is Azure API Management?" explains Azure API Management key concepts.
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/api-management-key-concepts
```

azd keeps the conversation, so a second `invoke`, such as `"Shorten that to ten words."`, continues it. Add
`--new-conversation` to start over.

### Find the agent in Foundry

```bash
azd ai agent show gateway-agent
```

The output shows **Status** `active`, the agent's own identity, its Responses endpoint, and a **Playground URL**.
Open that URL to chat with the agent in the Foundry portal.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd ai agent show gateway-agent` reports `active`, and `azd ai agent invoke` returns an answer with a Learn URL.

## See the agent in Monitoring

The `hosted-agent` key is a caller identity of its own. With monitoring set up as in
[Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), invoke the agent a few times, wait a few minutes, then
open **Monitoring** in the portal:

- **Models**: use the **All caller identities** filter to select `hosted-agent`. You see the agent's calls, tokens,
  and estimated cost for your alias.
- **Tools**: the `learn` tool server under **Usage by tool server**, with the tools the agent called under
  **Top tools within tool servers**.
- **Traces**: one row per model or tool call, with the policies the gateway applied.

## Cap the agent's tokens

Give the agent's alias a strict token limit counted per caller identity, then watch the gateway enforce it without
any change to the agent. Pick one track.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add the token limit

1. Select **Policies** › **Add policy**.
2. On **Type**, select **Token rate limit**.
3. On **Scope**, select **Individual assets** and pick your alias.
4. On **Configure**, set **Time period** to **Per minute**, **Allowed tokens** to `1000`, and
   **Counter dimensions** to **Caller identity**, then select **Create**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Add the token limit

Find the alias resource by its alias name, which works even when a portal-created alias contains `/`. A `PATCH` of
`properties.policies` replaces the whole array, so these commands keep the alias's other policies:

```bash title="Bash"
ALIAS_ID="$(az rest --url "$WS/aliases?$API" \
  --query "value[?properties.aliasName=='$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL'].id | [0]" -o tsv)"
ALIAS_URL="https://management.azure.com$ALIAS_ID"
az rest --url "$ALIAS_URL?$API" -o json \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:([(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit") | del(.scope)] + [{type:"tokenLimit",period:"minute",count:1000,counterKey:["identity"]}])}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$ALIAS_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$ALIAS_ID = az rest --url "$WS/aliases?$API" `
  --query "value[?properties.aliasName=='$($env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL)'].id | [0]" -o tsv
$ALIAS_URL = "https://management.azure.com$ALIAS_ID"
$alias = az rest --url "$ALIAS_URL`?$API" -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$p = @($alias.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' } |
  Select-Object * -ExcludeProperty scope) +
  @(@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; period = 'minute'; count = 1000; counterKey = @('identity') })
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$ALIAS_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
```

<!-- /tracks -->

<!-- steps -->

### Trigger the limit

Wait about 30 seconds for the policy to apply, then invoke the hosted agent twice:

```bash
azd ai agent invoke gateway-agent --new-conversation "Summarize Azure API Management in three sentences with Learn links."
azd ai agent invoke gateway-agent --new-conversation "Summarize Azure API Management in three sentences with Learn links."
```

The gateway counts tokens when a call completes, so the first invoke usually succeeds and uses well over 1,000
tokens, because Learn tool results are long. The second invoke fails, and the agent reports the gateway's `429`:

```text
ERROR: agent failed (server_error): (... Error code: 429 - {'statusCode': 429, 'message': 'Token limit is exceeded. Try again in <n> seconds.'} ...)
```

The counter belongs to the `hosted-agent` key. Your other apps, with their own keys, keep their full allowance on
the same alias. For more on limits, see
[Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md).

### Remove the limit

In the portal, select **Policies**, open the **Token rate limit** you created for your alias, and delete it. With
the CLI, remove the `tokenLimit` policy the same way you added it:

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$ALIAS_URL?$API" -o json \
  | jq -c '{properties:{policies:[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit") | del(.scope)]}}' > policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$ALIAS_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$alias = az rest --url "$ALIAS_URL`?$API" -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$p = @($alias.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' } |
  Select-Object * -ExcludeProperty scope)
@{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
az rest --method patch --url "$ALIAS_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
Remove-Item policies.json
```

If your alias had its own token limit before this lab, the CLI commands remove it too: add it back with the count
it had.

<!-- /steps -->

## Verify

> **Verify**
> - `azd ai agent invoke --local` and `azd ai agent invoke` both return an answer with a Microsoft Learn URL.
> - The Foundry project has no model deployments, yet the agent answers: its model calls go through the gateway.
> - With the token limit in place, the agent got `429` from the gateway without any code change.
> - With monitoring set up, **Monitoring** › **Models** shows calls from the `hosted-agent` caller identity.

## Go further

- **Go keyless.** The hosted agent has its own Microsoft Entra identity, shown by `azd ai agent show gateway-agent`.
  Give it the **AI Gateway User** role, which covers models and MCP tools, as in
  [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md). Then send a Microsoft Entra token from
  `DefaultAzureCredential` to both endpoints instead of the key.
- **Keep the key out of the agent definition.** Store it in Azure Key Vault and read it at startup with the agent's
  identity, instead of passing it as an environment variable.
- **Lock down egress.** Foundry can restrict where a hosted agent may connect. Allow only your gateway's host name,
  so the gateway is the agent's only way out. See the
  [egress control sample](https://github.com/microsoft-foundry/foundry-samples/tree/main/samples/python/hosted-agents/agent-framework/responses/18-egress-control).
- **Use another framework.** Swap the agent's internals for the OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph, as in
  [Connect agent frameworks to models and tools](../15-agent-frameworks/README.md). The gateway settings stay the
  same.
- **Charge the agent back.** Attribute its tokens and estimated cost with
  [Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry](../14-otel-chargeback/README.md).

## Clean up

Delete the Foundry resource group and the hosted agent. `--purge` also purges the soft-deleted Foundry resource so
you can reuse its name:

```bash
azd down --purge
```

Then delete the `hosted-agent` key: in **Access** › **Keys**, select **…** (**More actions**) on its row and delete
it, or run `az rest --method delete --url "$GW/apiKeys/hosted-agent?$API"`. Delete the `.azure` folder in `infra` if
you no longer need the environment, because it holds the key value.

Your gateway, its alias, and the `learn` MCP server aren't affected.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `400` "Specify either an API key or an Authorization header, not both" | The code sends the key as the SDK's API key and also in an `api-key` header | Pass the key only as the SDK's `api_key`, and remove the `api-key` default header from the model client. |
| `401` from the MCP endpoint | The key went in `Authorization: Bearer` | The MCP endpoint takes keys only in the `api-key` header, as in `main.py`. |
| `401` from the model endpoint | The key is wrong, suspended, or deleted | Check `hosted-agent` in **Access** › **Keys**, load the value again, run `azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`, then `azd deploy`. |
| `404` from the model endpoint | `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL` doesn't match an alias | Copy the alias exactly from the model's **Aliases** tab, run `azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`, then `azd deploy`. |
| `429` "Token limit is exceeded" | A token limit on the alias, such as the one from this lab | Wait for the time in the message, or remove the policy. |
| `429` from tool calls | A request rate limit on the `learn` server, for example from [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md) | Wait for the `Retry-After` time, or remove the policy from the MCP server. |
| `RuntimeError: Set AI_GATEWAY_URL` | An azd environment value is missing | Run `azd env set` for the missing value, then `azd ai agent run` or `azd deploy`. |
| The hosted agent still uses an old value | Foundry reads environment variables when the agent version is created | Run `azd deploy` after every `azd env set`. |
| `[CodeError] [tool.poetry] section not found` during deployment | A `pyproject.toml` without a lock file was added to `src/gateway-agent` | Keep `requirements.txt` as the dependency file, or commit a `uv.lock` next to `pyproject.toml`. |
| `azd ai agent run` can't download packages, with a certificate error | A proxy on your network inspects TLS traffic | Set `UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=true` (`UV_NATIVE_TLS=true` in older uv versions) so uv trusts your system certificates, then run it again. |

  identity.

  [Deploy a hosted agent](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/deploy-hosted-agent)

# Build on your gateway with coding agents

Your platform team publishes models and MCP tools behind AI Gateway, and product developers want to use them
without reading gateway settings or passing keys around in chat. The AI Gateway plugin teaches coding agents
such as GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI what your gateway offers. It then generates
code that uses the right endpoint, model name, and auth header. The plugin only reads from the gateway, so
developers build on top of your governance instead of around it.

![AI Gateway architecture with coding agents among the clients that call one gateway](../assets/diagrams/architecture.svg "Coding agents call the same gateway as apps and agents. The code they generate goes through the gateway's access checks, policies, and telemetry like any other client.")

## Before you begin

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need the
  gateway, a model that answers, and its alias.
- Optional: complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md) so the gateway
  also has MCP tools to discover.
- One coding agent, installed and signed in: GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI. Each agent
  documents its plugin support: [GitHub Copilot CLI](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/plugins-finding-installing),
  [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins), [Cursor](https://cursor.com/docs/plugins), and
  [Gemini CLI](https://geminicli.com/docs/extensions/).
- The [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with `az login`.
  The plugin uses your Azure sign-in to read the gateway, so your account needs read access to it. The commands in
  this lab call the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't
  manage the new `aigateways` resource type yet.
- Python 3.10 or later to run the generated app. To scaffold a standalone agent, you also need the GitHub Copilot
  CLI, because the GitHub Copilot SDK uses it.

Set these variables in the shell that you'll start your coding agent from. Create a key for this app so you can
revoke it on its own later.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-name>"   # the alias from lab 02
export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"

az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-coding-agent?$API" --body '{"properties":{}}' -o none
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-coding-agent/listSecrets?$API" \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)" && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG      = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY = "<gateway>"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-name>"   # the alias from lab 02
$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS         = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"

@{ properties = @{} } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-coding-agent?$API" --body "@body.json" -o none
Remove-Item body.json
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-coding-agent/listSecrets?$API" `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
```

Then print the gateway's Azure resource ID. You pass it to the plugin.

```bash title="Bash"
echo "$GATEWAY_ID"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$GATEWAY_ID
```

It looks like
`/subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/<gateway>`.

## How it works

The plugin bundles one skill and two commands. The skill holds the know-how: which endpoints to call, which
model name the gateway accepts, and how to send the key. The commands run that skill for a task.

Discovery goes through Azure Resource Manager, which is why the plugin needs the resource ID and your Azure
sign-in. Your app then calls the gateway's runtime URL with a runtime key, like any other client. The plugin is
read-only against the gateway: it never creates, updates, or deletes gateways, models, tools, or keys. Creating
those stays an administrator task in the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com).

| Piece | Invoked as | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Skill `use-ai-gateway` | `/ai-gateway:use-ai-gateway` | The full discover, select, credential, and integrate workflow. The commands use it too. |
| Command `discover` | `/ai-gateway:discover <resource ID>` | Lists the gateway's models and MCP tool servers and suggests the ones that fit your use case. Stops there. |
| Command `build` | `/ai-gateway:build <resource ID> <description>` | Discovers, gets a key, integrates the assets into your app, then runs the code once to check it. |

What the generated code relies on:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Model base URL (OpenAI-compatible) | `<gateway URL>/default/models/openai/v1` |
| MCP endpoint | `<gateway URL>/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp` |
| Auth header | `api-key: <runtime key>`. The plugin writes it as `Api-Key`; header names aren't case-sensitive. |
| Key source | The `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` environment variable, loaded from a git-ignored `.env` file |
| Model name | The model's deployment name as the gateway publishes it, for example `gpt-6-luna` |
| Agent scaffold | GitHub Copilot SDK, `github-copilot-sdk>=1.0.0`, Python unless you ask for TypeScript |

## Install the plugin

<!-- steps -->

### Create a project folder

Start in an empty folder with Git, so you can check later that no secret gets committed.

```bash title="Bash"
mkdir ticket-summarizer && cd ticket-summarizer && git init -q
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
New-Item -ItemType Directory ticket-summarizer | Out-Null; Set-Location ticket-summarizer; git init -q
```

### Add the plugin to your agent

The plugin lives in the [Azure/ai-gateway](https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway) repository and follows each
agent's plugin format. In GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, start a session in the folder (`copilot` or
`claude`) and run the slash commands. In Gemini CLI, run the command in your shell, then start `gemini` in the
folder. In Cursor, use the dashboard, then open the folder.

```text title="GitHub Copilot CLI"
/plugin marketplace add Azure/ai-gateway
/plugin install ai-gateway@azure
```

```text title="Claude Code"
/plugin marketplace add Azure/ai-gateway
/plugin install ai-gateway@azure
```

```text title="Cursor"
In the Cursor dashboard, open Plugins and select Add Marketplace.
Import https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway.
Install ai-gateway from Customize.
```

```bash title="Gemini CLI"
gemini extensions install https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway
```

The marketplace is named `azure` and the plugin `ai-gateway`.

### Check that the commands are available

In your agent, run the discover command without a resource ID:

```text
/ai-gateway:discover
```

The plugin asks you for the gateway's resource ID before it makes any call. That's how you know it's loaded.
Answer with the ID you printed, or continue with the next step.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `/ai-gateway:discover` is recognized and asks for a gateway resource ID.

## Discover what the gateway offers

<!-- steps -->

### Run discover with your resource ID

Paste the gateway ID that you printed in [Before you begin](#before-you-begin):

```text
/ai-gateway:discover /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/<gateway>
```

When your agent asks to run `az` or `curl` commands, approve the ones that read: getting a token, `GET` requests
to `management.azure.com`, and MCP calls to your gateway URL. Deny any `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`. The plugin
never needs them.

### Read the summary

The plugin reads the gateway's runtime URL, lists the models with the exact name each one accepts, and lists the
MCP tool servers with their endpoints. It checks each tool server with a full MCP handshake and reports how many
tools it exposes. Then it highlights the best matches and asks which assets you want. Ask follow-up questions in
plain language, for example:

```text
Which model fits short summaries? Do any tool servers search Microsoft Learn?
```

Discover doesn't retrieve keys or write code. Stop here, or move on to `build`.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The summary lists the model you published in lab 02 and, if you did lab 04, the `learn` tool server.

## Build an app with the gateway

<!-- steps -->

### Describe what to build

Run `build` with the same resource ID and a short description. To use the key you created for this app instead of
letting the plugin pick one, say so in the description:

```text
/ai-gateway:build /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/<gateway> a Python command-line script that summarizes a support ticket from a text file. Use the <model-name> model and read the key from the AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY environment variable.
```

Other descriptions to try:

| You want | Describe it as |
|---|---|
| A model call in an app you already have | `add a /summarize endpoint to my FastAPI app that calls the gateway model` |
| Tools in your own MCP client | `connect my app to the learn MCP tools` |
| A ready-to-run agent | `a standalone agent that answers Azure questions with the learn tools` |

### Answer the plugin's questions

`build` runs the discovery again and asks you to confirm the model and tools. Then it gets a key and asks what
you're building, if your description didn't say:

- **Call a model**: code for the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, in your project's language.
- **Connect MCP tools**: configuration for an MCP-capable client or app.
- **Scaffold a standalone agent**: a complete GitHub Copilot SDK project with agent code, `.env`, `.env.example`,
  `.gitignore`, `requirements.txt` or `package.json`, and a `README.md`.

If you didn't name a key, the plugin lists the gateway's keys and reads the secret of an active one. That needs
permission to list key secrets on the gateway. When the plugin writes a key to `.env`, it's a live secret in
plain text, kept out of Git by `.gitignore`.

### Review the generated code

Read the code before you run it again or commit it. Check that:

- The base URL is your gateway URL followed by `/default/models/openai/v1`, or `/default/toolservers/<name>/mcp`
  for tools. Without `/default/`, calls return `404`.
- The `model` value is a name your gateway accepts. To retarget models later without a code change, ask the agent
  to use your alias, as explained in
  [Publish models from any provider behind stable aliases](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md).
- The key comes from `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` and goes in the `api-key` header. No key value appears in code,
  `README.md`, or config files, and `.env.example` holds only a placeholder.
- `.gitignore` lists `.env`.
- The app calls only the gateway's runtime URL, never `management.azure.com`.
- For a scaffolded agent: `requirements.txt` pins `github-copilot-sdk>=1.0.0`, each MCP server lists the selected
  tools by name instead of `"*"`, and tool permission requests wait for your approval.

### Run the app

`build` already ran the code once and reported the result. Run it yourself from the shell where you set
`AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`, using the command in the generated `README.md`. For a Python project, that's usually:

```bash title="Bash"
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
python -m venv .venv; .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Then start the entry point that the README names, for example `python summarize.py ticket.txt`.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The generated app prints a model response that came through your gateway.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Confirm the key and model outside the generated code

If the app fails, this call tells you whether the problem is in the gateway setup or in the code.

```bash title="Bash"
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "ping" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
(Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck).StatusCode
```

Expect `HTTP 200`.

### Check that no secret can be committed

Run this in the project folder. It checks that Git ignores `.env` and that your key appears in no other file.

```bash title="Bash"
git check-ignore -q .env && echo ".env is ignored" || echo "WARNING: .env is not ignored"
if grep -rIlF --exclude=.env --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=.venv --exclude-dir=node_modules -- "$AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" .; then
  echo "WARNING: the key appears in the files above"
else
  echo "No key in project files"
fi
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
git check-ignore -q .env; if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { ".env is ignored" } else { "WARNING: .env is not ignored" }
$hits = Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -Force |
  Where-Object { $_.Name -ne ".env" -and $_.FullName -notmatch '[\\/](\.git|\.venv|node_modules)[\\/]' } |
  Select-String -SimpleMatch -Pattern $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY -List
if ($hits) { "WARNING: the key appears in:"; $hits.Path } else { "No key in project files" }
```

Expect `.env is ignored` and `No key in project files`. If the plugin wrote a different key to `.env`, run the
check again with that key in `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The direct call returns `200`, the app works, and no key can reach Git.

## Go further

### Use the gateway's tools in VS Code agent mode

VS Code reads MCP servers from `.vscode/mcp.json`. To give agent mode the tools that you federated in
[Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md), save this file as
`.vscode/mcp.json` in your project. Replace `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com` with your gateway
URL (`echo $AI_GATEWAY_URL`) and `learn` with any tool server name that discover listed. To copy a tool server's
exact MCP URL, run `az rest --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --query "properties.gatewayEndpoints[0].url" -o tsv`.

<!-- include: infra/mcp.json -->

On GitHub, open [infra/mcp.json](infra/mcp.json).

Start the server from the `mcp.json` editor and paste your runtime key when VS Code prompts for it. The `inputs`
entry keeps the key out of the file.

### Go keyless

The plugin generates code that uses a runtime key. For production apps, switch to Microsoft Entra ID tokens with
the audience `https://azure-api.net/aigateway`, as shown in
[Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).

## Clean up

Keep the gateway, model, and alias. Other labs use them.

Delete the key you created for this lab. Then delete the `ticket-summarizer` folder when you're done, because its
`.env` file can hold a live key.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method delete --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-coding-agent?$API"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az rest --method delete --url "$GW/apiKeys/app-coding-agent?$API"
```

If the plugin wrote another gateway key to `.env` and that file was shared or committed, regenerate that key as
shown in [Issue and rotate runtime API keys](../10-api-keys/README.md). Remove the `ai-gateway-learn` entry from
`.vscode/mcp.json` if you added it.

Optionally, remove the plugin. In Cursor, remove it where you installed it.

```text title="GitHub Copilot CLI"
/plugin uninstall ai-gateway
/plugin marketplace remove azure
```

```text title="Claude Code"
/plugin uninstall ai-gateway@azure
/plugin marketplace remove azure
```

```bash title="Gemini CLI"
gemini extensions uninstall ai-gateway
```

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `/ai-gateway:discover` isn't recognized | The plugin isn't installed or the client hasn't reloaded it | Repeat the install for your agent, then restart it. Check with `copilot plugin list` in GitHub Copilot CLI or `gemini extensions list` in Gemini CLI. |
| The plugin can't list models, or Azure returns `401` or `403` | `az` is signed in to another tenant or subscription, or your account can't read the gateway | Run `az account show`, then `az account set --subscription <subscription-id>`. Ask for read access to the gateway. |
| The plugin stops at the credential step | Your account can't list key secrets on the gateway | Create or get a key as in **Before you begin**, and tell the agent to read it from `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`. |
| `404 Resource not found` from the gateway | The URL is missing the `/default/` segment | Use `<gateway URL>/default/models/openai/v1` or `<gateway URL>/default/toolservers/<name>/mcp`. |
| `unknown_model` | The model name isn't one the gateway publishes, the client uses another protocol than the model supports, or a GitHub Copilot SDK older than 1.0.0 drops the key header | Use the name that discover reported or your alias. Pin `github-copilot-sdk>=1.0.0`. |
| `401` from the gateway | The key is missing or deleted, or an MCP call sends it as a bearer token. The MCP endpoint reads keys only from the `api-key` header. | Send the key in the `api-key` header. Create a new key if you deleted it. |
| `400` "Specify either an API key or an Authorization header, not both" | The client sends the key in `api-key` and also an `Authorization` header, as SDKs do when you pass a placeholder key | Send only one. For the model endpoint, pass the runtime key as the SDK's API key and drop the extra `api-key` header. |
| `KeyError: 'AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY'` | `.env` wasn't loaded, often because PowerShell saved it with a byte order mark | Export the variable in your shell, or save `.env` as UTF-8 without a byte order mark. |
| `429` | A token limit or the backend's quota | The wiring works. See [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md). |
| A tool server shows `0` tools | The server exposes no tools, or tool availability hides them | Check the server's tools in the portal, or see [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). |
