# Lock down backend traffic with private networking

Your security team wants model traffic kept off the public internet wherever the platform allows it. With AI
Gateway today, that's the hop from the gateway to your backends. In this lab you create a gateway with **private
routing**, so its outbound calls leave through a subnet in your virtual network. Then you give the Foundry
resource a private endpoint, turn off Foundry's public access, and prove that the gateway still reaches the model
while the internet can't.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Inbound private endpoints and disabling public network access aren't available for AI Gateway
> (`Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways`) yet. In the portal's create dialog, **Public network access** ›
> **Disabled** is greyed out with "Unavailable until private frontend access is supported", the gateway has no
> private endpoint connections, and setting `publicNetworkAccess` to `Disabled` through Azure Resource Manager has
> no effect. Clients keep calling the gateway on its public endpoint, so protect it with runtime keys or Microsoft
> Entra ID ([Issue and rotate runtime API keys](../10-api-keys/README.md),
> [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md)) and an `ipFilter` policy
> ([Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md)).

## Before you begin

- Complete [Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md) and
  [Call backends with managed identities](../12-backend-identity/README.md). You need a Foundry resource with a
  chat model deployment, for example `gpt-6-luna`.
- Private routing can only be chosen when a gateway is created, so this lab creates a **new** gateway. The
  gateway from the earlier labs stays as it is.
- The [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with
  `az login`, plus `jq` for the Bash snippets. Every track uses the CLI for the checks. The CLI track calls the
  Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, so you don't need a CLI extension.
- Permission to create a resource group, network resources, and a gateway, to change the Foundry resource, and
  to assign roles on it, for example **Owner**, or **Contributor** plus **Role Based Access Control
  Administrator**.
- AI Gateway is in preview in East US 2 and Sweden Central. The virtual network must be in the gateway's
  subscription and region.

> [!WARNING]
> Turning off public access on the Foundry resource blocks every caller that reaches it over the internet,
> including the gateway from the earlier labs, which has no private routing, and tools on your workstation. Use a
> dedicated Foundry resource for this lab if others depend on it, and re-enable public access when you clean up.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This lab creates billable resources: a private endpoint and private DNS zones. The AI Gateway tier is free
> during the preview. Follow [Clean up](#clean-up) when you finish.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them. The lab puts the new gateway and
the network in their own resource group, so clean-up is one command.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="rg-ai-gateway-private"            # a new resource group for this lab
export LOCATION="eastus2"                    # eastus2 or swedencentral
export GATEWAY="<private-gateway>"           # a NEW, globally unique name, 24 characters or fewer
export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export SUBSCRIPTION_ID="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
export GATEWAY_ID="/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"

export VNET="vnet-aigw"
export INTEGRATION_SUBNET="snet-aigw-integration"
export PE_SUBNET="snet-private-endpoints"
export NSG="nsg-aigw-integration"
export FOUNDRY_PE="pe-foundry-$GATEWAY"

# The Foundry resource and deployment from the earlier labs
export FOUNDRY_RG="<foundry-resource-group>"
export FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT="<foundry-account-name>"
export DEPLOYMENT="gpt-6-luna"
export FOUNDRY_ID="$(az cognitiveservices account show -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --query id -o tsv)"
export FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT="$(az cognitiveservices account show -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --query properties.endpoint -o tsv)"

# What the lab publishes on the new gateway
export PROVIDER="foundry-private"
export ALIAS="private-chat"
export KEY_NAME="private-net-lab"

az group create -n "$RG" -l "$LOCATION" -o none
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG              = "rg-ai-gateway-private"   # a new resource group for this lab
$LOCATION        = "eastus2"                 # eastus2 or swedencentral
$GATEWAY         = "<private-gateway>"       # a NEW, globally unique name, 24 characters or fewer
$API             = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$SUBSCRIPTION_ID = az account show --query id -o tsv
$GATEWAY_ID      = "/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY"
$GW              = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS              = "$GW/workspaces/default"

$VNET               = "vnet-aigw"
$INTEGRATION_SUBNET = "snet-aigw-integration"
$PE_SUBNET          = "snet-private-endpoints"
$NSG                = "nsg-aigw-integration"
$FOUNDRY_PE         = "pe-foundry-$GATEWAY"

# The Foundry resource and deployment from the earlier labs
$FOUNDRY_RG       = "<foundry-resource-group>"
$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT  = "<foundry-account-name>"
$DEPLOYMENT       = "gpt-6-luna"
$FOUNDRY_ID       = az cognitiveservices account show -g $FOUNDRY_RG -n $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT --query id -o tsv
$FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT = az cognitiveservices account show -g $FOUNDRY_RG -n $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT --query properties.endpoint -o tsv

# What the lab publishes on the new gateway
$PROVIDER = "foundry-private"
$ALIAS    = "private-chat"
$KEY_NAME = "private-net-lab"

az group create -n $RG -l $LOCATION -o none
```

> [!TIP]
> Single-line commands and the `az network` commands in the tracks work in both shells. In PowerShell, replace
> the Bash line continuation (`\`) with a backtick (`` ` ``) or put the command on one line. Snippets that build
> JSON bodies or URLs have separate Bash and PowerShell tabs.

## How it works

A gateway has two network directions. **Inbound**, clients call the gateway's frontend on
`https://<gateway>.<region>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com`. **Outbound**, the gateway calls models, MCP servers, and
APIs. With **private routing**, the gateway joins a dedicated, delegated subnet in your virtual network and sends
its outbound calls through it, so it can reach backends on private IPs. When a backend's private DNS zones are
linked to that virtual network, the gateway resolves the backend's usual host name to its private endpoint IP.

You choose private routing when you create the gateway, and you can't add, change, or remove it afterwards: "Virtual
network integration for Azure AI Gateway can only be configured during creation." Most connectivity problems
after that are DNS: the gateway must resolve each backend to its private IP.

| Piece | Direction | Available today | Where you set it | Key values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Integration subnet | Outbound | Yes | Your virtual network | At least `/27` (`/24` recommended), same subscription and region as the gateway, dedicated to one gateway, delegated to `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms`, NSG allows outbound TCP 443 to `Storage` and `AzureKeyVault` |
| Private routing | Outbound | Yes, at creation only | **Create AI gateway** › **Advanced** › **Private routing** | `properties.backend.subnet.id` set to the integration subnet |
| Backend private endpoints | Outbound | Yes | Each backend, plus its private DNS zones linked to the virtual network | Foundry uses the `account` group ID |
| Gateway private endpoint | Inbound | Not yet | — | The gateway has no private link resources |
| Public network access | Inbound | Always **Enabled** | — | **Disabled** is "Unavailable until private frontend access is supported" |
| IP filter | Inbound | Yes | Gateway-wide policy ([lab 09](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md)) | `ipFilter` with `action: Allow` and `cidrRanges` |

## Prepare the virtual network

You create one virtual network with two subnets. The integration subnet belongs to the new gateway alone, and
backend private endpoints get their own subnet.

| Subnet | Prefix | Used for | Settings |
|---|---|---|---|
| `snet-aigw-integration` | `10.20.0.0/24` | Gateway private routing (outbound) | NSG `nsg-aigw-integration`, delegated to `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms`, nothing else deployed in it |
| `snet-private-endpoints` | `10.20.1.0/24` | Private endpoints to backends such as Foundry | None |

Pick one track. The IaC track declares the network, the gateway, and the Foundry private endpoint in one
template, so you deploy it once in the next section.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Create the network security group

In the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), create a network security group named `nsg-aigw-integration`
in the lab's resource group and region. Add two **outbound** security rules:

| Name | Priority | Source | Destination (service tag) | Protocol | Destination port | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AllowStorageOutbound` | 100 | `VirtualNetwork` | `Storage` | TCP | `443` | Allow |
| `AllowKeyVaultOutbound` | 110 | `VirtualNetwork` | `AzureKeyVault` | TCP | `443` | Allow |

### Create the virtual network and subnets

Create a virtual network named `vnet-aigw` in the **same subscription and region as the new gateway**, with the
address space `10.20.0.0/16`. Add the two subnets from the table above. On `snet-aigw-integration`, select the
`nsg-aigw-integration` network security group and delegate the subnet to `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms`.

> **Checkpoint**
> The virtual network shows two subnets, and `snet-aigw-integration` lists the delegation
> `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms` and the NSG `nsg-aigw-integration`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the network security group

```bash
az network nsg create -g "$RG" -n "$NSG" -l "$LOCATION"

az network nsg rule create -g "$RG" --nsg-name "$NSG" -n AllowStorageOutbound \
  --priority 100 --direction Outbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes VirtualNetwork \
  --destination-address-prefixes Storage --destination-port-ranges 443

az network nsg rule create -g "$RG" --nsg-name "$NSG" -n AllowKeyVaultOutbound \
  --priority 110 --direction Outbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes VirtualNetwork \
  --destination-address-prefixes AzureKeyVault --destination-port-ranges 443
```

### Create the virtual network and subnets

```bash
az network vnet create -g "$RG" -n "$VNET" -l "$LOCATION" --address-prefixes 10.20.0.0/16

az network vnet subnet create -g "$RG" --vnet-name "$VNET" -n "$INTEGRATION_SUBNET" \
  --address-prefixes 10.20.0.0/24 \
  --delegations Microsoft.Web/serverFarms --network-security-group "$NSG"

az network vnet subnet create -g "$RG" --vnet-name "$VNET" -n "$PE_SUBNET" --address-prefixes 10.20.1.0/24
```

> **Checkpoint**
> This command shows the `/24` prefix, the `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms` delegation, and the NSG:
>
> ```bash
> az network vnet subnet show -g "$RG" --vnet-name "$VNET" -n "$INTEGRATION_SUBNET" \
>   --query "{prefix:addressPrefix, delegation:delegations[0].serviceName, nsg:networkSecurityGroup.id}"
> ```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Review the template

The template declares the NSG, the virtual network and its two subnets, and the gateway itself. It creates the
gateway with the template from [Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md), used as a module,
and passes the integration subnet in its `backendSubnetId` parameter, which becomes
`properties.backend.subnet.id`. When you pass a Foundry resource ID in `foundryAccountId`, it also adds a private
endpoint to Foundry with the `account` group ID, the three Foundry private DNS zones, their virtual network
links, and a DNS zone group.

There's no inbound private endpoint and no `publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled'` in the template, because the
`aigateways` resource type doesn't support them yet.

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

On GitHub, open [infra/main.bicep](infra/main.bicep).

> **Checkpoint**
> You know which parameters you pass: `gatewayName`, `location`, and `foundryAccountId`. You deploy the template
> in the next section.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Create the gateway with private routing

Private routing is part of the create request. Select the integration subnet now: if you skip it, the only way to
add it later is to create another gateway.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Enter the gateway details

1. Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com). Open the gateway switcher in the top bar and start
   creating a new gateway.
2. In **Create AI gateway**, enter the new gateway's **Name**, then choose the subscription, the
   `rg-ai-gateway-private` **Resource group** (**Existing**), and the **Region** that matches the virtual network.
3. Under **Advanced**, keep **Enable system-assigned managed identity** selected and **Public network access**
   set to **Enabled**. **Disabled** is greyed out: "Unavailable until private frontend access is supported".

### Choose private routing

1. Select **Private routing** ("Allow access to private backends through secure outbound connections").
2. In **Virtual network**, select `vnet-aigw`. In **Subnet**, select `snet-aigw-integration`.
3. The portal checks the subnet: same subscription and region as the gateway, at least `/27` (`/24` leaves room to
   scale), delegated to `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms`, dedicated to one gateway, and an NSG that allows outbound
   TCP 443 to the `Storage` and `AzureKeyVault` service tags. Fix anything it flags before you continue.
4. Select **Create gateway** and wait for provisioning to finish.

> **Checkpoint**
> The gateway switcher shows the new gateway, and **Home** opens with the setup guide.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Register the resource providers

```bash
az provider register -n Microsoft.ApiManagement --wait
az provider register -n Microsoft.Web --wait
```

### Create the connector gateway

Every AI gateway has a companion `Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways` resource with the same name, created first.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method put \
  --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways/$GATEWAY?api-version=2026-05-01-preview" \
  --body "$(jq -cn --arg location "$LOCATION" '{location: $location, properties: {}}')" -o none
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
@{ location = $LOCATION; properties = @{} } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put `
  --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways/${GATEWAY}?api-version=2026-05-01-preview" `
  --body "@body.json" -o none
```

### Create the gateway in the integration subnet

The request is the same as in lab 01, plus `properties.backend.subnet.id`.

```bash title="Bash"
SUBNET_ID="$(az network vnet subnet show -g "$RG" --vnet-name "$VNET" -n "$INTEGRATION_SUBNET" --query id -o tsv)"

az rest --method put --url "$GW?$API" \
  --body "$(jq -cn --arg location "$LOCATION" --arg subnet "$SUBNET_ID" \
    '{location: $location, identity: {type: "SystemAssigned"},
      properties: {publicNetworkAccess: "Enabled", backend: {subnet: {id: $subnet}}}}')" -o none

az resource wait --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --api-version 2025-09-01-preview \
  --custom "properties.provisioningState=='Succeeded'"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$SUBNET_ID = az network vnet subnet show -g $RG --vnet-name $VNET -n $INTEGRATION_SUBNET --query id -o tsv

@{
  location   = $LOCATION
  identity   = @{ type = "SystemAssigned" }
  properties = @{ publicNetworkAccess = "Enabled"; backend = @{ subnet = @{ id = $SUBNET_ID } } }
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5 -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put --url "${GW}?$API" --body "@body.json" -o none
Remove-Item body.json

az resource wait --ids $GATEWAY_ID --api-version 2025-09-01-preview `
  --custom "properties.provisioningState=='Succeeded'"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `az resource wait` returns without an error, usually within a few minutes.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Deploy the network, the gateway, and the Foundry private endpoint

From the lab folder, register the resource providers once, then deploy the template:

```bash title="Bash"
az provider register -n Microsoft.ApiManagement --wait
az provider register -n Microsoft.Web --wait

az deployment group create -g "$RG" \
  --template-file infra/main.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" location="$LOCATION" foundryAccountId="$FOUNDRY_ID" \
  --query properties.outputs
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az provider register -n Microsoft.ApiManagement --wait
az provider register -n Microsoft.Web --wait

az deployment group create -g $RG `
  --template-file infra/main.bicep `
  --parameters gatewayName=$GATEWAY location=$LOCATION foundryAccountId=$FOUNDRY_ID `
  --query properties.outputs
```

`BCP081` warnings about `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways` and `Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways` are expected:
Bicep has no type definitions for these preview types yet.

> **Checkpoint**
> The outputs include `gatewayUrl`, `integrationSubnetId`, and `foundryPrivateEndpointName`
> (`pe-foundry-<private-gateway>`).

<!-- /tracks -->

Whichever track you used, load the runtime URL and confirm that the gateway uses the integration subnet:

```bash title="Bash"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"

az rest --url "$GW?$API" \
  --query "{state:properties.provisioningState, backendSubnet:properties.backend.subnet.id, host:properties.frontend.defaultHostname}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"

az rest --url "${GW}?$API" `
  --query "{state:properties.provisioningState, backendSubnet:properties.backend.subnet.id, host:properties.frontend.defaultHostname}"
```

Expected output:

```json
{
  "state": "Succeeded",
  "backendSubnet": "/subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/rg-ai-gateway-private/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/vnet-aigw/subnets/snet-aigw-integration",
  "host": "<private-gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com"
}
```

## Give Foundry a private endpoint

The gateway now sends outbound calls through your virtual network, but Foundry still resolves to its public IP.
Give the Foundry resource a private endpoint in `snet-private-endpoints` and link its private DNS zones to the
virtual network, so the gateway resolves Foundry to a private IP.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add a private endpoint to Foundry

In the Azure portal, open your Foundry resource and add a private endpoint named `pe-foundry-<private-gateway>`
in the lab's resource group, in `vnet-aigw` › `snet-private-endpoints`, for the `account` sub-resource, with
private DNS integration turned on. The private DNS zones for Foundry are
`privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com`, `privatelink.openai.azure.com`, and `privatelink.services.ai.azure.com`.
For the full walkthrough, see
[How to configure network isolation for Microsoft Foundry](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/ai-foundry/how-to/configure-private-link).

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Add a private endpoint to Foundry

```bash
az network private-endpoint create -g "$RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_PE" -l "$LOCATION" \
  --vnet-name "$VNET" --subnet "$PE_SUBNET" \
  --private-connection-resource-id "$FOUNDRY_ID" --group-id account --connection-name foundry
```

### Link the Foundry private DNS zones

Create each zone, link it to the virtual network, and add it to the endpoint's DNS zone group:

```bash title="Bash"
first=true
for zone in privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com privatelink.openai.azure.com privatelink.services.ai.azure.com; do
  az network private-dns zone create -g "$RG" -n "$zone" -o none
  az network private-dns link vnet create -g "$RG" -z "$zone" -n "$VNET-link" -v "$VNET" -e false -o none
  if $first; then action=create; first=false; else action=add; fi
  az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group "$action" -g "$RG" --endpoint-name "$FOUNDRY_PE" \
    -n default --private-dns-zone "$zone" --zone-name "${zone//./-}" -o none
done
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$zones = "privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com", "privatelink.openai.azure.com", "privatelink.services.ai.azure.com"
foreach ($zone in $zones) {
  az network private-dns zone create -g $RG -n $zone -o none
  az network private-dns link vnet create -g $RG -z $zone -n "$VNET-link" -v $VNET -e false -o none
  $action = if ($zone -eq $zones[0]) { "create" } else { "add" }
  az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group $action -g $RG --endpoint-name $FOUNDRY_PE `
    -n default --private-dns-zone $zone --zone-name $zone.Replace('.', '-') -o none
}
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Check what the deployment created

You passed `foundryAccountId` in the previous section, so the deployment already created the private endpoint,
the three private DNS zones, their virtual network links, and the DNS zone group. If you left `foundryAccountId`
out, run the CLI track's commands for this section instead of redeploying, because the template also declares
the gateway, and its private routing can't change after creation.

<!-- /tracks -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The private endpoint is approved, and the Foundry host has an `A` record in the `10.20.1.0/24` range:
>
> ```bash
> az network private-endpoint show -g "$RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_PE" \
>   --query "privateLinkServiceConnections[0].privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status" -o tsv
> az network private-dns record-set a list -g "$RG" -z privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com \
>   --query "[].{name:name, ip:aRecords[0].ipv4Address}" -o table
> ```
>
> The first command prints `Approved`, and the table shows `<foundry-account-name>` with an IP like `10.20.1.4`.

## Publish a model on the new gateway

The new gateway starts empty. Publish your Foundry deployment on it, as in
[Make your first model call](../02-first-model-call/README.md), and create a runtime API key. The gateway calls
Foundry with its own system-assigned managed identity, which needs the **Foundry User** role on the account.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Import the deployment from Foundry

1. In the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), select the new gateway in the top bar.
2. Select **Models** › **Add** › **Models from Microsoft Foundry**.
3. Select the subscription and resource group of your Foundry account, then select your deployment and keep
   **Managed identity** as the **Authentication method**.
4. Under **Aliases**, keep **Create an alias for each model** selected, then select **Add models**.
5. Open the imported model on **Models**, open the **Aliases** tab, and copy the alias exactly as shown.

### Create a runtime API key

Select **Access** › **Keys** › **Create API key**, enter `private-net-lab` in **Key name**, select **Create**,
and copy the value. Then set both values in your shell without echoing the key:

```bash title="Bash"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-name>"    # the alias from the Aliases tab
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = "<model-name>"  # the alias from the Aliases tab
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Grant the gateway access to Foundry

```bash title="Bash"
PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query identity.principalId -o tsv)"
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope "$FOUNDRY_ID" -o none
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$PRINCIPAL_ID = az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query identity.principalId -o tsv
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id $PRINCIPAL_ID --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal `
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope $FOUNDRY_ID -o none
```

`53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d` is the **Foundry User** role.

### Publish the deployment and an alias

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method put --url "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER?$API" -o none \
  --body "$(jq -cn --arg endpoint "$FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT" --arg id "$FOUNDRY_ID" \
    '{properties: {kind: "Foundry", displayName: "Foundry (private)", foundry: {endpoint: $endpoint, resourceIds: [$id],
      authentication: {kind: "ManagedIdentity", managedIdentity: {resource: "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/"}}}}}')"

az rest --method put --url "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT?$API" -o none \
  --body "$(jq -cn --arg d "$DEPLOYMENT" --arg id "$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT" \
    '{properties: {displayName: $d, apiFormat: "OpenAIChatCompletions",
      supportedEndpoints: ["/openai/v1/chat/completions", "/openai/v1/responses"],
      deployment: {resourceId: $id, modelName: $d}}}')"

MODEL_ID="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT"
az rest --method put --url "$WS/aliases/$ALIAS?$API" -o none \
  --body "$(jq -cn --arg m "$MODEL_ID" '{properties: {backendModels: [{resourceId: $m}]}}')"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
@{ properties = @{
    kind = "Foundry"; displayName = "Foundry (private)"
    foundry = @{
      endpoint = $FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT; resourceIds = @($FOUNDRY_ID)
      authentication = @{ kind = "ManagedIdentity"; managedIdentity = @{ resource = "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/" } }
    } } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put --url "$WS/modelProviders/${PROVIDER}?$API" --body "@body.json" -o none

@{ properties = @{
    displayName = $DEPLOYMENT; apiFormat = "OpenAIChatCompletions"
    supportedEndpoints = @("/openai/v1/chat/completions", "/openai/v1/responses")
    deployment = @{ resourceId = "$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT"; modelName = $DEPLOYMENT }
  } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put --url "$WS/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/${DEPLOYMENT}?$API" --body "@body.json" -o none

$MODEL_ID = "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT"
@{ properties = @{ backendModels = @(@{ resourceId = $MODEL_ID }) } } |
  ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put --url "$WS/aliases/${ALIAS}?$API" --body "@body.json" -o none
Remove-Item body.json
```

### Create a runtime API key

Read the generated value straight into a variable, so it never appears on screen.

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/$KEY_NAME?$API" --body '{"properties":{}}' -o none
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/$KEY_NAME/listSecrets?$API" --query primaryKey -o tsv)" \
  && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$ALIAS"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
@{ properties = @{} } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress | Set-Content body.json
az rest --method put --url "$GW/apiKeys/${KEY_NAME}?$API" --body "@body.json" -o none
Remove-Item body.json
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/$KEY_NAME/listSecrets?$API" --query primaryKey -o tsv
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = $ALIAS
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Deploy the model template from lab 02

The template from [Make your first model call](../02-first-model-call/README.md) publishes a Foundry deployment
on an existing gateway: it grants the gateway's identity the **Foundry User** role, creates the provider, the
model, and an alias, and creates a runtime API key. Run it from this lab's folder against the new gateway:

```bash title="Bash"
az deployment group create -g "$RG" \
  --template-file ../02-first-model-call/infra/main.bicep \
  --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" foundryAccountId="$FOUNDRY_ID" deploymentName="$DEPLOYMENT" \
               providerName="$PROVIDER" aliasName="$ALIAS" apiKeyName="$KEY_NAME" \
  --query properties.outputs
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az deployment group create -g $RG `
  --template-file ../02-first-model-call/infra/main.bicep `
  --parameters gatewayName=$GATEWAY foundryAccountId=$FOUNDRY_ID deploymentName=$DEPLOYMENT `
               providerName=$PROVIDER aliasName=$ALIAS apiKeyName=$KEY_NAME `
  --query properties.outputs
```

### Read the alias and key

Template outputs never contain the key value. Read it straight into a variable.

```bash title="Bash"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$ALIAS"
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/$KEY_NAME/listSecrets?$API" --query primaryKey -o tsv)" \
  && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = $ALIAS
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az rest --method post --url "$GW/apiKeys/$KEY_NAME/listSecrets?$API" --query primaryKey -o tsv
```

<!-- /tracks -->

> **Checkpoint**
> Call the model through the new gateway. Foundry's public access is still on, so a `200` proves that the
> gateway, the model, and the key work before you lock anything down:
>
> ```bash title="Bash"
> curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
>   -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
>   -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Reply with exactly one word: ok\"}],\"max_completion_tokens\":128}"
> ```
>
> ```powershell title="PowerShell"
> $body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; max_completion_tokens = 128
>   messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "Reply with exactly one word: ok" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
> $r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
>   -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck
> "HTTP $($r.StatusCode)"
> ```
>
> If the first call returns `401` or `403` from the backend, the role assignment hasn't taken effect yet. Wait a
> few minutes and try again.

## Turn off public access to Foundry

The gateway resolves Foundry through the private DNS zones, so its calls already use the private endpoint. Turn
off Foundry's public access, so the private endpoint is the only way in.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Disable public network access on Foundry

After the private endpoint shows as approved, open the Foundry resource's networking settings in the Azure portal
and disable public network access. See
[Configure virtual networks for Foundry Tools](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/ai-services/cognitive-services-virtual-networks).

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Disable public network access on Foundry

```bash
az resource update --ids "$FOUNDRY_ID" --set properties.publicNetworkAccess=Disabled \
  --query properties.publicNetworkAccess -o tsv
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep -->

### Disable public network access on Foundry

The Foundry resource lives in its own template, so change only its public access setting here instead of
redeclaring it:

```bash
az resource update --ids "$FOUNDRY_ID" --set properties.publicNetworkAccess=Disabled \
  --query properties.publicNetworkAccess -o tsv
```

If you deploy Foundry with Bicep yourself, set `publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled'` in that template instead.

<!-- /tracks -->

The change can take a few minutes to apply.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Check the gateway's private routing

```bash title="Bash"
az rest --url "$GW?$API" --query "properties.backend.subnet.id" -o tsv
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az rest --url "${GW}?$API" --query "properties.backend.subnet.id" -o tsv
```

The output ends with `/virtualNetworks/vnet-aigw/subnets/snet-aigw-integration`.

### Check name resolution for Foundry

```bash
az network private-dns record-set a list -g "$RG" -z privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com \
  --query "[].{name:name, ip:aRecords[0].ipv4Address}" -o table
```

The Foundry account resolves to an IP in `snet-private-endpoints` (`10.20.1.x`) for anything that uses the
virtual network's DNS, including the gateway.

### Call the model through the gateway

```bash title="Bash"
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Reply with exactly one word: ok\"}],\"max_completion_tokens\":128}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; max_completion_tokens = 128
  messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "Reply with exactly one word: ok" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck
"HTTP $($r.StatusCode)"
```

The call still returns `HTTP 200`. Your workstation reaches the gateway on its public endpoint, and the gateway
reaches Foundry through the integration subnet and the private endpoint.

### Call Foundry directly from your workstation

```bash title="Bash"
TOKEN="$(az account get-access-token --resource https://cognitiveservices.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv)"
curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' "${FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT%/}/openai/v1/models" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$TOKEN = az account get-access-token --resource https://cognitiveservices.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$($FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT.TrimEnd('/'))/openai/v1/models" `
  -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $TOKEN" } -SkipHttpErrorCheck
"HTTP $($r.StatusCode)"; $r.Content
```

The call returns `HTTP 403` with a message that public access is disabled: the internet can't reach Foundry
anymore, but the gateway can.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The new gateway uses private routing through `snet-aigw-integration`, Foundry resolves to a `10.20.1.x` address
> inside the virtual network, model calls through the gateway return `200`, and direct calls to Foundry from the
> internet return `403`.

## Go further

- **Filter who can call the gateway.** While the frontend stays public, add a gateway-wide `ipFilter` policy
  (`action: Allow` with your egress `cidrRanges`) next to keys or Microsoft Entra ID. See
  [Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md).
- **Hub-and-spoke networks.** Keep backend private endpoints and their private DNS zones in a hub, peer the
  gateway's virtual network to it, and link the zones to the integrated virtual network. If you use your own DNS
  servers, forward the `privatelink` zones to Azure DNS. See
  [Azure private endpoint DNS configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-dns).
- **Private MCP servers and APIs.** Any backend with a private endpoint or a private IP that the integrated
  virtual network can reach works the same way, including the tool servers from
  [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md).
- **Data residency.** Residency follows the whole request path, so account for where your backends, tools, logs,
  and clients live, not only the gateway region.

## Clean up

Re-enable Foundry's public access first, because the gateway from the earlier labs and other callers reach it
over the internet. Then remove the new gateway's role assignment on Foundry and delete the lab's resource group,
which holds the gateway, its connector gateway, the private endpoint, the private DNS zones, the virtual network,
and the NSG.

```bash title="Bash"
az resource update --ids "$FOUNDRY_ID" --set properties.publicNetworkAccess=Enabled \
  --query properties.publicNetworkAccess -o tsv

PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query identity.principalId -o tsv)"
az role assignment delete --assignee "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope "$FOUNDRY_ID"

az group delete -n "$RG" --yes
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az resource update --ids $FOUNDRY_ID --set properties.publicNetworkAccess=Enabled `
  --query properties.publicNetworkAccess -o tsv

$PRINCIPAL_ID = az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query identity.principalId -o tsv
az role assignment delete --assignee $PRINCIPAL_ID --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope $FOUNDRY_ID

az group delete -n $RG --yes
```

In the portal, you can do the same: re-enable public network access on the Foundry resource, remove the new
gateway's **Foundry User** role assignment in its **Access control (IAM)**, and delete `rg-ai-gateway-private`.

If you put the lab's resources in a resource group you want to keep, delete them in this order instead: the
gateway and its connector gateway, then the private endpoint, the private DNS zone links and zones, the virtual
network, and the NSG.

```bash title="Bash"
az resource delete --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --api-version 2025-09-01-preview
az resource delete -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways --api-version 2026-05-01-preview
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
az resource delete --ids $GATEWAY_ID --api-version 2025-09-01-preview
az resource delete -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways --api-version 2026-05-01-preview
```

Keep the gateway, model, and key from the earlier labs. The next labs reuse them.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The create dialog flags the subnet, or the create request fails with a subnet error | The subnet is in another subscription or region, smaller than `/27`, not delegated to `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms`, used by another gateway or resource, or its NSG lacks the 443 rules | Fix each item. The NSG needs outbound TCP 443 allow rules to the `Storage` and `AzureKeyVault` service tags. |
| "Virtual network integration for Azure AI Gateway can only be configured during creation." | You tried to add, change, or remove private routing on an existing gateway | Create a new gateway with private routing. |
| Model calls through the new gateway fail after you turn off Foundry public access | The gateway resolves Foundry to its public IP: the zones aren't linked to the integrated virtual network, the private endpoint has no DNS zone group, or the gateway was created without private routing | Check the `A` records and zone links, and confirm that `properties.backend.subnet.id` points to the integration subnet. |
| The gateway from the earlier labs, or another app, now gets `403` from Foundry | It reaches Foundry over the internet, and Foundry's public access is disabled | Expected. Use a dedicated Foundry resource for this lab, or re-enable public access when you finish. |
| The first call after the import returns `401` or `403` from the backend | The **Foundry User** role assignment hasn't propagated yet | Wait a few minutes, and confirm that the role is assigned to the new gateway's principal ID on the Foundry resource. |
| **Public network access** › **Disabled** is greyed out, or a `PATCH` to `Disabled` doesn't stick | Private frontend access isn't available for AI Gateway yet | Expected. Protect the public endpoint with keys or Microsoft Entra ID and an `ipFilter` policy. |
| Deleting the resource group or the virtual network fails because the subnet is in use | The service is still releasing the gateway's integration subnet | Wait a few minutes after the gateway is gone, then delete again. |

  tools, policies, and telemetry in one repeatable deployment.

  frontend.

- [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md): confirm that private traffic still produces
  telemetry.
- Docs: [Networking](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/networking).

# Protect tool calls with Agent 365 threat protection

Your agents call tools that read web pages, tickets, and documents, and any of that content can carry a prompt
injection or leak sensitive data back to the model. Content filters on the model don't see what goes into a tool
or what comes out of it. In this lab you add **Agent 365 tool threat protection** to an MCP server, so Microsoft
Defender and Microsoft Purview evaluate each tool request, each tool result, or both, and the gateway only lets
allowed calls through.

![The gateway sends the tool request and the tool result to Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview for an allow decision](../assets/diagrams/threat-protection.svg "The gateway asks for an allow decision before the tool runs, after it returns, or both. Anything other than an allow fails closed.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). This lab protects the
  `learn` MCP server from that lab. Any MCP server in your gateway works.
- Complete [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md). Tool threat protection
  only works for callers that send a **delegated** Microsoft Entra ID bearer token issued for AI Gateway.
- A **Microsoft Defender or Microsoft Purview license** in your tenant.
- Permission to manage policies on the gateway, for example **Contributor** on its resource group, and permission
  to create role assignments if your user doesn't have a data-plane role yet.
- The [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with
  `az login` as a **user** (not a service principal). The CLI snippets call the Azure Resource Manager REST API
  with `az rest`, because the `az aigateway` extension doesn't manage the new `aigateways` resource type yet.
- For the test scripts and the Bash snippets: `curl` and `jq` (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later.

> [!NOTE]
> Agent 365 tool threat protection is an emerging capability of the AI Gateway tier preview, which is available
> in East US 2 and Sweden Central. Labels and behavior can change; see the
> [release note](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/releases/2026-10-08-tool-threat-protection). AI Gateway itself
> is free during the preview; Defender and Purview are licensed separately.

Set these variables once. The steps and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export MCP_SERVER="learn"                    # the MCP server you protect in this lab

export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export GW="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
export WS="$GW/workspaces/default"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. You use it once to see a key-only call fail closed.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"
$MCP_SERVER = "learn"                        # the MCP server you protect in this lab

$API                = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID         = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$GW                 = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID"
$WS                 = "$GW/workspaces/default"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. You use it once to see a key-only call fail closed.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

## How it works

Tool threat protection is a policy on one MCP server. It covers every tool on that server, whether the server is
backed by remote MCP endpoints, OpenAPI services, or both, and every caller. The gateway first runs its usual
authentication, authorization, and policies. Only requests that pass are sent for evaluation.

For each `tools/call`, the gateway exchanges the caller's delegated token on behalf of the user (OBO) and asks
Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview for a verdict on malicious content, prompt injection, and sensitive-data
risks. Discovery and session traffic, such as `initialize`, `tools/list`, and notifications, isn't evaluated.

The evaluation must return a valid **allow**. A denial, timeout, token-exchange failure, malformed verdict, or
unavailable evaluator fails closed: the caller gets a normal tool result over HTTP `200` with `isError: true`, a
denial code, and a correlation ID.

| Stage | What's evaluated | What it prevents | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Before tool invocation** | The tool name and arguments | The tool never runs, so there are no side effects | One evaluation round trip |
| **After tool invocation** | The tool result, including error results | The result never reaches the agent. The tool **already ran**. | One evaluation round trip |
| **Both** | Both of the above | Requires two allow decisions | Up to two round trips per call |

## Prepare a delegated caller

The policy evaluates each call on behalf of the signed-in user, so you test it with your own user token. Give
your user permission to call tools on the server, then make one call **before** you add the policy. That proves
the token and the role work, so any later failure comes from the policy.

<!-- steps -->

### Grant yourself the AI Gateway Tools User role

In the AI Gateway portal, select **Access**, then **Add role assignments**. Choose the **AI Gateway Tools User**
role, scope it to the `learn` MCP server, search for your user, and select **Review + assign**. The
[Entra ID lab](../11-entra-rbac/README.md) walks through this page.

The same assignment with the Azure CLI:

```bash
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" \
  --assignee-principal-type User \
  --role "dce03f8d-857f-4e40-a90d-67770fa6ecd2" \
  --scope "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
az role assignment create `
  --assignee-object-id (az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv) `
  --assignee-principal-type User `
  --role "dce03f8d-857f-4e40-a90d-67770fa6ecd2" `
  --scope "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER"
```

If you already have **AI Gateway User** or **AI Gateway Tools User** at the gateway scope, skip this step. Role
assignments can take several minutes to apply.

### Call a tool with your user token

The script below gets a token for `https://azure-api.net/aigateway` from the Azure CLI, checks that it's a
delegated user token, runs the MCP handshake, and calls the server's search tool with a harmless question.

<!-- include: infra/call-protected-tool.sh -->

On GitHub, open [infra/call-protected-tool.sh](infra/call-protected-tool.sh) or
[infra/call-protected-tool.ps1](infra/call-protected-tool.ps1).

```bash
chmod +x infra/call-protected-tool.sh
./infra/call-protected-tool.sh token "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
./infra/call-protected-tool.ps1 -Auth token -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
Delegated token for the signed-in user (scp: ...)
MCP endpoint: https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/learn/mcp
tools/list: HTTP 200, <n> tools (discovery isn't evaluated)
tools/call: learn_microsoft_docs_search with query: What is Azure API Management?
HTTP status: 200
isError: false (the result was returned)
...
```

The tool names and count depend on your server and can change as the Learn server evolves. If `tools/call` fails with HTTP `401` or `403`, fix the token or
the role before you continue.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> A tool call with your delegated token returns a result with `isError: false`.

## Add tool threat protection

You add the policy in the AI Gateway portal. Each MCP server can have only one tool threat protection policy,
and you can't set it at gateway scope or on a single tool.

<!-- steps -->

### Start a new policy

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies**, then **Add policy**.

### Choose the policy type

On the **Type** step, under **Security**, select **Agent 365 tool threat protection**. Its card carries the
**MCP server** badge and reads "Evaluate tool calls and results with Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview
for threats, prompt injection, and sensitive-data risks." Select **Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step, with Agent 365 tool threat protection selected under Security](../assets/screens/policy-tool-threat-protection.jpeg "Agent 365 tool threat protection sits in the Security group, next to Content safety and IP filter. It applies to MCP servers only.")

### Select the MCP server

On the **Scope** step, the wizard notes that this policy applies to individual MCP servers. Select the `learn`
MCP server, then select **Next**.

### Choose the evaluation stages

On the **Details** step, the wizard reminds you that Microsoft Entra ID is required for this policy, because the
evaluation runs on behalf of the caller. Select both stages:

- **Before tool invocation: Evaluate the request payload**
- **After tool invocation: Evaluate the tool output**

You must select at least one stage. Then select **Create**.

### Confirm the policy

The new policy appears in the **Policies** overview. The policy is stored on the MCP server, so you can also read
it with a control-plane `GET`:

```bash
az rest --method get --url "$WS/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER?$API" --query "properties.policies"
```

```powershell
az rest --method get --url "$WS/toolServers/${MCP_SERVER}?$API" --query "properties.policies"
```

The list includes an entry with `"type": "toolThreatProtection"`, `"preInvocation": true`, and
`"postInvocation": true`. The service adds `"scope": "resource"` when it returns a policy set on the server.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The `learn` MCP server has one `toolThreatProtection` policy with both stages turned on.

> [!CAUTION]
> A post-invocation denial withholds the result, but it can't undo what the tool already did. The gateway doesn't
> retry or reverse the call. Build agents so they **don't automatically retry** a tool call whose result was
> withheld, especially for tools that write, send, or delete. For those tools, keep **Before tool invocation**
> turned on so a risky request never runs.

## Understand verdicts and failures

The gateway doesn't decide what's risky. Microsoft Defender does, in the policy mode your security team sets in
Microsoft Defender. You can't change that mode at the gateway.

| Defender policy mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Disabled** | A permanent fail-open state. No inspection occurs. |
| **Audit** | Tool calls are logged without blocking. If the service lags or drops out, calls fail open. |
| **Block** | Explicit enforcement that fails closed. Withholding a result after invocation requires Block mode. |

When a call fails closed, the caller sees one of these codes in the result's
`_meta["com.microsoft.azure.ai.gateway/denial"].code`:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired` | The request has no usable bearer token, or the gateway can't read the token tenant it needs for the OBO exchange |
| `ToolEvaluationDenied` | The evaluation service denied the request or the result |
| `ToolEvaluationInvalidRequest` | The evaluation input isn't valid |
| `ToolEvaluationRequestTooLarge` | The evaluation input exceeds the supported size |
| `ToolEvaluationUnavailable` | Token exchange or evaluation failed, timed out, returned an invalid verdict, or was unavailable |

A denied call looks like this. The HTTP status is still `200`, so clients must check `result.isError`:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 42,
  "result": {
    "isError": true,
    "content": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "Tool 'mcp_tail_logs' requires a validated delegated caller token." }
    ],
    "_meta": {
      "com.microsoft.azure.ai.gateway/denial": {
        "code": "ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired",
        "correlationId": "9f2c1b6e-..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

> [!TIP]
> Log the `correlationId` with every denial in your agent. It's the value to share when you investigate a
> denial with your security team.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Call the protected tool with your user token

Run the same benign call as before. Allow a few seconds per call, because each enabled stage adds an evaluation
round trip.

```bash
./infra/call-protected-tool.sh token "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
./infra/call-protected-tool.ps1 -Auth token -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
...
tools/list: HTTP 200, <n> tools (discovery isn't evaluated)
tools/call: learn_microsoft_docs_search with query: What is Azure API Management?
HTTP status: 200
isError: false (the result was returned)
...
```

A harmless question about Azure is allowed at both stages, so the result comes back as before. If you see
`ToolEvaluationUnavailable` or `ToolEvaluationDenied` instead, see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

### Call it with a runtime key only

Now call the same tool with the API key and no bearer token. The key still authenticates you to the gateway, so
`initialize` and `tools/list` succeed. The `tools/call` needs an evaluation, and without a delegated token the
gateway can't run one, so it fails closed.

```bash
./infra/call-protected-tool.sh key "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
./infra/call-protected-tool.ps1 -Auth key -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
...
tools/list: HTTP 200, <n> tools (discovery isn't evaluated)
tools/call: learn_microsoft_docs_search with query: What is Azure API Management?
HTTP status: 200
isError: true
Denial code: ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired
Correlation ID: <guid>
Tool '...' requires a validated delegated caller token.
```

The denial text can differ. The code is what matters.

### Look for the call in Monitoring

If you set up Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring**. The **Tools** tab shows MCP tool executions, and **Traces** shows each request with its policy
steps. Find your calls by time and compare the allowed call with the key-only call.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> A delegated call returns its result. A key-only call to the same tool returns `isError: true` with
> `ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired`, while `tools/list` still works.

## Go further

- **Choose stages per server.** Keep **Before tool invocation** on for tools with side effects, such as sending
  mail or changing records. Add **After tool invocation** for tools that return untrusted content, such as web
  pages, tickets, or documents. For read-only tools that only return trusted content, weigh the extra round trip.
- **Move your agents to delegated tokens.** Agents that call tools with runtime keys or app-only tokens, such as a
  managed identity, can't use protected servers. Plan an on-behalf-of flow with the scope
  `https://azure-api.net/aigateway/Data.All` before you protect a server they depend on.
- **Roll out in Audit mode first.** Ask your security team to start Defender in **Audit**, review what it flags,
  and then switch to **Block**. Defender's
  [runtime protection guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/configure-ai-agent-runtime-protection#enable-runtime-protection)
  recommends the same phased rollout, with alerts reviewed in the Microsoft Defender portal.
- **Automate the policy.** The policy is the `toolThreatProtection` entry in the MCP server's
  `properties.policies`, as described in
  [Protect tool calls with Defender and Purview](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/ai-gateway-policy-tool-threat).
  A `PATCH` replaces the whole `policies` array, so read the current array first and keep any other policies,
  such as the request rate limits from [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md):

  ```bash title="Bash"
  TS_URL="$WS/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER"
  az rest --url "$TS_URL?$API" --query properties -o json \
    | jq -c '{properties:{policies:([(.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "toolThreatProtection") | del(.scope)]
        + [{type:"toolThreatProtection",preInvocation:true,postInvocation:true}])}}' > policies.json
  az rest --method patch --url "$TS_URL?$API" --body @policies.json --query properties.policies
  rm policies.json
  ```

  ```powershell title="PowerShell"
  $TS_URL = "$WS/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER"
  $p = az rest --url "$TS_URL`?$API" --query properties.policies -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
  $p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'toolThreatProtection' } | Select-Object * -ExcludeProperty scope) +
       @(@{ type = 'toolThreatProtection'; preInvocation = $true; postInvocation = $true })
  @{ properties = @{ policies = $p } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json
  az rest --method patch --url "$TS_URL`?$API" --body "@policies.json" --query properties.policies
  Remove-Item policies.json
  ```

- **Govern servers centrally.** [Govern MCP servers with Agent 365](../20-agent-365-governance/README.md) adds
  inventory and blocking from the Microsoft 365 admin center on top of this policy.

## Clean up

<!-- steps -->

### Delete the policy

In the AI Gateway portal, select **Policies**, select the **Agent 365 tool threat protection** policy, and select
**Delete**. Confirm with **Delete**. Tool calls with a runtime key work again.

### Remove the role assignment

If you added **AI Gateway Tools User** only for this lab, remove it in **Access**, or run:

```bash
az role assignment delete \
  --assignee "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" \
  --role "dce03f8d-857f-4e40-a90d-67770fa6ecd2" \
  --scope "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
az role assignment delete `
  --assignee (az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv) `
  --role "dce03f8d-857f-4e40-a90d-67770fa6ecd2" `
  --scope "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER"
```

<!-- /steps -->

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Every protected call returns `ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired` | The call has no bearer token, or the token isn't a delegated user token. App-only tokens and runtime keys can't be used for OBO. | Sign in with `az login` as a user, get a token for `https://azure-api.net/aigateway`, and send it as `Authorization: Bearer`. Check that the token has an `scp` claim. |
| `tools/call` returns HTTP `401` or `403` with a bearer token | The user has no data-plane role on the MCP server, or the assignment hasn't applied yet | Assign **AI Gateway Tools User** at the MCP server or gateway scope and wait a few minutes |
| Calls return `ToolEvaluationUnavailable` | The token exchange or the evaluation failed, timed out, returned an invalid verdict, or the evaluator was unavailable | Retry later. If it persists, confirm the Microsoft Defender or Microsoft Purview license and the Defender policy mode with your security team, and share the `correlationId`. |
| A benign call returns `ToolEvaluationDenied` | Defender or Purview flagged the request or the result | Review the call with your security team using the `correlationId`. If the tool already ran (after-invocation stage), don't retry it automatically. |
| You can't add a second tool threat protection policy to the server | Each MCP server can have only one tool threat protection policy | Keep the existing policy, or delete it and add a new one with the stages you want |
| Tool calls got noticeably slower | Each enabled stage adds an evaluation round trip | Keep both stages where you need them, and use only **Before tool invocation** where results are trusted |

# Govern MCP servers with Agent 365

Your platform team runs the gateway, but the people who decide which tools agents may use sit in IT and security,
and they work in the Microsoft 365 admin center, not in Azure. When a tool is found to be risky, they need to
switch it off across every gateway in minutes, without filing a ticket. In this lab you connect Microsoft Agent
365 to your gateways, block one tool and then a whole MCP server from the admin center, and watch the gateway
enforce each decision on live traffic.

![Microsoft Agent 365 keeps the inventory and the decisions, and the gateway enforces them inline on MCP traffic](../assets/diagrams/agent-365.svg "Agent 365 defines governance intent, inventory, and access decisions. API Management enforces them on every request to the MCP server.")

<!-- widget: tool-patterns {"tools":["learn_microsoft_docs_search","learn_microsoft_code_sample_search","learn_microsoft_docs_fetch"],"allow":["learn_microsoft_docs_search","learn_microsoft_code_sample_search","learn_microsoft_docs_fetch"],"block":["learn_microsoft_docs_fetch"]} -->

## Before you begin

- Complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md) and
  [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md). This lab governs the `learn` MCP
  server, and you edit its **Tool availability** the same way you did in lab 05.
- A Microsoft Agent 365 tenant, and a **tenant administrator** who can grant tenant-level consent in the
  [Microsoft 365 admin center](https://admin.microsoft.com). After consent, Agent 365 administrators don't need
  Azure permissions of their own.
- Permission to edit the MCP server in the AI Gateway portal, for example **Contributor** on the gateway's resource
  group, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- For the test script: `curl` and `jq` (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later. Get the gateway URL from the portal or
  with the [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later, signed in with
  `az login`. The CLI reads the new `aigateways` resource type with `az resource`, because the `az aigateway`
  extension doesn't manage it yet.

> [!NOTE]
> The Agent 365 integration is an emerging preview capability. Labels and behavior can change; see the
> [release note](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/releases/2026-10-08-agent-365). AI Gateway itself is free
> during the preview; Agent 365 is licensed separately.

Set these variables once. The steps and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export MCP_SERVER="learn"

export GATEWAY_ID="$(az resource show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az resource show --ids "$GATEWAY_ID" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"
$MCP_SERVER = "learn"

$GATEWAY_ID         = az resource show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways --query id -o tsv
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az resource show --ids $GATEWAY_ID --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys. Don't commit it or write it to a file.
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
```

## How it works

The integration separates governance from enforcement. **Microsoft Agent 365** keeps the inventory and the access
decisions. **Azure API Management** enforces them inline on every request to an MCP server, and emits runtime
signals for auditing and investigation.

After a tenant administrator consents once, Agent 365 discovers `Microsoft.ApiManagement` resources across the
tenant's subscriptions, including subscriptions you add later, and lists their MCP servers and tools with metadata
such as endpoints, access scopes, and service identities. When an administrator blocks a server or a tool, Agent
365 uses API Management control-plane operations to insert a **managed policy** into that server. Unblocking
removes it. Existing agents keep using the same gateway endpoints.

| Control | Where you set it | What callers get |
|---|---|---|
| Block a tool (Agent 365) | Admin center › **Agents** › **Tools** › server › **Tools** tab | HTTP `200`, `isError: true`, denial code `ToolNotAvailable` |
| Block a server (Agent 365) | Admin center › **Agents** › **Tools** › server › **Block** | HTTP `403`, error code `AccessBlockedByGateway` |
| **Blocked tools** (gateway) | AI Gateway portal › MCP server › **Tools** step | The tool stays visible, but the gateway blocks its execution |
| **MCP server access** (gateway) | AI Gateway portal › MCP server › **Basic info** step | **Blocked** servers can't be reached by clients |

Tool-level blocking needs a **static list of allowed tools** on the server, so Agent 365 can read the tool list.
It isn't available for servers with dynamic allowed tools, such as **Allow all tools**.

| Capability | API Management v2 tiers | AI Gateway tier |
|---|---|---|
| Centralized MCP server inventory | Yes | Yes |
| Block or unblock MCP servers | Yes | Yes |
| Tool-level blocking | No | Yes |
| Tool activity observability | No | Yes |
| Tool threat protection | No | Yes |

API Management v1 tiers aren't supported.

## Publish a static list of allowed tools

Agent 365 can only list and block individual tools when the MCP server publishes a fixed set of tools. You set
that in the AI Gateway portal.

<!-- steps -->

### Open the Tools step

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **MCP servers**, then `learn`, then **Edit**, and go to the **Tools** step.

### Select exact tools

Under **Tool availability**, choose **Select exact tools**, and select the three `learn_` tools:
`learn_microsoft_docs_search`, `learn_microsoft_code_sample_search`, and `learn_microsoft_docs_fetch`.
Leave **Blocked tools** empty, so the only blocks in this lab come from Agent 365. Select **Save**.

If your portal doesn't offer **Select exact tools** yet, Agent 365 can't read this server's tool list. You can
still block the whole server from Agent 365, and block single tools under **Blocked tools** in the AI Gateway
portal, as in [lab 05](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md).

### Check the catalog

List the tools through the gateway. The script runs the MCP handshake with your runtime key and prints the
gateway's answer even when a call is blocked.

<!-- include: infra/call-tool.sh -->

On GitHub, open [infra/call-tool.sh](infra/call-tool.sh) or [infra/call-tool.ps1](infra/call-tool.ps1).

```bash
chmod +x infra/call-tool.sh
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
MCP endpoint: https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/learn/mcp
tools/list: HTTP 200
  learn_microsoft_docs_search
  learn_microsoft_code_sample_search
  learn_microsoft_docs_fetch
```

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The `learn` server publishes exactly the tools you selected.

## Connect Agent 365 to your gateways

A tenant administrator grants consent once. The consent gives the Agent 365 service identity the **A365 MCP
Gateway Policy Operator** Azure role at tenant level, which lets it read API Management resources, read and write
API-scoped policies, and discover supported resources in existing and future subscriptions in the tenant.

<!-- steps -->

### Grant consent

Sign in to the [Microsoft 365 admin center](https://admin.microsoft.com) as a tenant administrator. Under
**Agents**, select **Settings**, then **Gateways**. Turn on **Azure API Management service and AI Gateway**. By
consenting, you let the organization read the tools published through the gateway.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The consent covers every API Management instance in the tenant, not just this gateway, and lets Agent 365
> change API-scoped policies. Agree on who may block servers and tools in Agent 365 before you turn it on.

### Find your MCP server

Under **Agents**, select **Tools**. Search for `learn`, or look for servers whose publisher is **AI Gateway**.
Select the server to see its metadata, such as its endpoint, access scope, and service identity.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The `learn` server from your gateway is in the Agent 365 inventory, with **AI Gateway** as its publisher.

## Block a tool

Your security team decides that agents shouldn't fetch arbitrary pages. You turn off one tool and leave the rest
of the server working.

<!-- steps -->

### Turn off the tool in Agent 365

In the admin center, under **Agents**, select **Tools**, then the `learn` server. Select the **Tools** tab and
disable `learn_microsoft_docs_fetch`. Agent 365 inserts a managed policy into the server to stop that tool from
running.

### Call the blocked tool

```bash
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER" learn_microsoft_docs_fetch \
  '{"url":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/agent-365"}'
```

```powershell
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_fetch `
  -Arguments '{"url":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/agent-365"}'
```

```text title="Expected output"
...
tools/call: learn_microsoft_docs_fetch {"url":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/agent-365"}
HTTP status: 200
isError: true
Denial code: ToolNotAvailable
Correlation ID: <guid>
Tool 'learn_microsoft_docs_fetch' is blocked by the gateway. Do not retry this tool.
```

The message text can differ; the denial code is what matters. The call returns HTTP `200` with a JSON-RPC
result, not an HTTP error. The `isError` flag and the "Do not retry" text tell the agent the tool is off on
purpose, so a well-behaved agent stops retrying it. The documented response, for a tool named `delete_file`, is:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 42,
  "result": {
    "content": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "Tool 'delete_file' is blocked by the gateway. Do not retry this tool." }
    ],
    "isError": true,
    "_meta": {
      "com.microsoft.azure.ai.gateway/denial": {
        "code": "ToolNotAvailable",
        "correlationId": "9f2c1b6e-..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Call a tool that's still allowed

```bash
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER" learn_microsoft_docs_search '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

```powershell
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_search `
  -Arguments '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

The search returns results with `isError: false`.

### Turn the tool back on

In the admin center, on the `learn` server's **Tools** tab, enable `learn_microsoft_docs_fetch` again.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> While the tool was off, calls to it returned `ToolNotAvailable` and the other tools kept working.

## Block the whole server

During an incident, you may need to cut off every tool on a server at once. Blocking the server in Agent 365
inserts a managed `return-response` policy at the start of the server's inbound policy, so the gateway answers
before it reaches any backend.

<!-- steps -->

### Block the server in Agent 365

In the admin center, under **Agents**, select **Tools**, select the `learn` server, and select **Block**.

### Try to connect

```bash
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
MCP endpoint: https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/learn/mcp
initialize: HTTP 403 (x-correlation-id: <guid>)
{
  "error": {
    "code": "AccessBlockedByGateway",
    "message": "Access to server 'learn' is blocked.",
    "target": "learn",
    "correlationId": "<guid>"
  }
}
```

The message names your server. Every request to the server, including `initialize` and `tools/list`, now
returns `403`.

### Unblock the server

In the admin center, select the `learn` server again and unblock it. Agent 365 removes the managed policy, and
the script lists the tools again.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> While the server was blocked, every request returned `403 AccessBlockedByGateway`. After you unblocked it, the
> handshake and `tools/list` succeed.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Confirm the inventory

In the admin center, under **Agents** › **Tools**, the `learn` server is listed with **AI Gateway** as its
publisher, isn't blocked, and its **Tools** tab shows all three tools enabled.

### Confirm the server works end to end

```bash
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER" learn_microsoft_docs_search '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

```powershell
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_search `
  -Arguments '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

`tools/list` returns the three tools, and the search returns `isError: false`.

### Trace a denial

Each denial carries a correlation ID, in the `x-correlation-id` response header and in the response body. Record
it with the agent's logs, so you can match a blocked call with the gateway's runtime signals. If you set up
Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), **Monitoring** › **Tools**
shows the server's tool executions and **Traces** shows each request.

<!-- /steps -->

## Go further

- **Close the side door.** Agent 365 doesn't route agents through the gateway for you. Each agent must use the
  gateway's MCP endpoint, and a block only works if agents can't reach the MCP server directly. Restrict the
  backend so the gateway is its only caller, for example with
  [private networking](../18-private-networking/README.md).
- **Add threat protection.** On the AI Gateway tier, add
  [Agent 365 tool threat protection](../19-tool-threat-protection/README.md) so Microsoft Defender and Microsoft
  Purview evaluate the calls that you allow.
- **Decide who owns which switch.** Agent 365 blocks are tenant-wide governance decisions. The gateway's own
  **Blocked tools** and **MCP server access** settings belong to the platform team. Write down which team uses
  which control, so a block set in one place isn't undone in the other.
- **Govern every server the same way.** Prefer **Select exact tools** for servers that Agent 365 governs. New
  tools then stay unpublished until someone reviews and adds them.

## Clean up

<!-- steps -->

### Clear Agent 365 blocks

In the admin center, make sure the `learn` server isn't blocked and all its tools are enabled. The gateway
consent is tenant-wide, so leave it on if your organization plans to keep using the integration. Otherwise, ask a
tenant administrator to review **Azure API Management service and AI Gateway** under **Agents** › **Settings** ›
**Gateways**.

### Restore the tool availability

In the AI Gateway portal, open **MCP servers** › `learn` › **Edit** › **Tools**. Select **Allow all tools**, then
select **Save**.

<!-- /steps -->

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The gateway's MCP servers don't appear under **Agents** › **Tools** | Consent isn't granted, or the instance is on an API Management v1 tier | Have a tenant administrator turn on **Azure API Management service and AI Gateway** under **Agents** › **Settings** › **Gateways**. Use a v2 tier or the AI Gateway tier. |
| The server's **Tools** tab can't list its tools | The server doesn't have a static list of allowed tools, for example it uses **Allow all tools** | In the AI Gateway portal, choose **Select exact tools** on the server's **Tools** step. Otherwise, block tools in the AI Gateway portal. |
| You can't block individual tools | The instance is on an API Management v2 tier | Tool-level blocking needs the AI Gateway tier. Block the whole server instead. |
| A blocked tool still runs for some agents | Those agents call the MCP server directly, not through the gateway | Point every agent at the gateway's MCP endpoint and restrict direct access to the backend |
| An agent keeps retrying a blocked tool | The agent ignores `isError` | Check `result.isError` and the `ToolNotAvailable` denial code, and stop retrying that tool |
| Calls still fail after you unblock | Another control blocks them, such as the gateway's **Blocked tools**, **MCP server access**, or a policy | Check the server's **Basic info** and **Tools** steps and its policies in the AI Gateway portal |

## Next steps

- [Protect tool calls with Agent 365 threat protection](../19-tool-threat-protection/README.md)
- [Lock down backend traffic with private networking](../18-private-networking/README.md)
- [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md)
- [Govern tools with Microsoft Agent 365 and Azure API Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/agent-365) on Microsoft Learn
